Tapu (the source, via Captain Cook, of the English word taboo ) is the sacred-forbidden: the state of being so charged with the sacred that contact is dangerous and restricted. The two are inseparable — what has great mana is tapu — and together they ordered all of life, from the chief's person to the preparation of food; the violation of an important tapu could be punishable by death . Society was ranked by mana: the ariki (chiefs) held it by descent from the gods, and the tohunga (Hawaiian kahuna ), the priest-experts, knew how to wield and contain it. The gods and the world-parents Polynesian creation begins, in the classic Māori account, with Rangi , the Sky Father, and Papa , the Earth Mother, locked in embrace in the darkness, until their children force them apart to let in the light and make the world (the world-parent cosmogony of ch46). From them come the great gods, worshipped across Polynesia under related names: Tangaroa (Hawaiian Kanaloa ), god of the sea; Tāne ( Kāne ), god of forests, birds, and light; Tū ( Kū ), god of war; and Rongo ( Lono ), god of agriculture and peace. Beloved above all is Māui , the trickster-hero who fished up the islands from the sea, snared the sun to slow it, and died seeking immortality for humankind. Regional deities loom large — the Hawaiian volcano goddess Pele , beautiful and destroying. Worship centered on the open sacred precinct, the marae (Hawaiian heiau ), with offerings, chant, feasting, and — in some societies — human sacrifice to the war-god. Rapa Nui: the ancestors in stone Rapa Nui developed a self-contained Polynesian religious world of…

title: Pentecostalism & Global Christianity
summary: The fire and the southern shift — the fastest-growing movement in modern religion, and the transformation of Christianity into a Global-South faith. The Azusa Street Revival (1906) under William Seymour and the Holiness roots (Parham, 1901); the baptism in the Holy Spirit and the restored gifts — speaking in tongues, prophecy, and divine healing, modeled on Acts 2; the three waves (classical Pentecostal denominations, the 1960s Charismatic movement into the mainline and Catholic churches, and the neo-charismatic independents); the prosperity gospel, reported honestly and contested; and the demographic shift of the Christian majority to Africa, Latin America, and Asia. A symbology of the tongues of fire, the raised hands, and the laying on of hands — an aniconic Christianity of direct experience, with its theological claims marked as faith.
text: In April 1906, in a run-down former Methodist church on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, something broke loose that would remake world Christianity. Led by William J. Seymour , the one-eyed son of former slaves, a crowd of Black, white, Latino, and Asian worshippers prayed, wept, sang, fell to the floor, and — most astonishingly to onlookers — spoke in tongues , uttering syllables they believed the Holy Spirit was giving them directly. The revival ran day and night for three years and sent missionaries around the globe. From that stable-like mission grew the fastest-growing religious movement of the modern age. The third force Pentecostalism is often called the " third force " in Christianity, standing alongside Catholicism and Protestantism as a distinct stream — and today the most dynamic of the three. Born at the very start of the 20th century, it has grown from almost nothing to some 600 million adherents (counting the wider charismatic movement), and it is the leading edge of the single greatest shift in modern religion: the movement of Christianity's center of gravity from the West to the Global South . The fire falls Pentecostalism grew out of the 19th-century Holiness movement , itself rooted in John Wesley's teaching of a " second blessing " of sanctification after conversion. The Holiness preacher Charles Fox Parham , at his Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, in 1901 , taught that there was a further, "third" experience — a baptism in the Holy Spirit — and that its biblical evidence was speaking in tongues . His student William J. Seymour carried the teaching to Los Angeles, where in 1906 the Azusa Street Revival ignited. What made Azusa historic was not only the ecstatic experience but its interracial character — extraordinary for its time (a Black pastor leading whites and Blacks together, though the interracial unity soon fractured under the pressures of a segregated society) — and its missionary energy, which broadcast the movement worldwide within a few years. Seymour chronicled it in a periodical, The Apostolic Faith . The baptism in the Spirit The heart of Pentecostalism is the conviction that the gifts of the Holy Spirit described in the New Testament — the charismata of 1 Corinthians 12 — are available to believers today , not confined to the apostolic past. Central is the baptism in the Holy Spirit , a direct, overwhelming experience of God typically evidenced by glossolalia (speaking in tongues), modeled on the first Pentecost in Acts 2, when the Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire and they spoke in other languages. With it come the other gifts: prophecy , divine healing , miracles, and the discernment and casting-out of spirits. Pentecostalism is, above all, a religion of direct, felt, ecstatic experience of the divine — not primarily creed, sacrament, or institution, but the living presence of the Spirit, now. Three waves The movement spread in three great waves. Classical Pentecostalism built new denominations — the Assemblies of God , the largely African-American Church of God in Christ , and many more. Then, from the 1960s , the Charismatic movement carried the gifts into the existing churches : Spirit…

title: Bahá'í & New Faiths
summary: One God, one religion, one humanity — the archive’s closing chapter, on the faith that tries to hold all the others in a single embrace. The Bahá'í Faith: the Báb (executed 1850) and Bahá'u’lláh (1817–1892), exiled to ʾAkká; the three onenesses and the doctrine of progressive revelation, which gathers Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá'u’lláh into one unfolding succession of Manifestations; the strikingly modern social teachings (equality of the sexes, harmony of science and religion, world peace); a clergy-less order under the Universal House of Justice in Haifa; and the systematic persecution of Bahá’ís in Iran. Plus the wider modern ‘new world faiths’ — Caodaism, the Ahmadiyya, Tenrikyo. A symbology of the nine-pointed star, the Greatest Name, and the terraced mountain — with progressive revelation flagged as the faith’s own framework, not neutral history.
text: In July 1850, in the Persian city of Tabriz, a young man who called himself the Báb — "the Gate" — was suspended by ropes before a firing squad of 750 soldiers. The first volley, it is said, cut his ropes and left him unharmed; when the smoke cleared he had vanished, found back in his cell finishing a conversation. A second regiment was brought; the second volley killed him. He was thirty. He had proclaimed that a new messenger of God was about to appear — and out of the movement he founded grew what may be the only major independent world religion born in the modern age: the Bahá'í Faith , whose whole purpose is to declare that all religions are one. A faith for a united world The Bahá'í Faith rests on three "onenesses": the oneness of God , the oneness of religion , and the oneness of humanity . It teaches that there is one God, unknowable in essence; that all the great religions come from that one God and form a single unfolding story; and that humankind is one family, now come of age and destined for unity. It is at once one of the youngest of the world's religions and one of the most geographically widespread, with communities in virtually every country on earth. The Báb and Bahá'u'lláh The faith has two founding figures. The Báb (Siyyid ʿAlí Muḥammad, 1819–1850), a merchant of Shiraz, declared in 1844 that he was the herald of one greater than himself, and his Bábí movement spread rapidly through Persia — and was savagely persecuted, with thousands of followers killed and the Báb himself executed in 1850. Among the Bábís was Bahá'u'lláh (Mírzá Ḥusayn-ʿAlí, 1817–1892), a Persian nobleman who, in 1863, declared that he was the one the Báb had foretold — the promised Manifestation of God for this age. Exiled by the Persian and Ottoman authorities ever farther from home — to Baghdad, Constantinople, Adrianople, and at last to the prison-city of ʿAkká (Acre) in Ottoman Palestine — he spent the rest of his life a prisoner, writing the enormous body of scripture on which the faith is built. It is from ʿAkká and neighboring Haifa , on Mount Carmel , that the Bahá'í world center grew, its golden-domed Shrine of the Báb and terraced gardens now among the most famous sights of the region. Progressive revelation The intellectual heart of the Bahá'í Faith is the doctrine of progressive revelation . God, it teaches, has never left humanity without guidance, but has sent a succession of Manifestations of God — Divine Educators — each renewing religion for a new age and preparing the way for the next, roughly every five hundred to a thousand years. Among these Manifestations Bahá'ís count Abraham, Krishna, Moses, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Báb, and Bahá'u'lláh . Each brought the same eternal truth in the form suited to their time and people; the apparent conflicts between religions are differences of social teaching fitted to different ages, not of essential truth. And the process has no end: future Manifestations will come. In this single framework the Bahá'í Faith attempts to gather the entire religious history this archive has surveyed into one continuous, divinely-guided story — an audacious and characteristically modern claim. The…

title: Minoan Crete
summary: A religion with no readable scripture: the peak sanctuaries and sacred caves of Bronze Age Crete, the palaces with their pillar crypts and lustral basins, the faience ‘Snake Goddess’ and the forgeries Evans’s vision inspired, the gold rings of epiphany, bull-leaping and bull sacrifice, the contested human sacrifice at Anemospilia, and the Greek gods of Mycenaean Knossos, including the ‘Mistress of the Labyrinth’. A symbology of the double axe, the horns of consecration and the undeciphered Linear A libation formula, with the Great Goddess and the peaceful matriarchy marked as interpretations, not findings.
text: In 1903 , in two stone-lined pits under the floor of the palace at Knossos , Arthur Evans's workmen found the broken pieces of several small figures in faience , a glazed quartz paste. Two of them were put back together in the months that followed. One was a woman in a flounced skirt and an open bodice, holding a snake in each outstretched hand; a small cat sat on her head. The other had snakes coiled over her arms and round her tall hat. Evans called the pits the Temple Repositories , and the figures a "Snake Goddess" and her votary. They became the most famous images of a religion that has left no readable scripture, no names of gods, no myths in its own words. They are also a good place to begin, because the missing head, the left arm and the cat of the best-known figure were supplied by Evans's restorers. Much of what the world believes about the religion of Bronze Age Crete was built the same way: from real fragments, joined by confident guesses. A civilization without a readable scripture The people now called Minoans (Evans's name, from the mythical King Minos) built a palace civilization on Crete from about 1950 BCE . Archaeologists divide it into the Protopalatial period (the first palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, c. 1950–1700), and the Neopalatial (rebuilt, grander palaces, c. 1700–1450), when Minoan art and influence reached across the Aegean. Around 1450 BCE most sites on the island were destroyed or abandoned; afterwards Knossos was run by Greek-speaking Mycenaeans , whose tablets in the Linear B script record the palace's last administration. The Minoans wrote. They used a hieroglyphic script on seals, and then Linear A , known from more than a thousand inscriptions, mostly clay accounting tablets. Linear A is not deciphered . Because Linear B was adapted from it, the sound values of many signs can be guessed, so Linear A can be pronounced after a fashion; but the language behind it is unknown, and no proposed identification (Greek, Luwian, Semitic, Indo-Iranian and others) has won acceptance. The famous Phaistos Disc (see the Vault, V56) is in yet another script, and unreadable. So Minoan religion has to be reconstructed almost entirely from places, objects and images : where people left offerings, what they left, and what their artists showed. That is a real limit, and this chapter keeps returning to it. Mountains and caves The earliest clear Minoan cult places are in the open country. Peak sanctuaries. From about 2000 BCE people climbed to hilltops and mountain summits within sight of their settlements to light fires and leave offerings. The first to be identified was Petsofas , above Palaikastro in the east; the greatest was Mount Iouktas (Juktas), the mountain south of Knossos whose profile looks, from the palace, like a face lying on its back. The offerings are humble and numerous: thousands of small clay figurines of men and women with raised or folded arms, of cattle, sheep and beetles, and of separate human limbs , arms, legs and heads, some apparently diseased, pierced to be hung up. They have been read as prayers for healing, much like the ex-votos of later Greek and Christian shrines, though what the…

title: Nubia & Kush
summary: Egypt’s southern twin: the great mounds and retainer burials of Kerma; Amun in the ‘Pure Mountain’ of Jebel Barkal; the Kushite pharaohs of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, Piye’s Victory Stela and the revival of the pyramid; Meroë’s own gods, the lion-headed Apedemak above all, and its ruling queens, the Kandake of Acts 8; the Nubian pilgrims who kept Isis’s temple at Philae open until the sixth century; and Christian Nubia and the paintings of Faras. A symbology of the uraeus mountain, the ram and the lion, and the Meroitic script, whose signs can be read but whose language still cannot.
text: On the right bank of the Nile, near the Fourth Cataract in northern Sudan, a flat-topped sandstone mountain rises about a hundred metres above the plain. At its southern corner a pinnacle about 75 metres high stands apart from the cliff. Seen from the right place, it looks like a rearing cobra, the uraeus that Egyptian kings wore on their brow, crowned with the tall white crown of Upper Egypt. The mountain is Jebel Barkal . Egyptian pharaohs of the New Kingdom called it the " Pure Mountain " and said that the god Amun lived inside it. When Egypt's hold on the south collapsed, a line of Nubian kings took over the claim: the god in the mountain, they said, had chosen them . Around 728 BCE one of them, Piye , marched north and conquered Egypt. For about seventy years, as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty , Nubian kings ruled as pharaohs from the Sudan to the Mediterranean, and their descendants went on attributing their kingship to the Amun of Jebel Barkal for nearly a thousand years more. Kush: names and periods Nubia is the Nile valley between the First Cataract at Aswan and the region of Khartoum, now divided between Egypt and Sudan. Egyptians called its southern kingdoms Kush ; Greeks and Romans called its people Aithiopes , "Ethiopians", which in the Bible and classical writers usually means Nubia, not modern Ethiopia. Its religious history falls into several periods, each with good archaeology: Kerma (c. 2500–1500 BCE), a powerful kingdom centred on the town of Kerma above the Third Cataract, destroyed by the armies of New Kingdom Egypt. Egyptian rule (c. 1500–1070 BCE), when pharaohs built temples to Amun at Jebel Barkal, Soleb and elsewhere and governed Nubia through a viceroy, the "King's Son of Kush". Napata (c. 800–300 BCE), the kingdom based at Jebel Barkal and its royal cemeteries at el-Kurru and Nuri , whose kings ruled Egypt as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. Meroë (c. 300 BCE–350 CE), when the royal centre moved south to Meroë, and a distinct Nubian religion, with its own gods and its own script, came fully into view. Christian Nubia (6th–15th centuries), the kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia. Kerma: the great mounds Kerma left no texts, so its religion is known only from buildings and graves. In the centre of the town stood the Western Deffufa , a massive solid mud-brick structure about 18 metres high, entered by a narrow stair: almost certainly a temple, with ceremonies held on its top. East of the town lay a cemetery of some 30,000 graves. The largest, the royal tumuli of the Classic Kerma period (c. 1750–1500 BCE), were circular mounds up to 90 metres across. When George Reisner excavated them between 1913 and 1916 he found, in a corridor across the largest ( KX ), the remains of hundreds of people buried at the same time as the ruler, many lying curled on their sides, and argued that they had been sacrificed to accompany him. Later study has supported the conclusion that large numbers of retainers died at royal funerals, though the exact counts are uncertain. The graves also held beds, sandals, bows, cattle skulls in their hundreds arranged in crescents, and Egyptian statues and objects carried off in raids. Cattle clearly mattered…

title: The Upanishads & the Hindu Synthesis
era: Axial Age · The Upanishads & the Hindu Synthesis
summary: From fire altar to temple: the Upanishads and their debates at Janaka’s court, the self (ātman) and the absolute (Brahman) and ‘that you are’; the first teachings of karma, rebirth and liberation; the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa and the Bhagavad Gītā; the Laws of Manu, varṇa and the stages and aims of life; the six philosophical ‘viewpoints’; and the Greek ambassador’s Garuḍa pillar, the Purāṇas and the first Gupta temples. A symbology of Om and the four states, the great sayings and the temple as cosmos, with epic chronologies, Rāma’s bridge and ‘Vedic science’ sorted from the evidence.
text: King Janaka of Videha, the story goes, was holding a great sacrifice with rich fees, and the learned brahmins of the Kuru and Pañcāla lands had come to it. He had a thousand cows penned, with gold tied to the horns of each, and announced that they would go to the most learned of the brahmins present. None dared claim them, until Yājñavalkya told his pupil to drive them home. The others were outraged and challenged him one after another. A woman, Gārgī Vācaknavī , pressed him so hard on what the world was "woven upon", warp and woof, that he warned her not to question too far, lest her head fall off; she came back later with two questions she compared to arrows, and was answered with the imperishable ( akṣara ), which "is not coarse, not fine, not short, not long", and on which space itself is woven. The scene is told in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad , one of the two oldest Upanishads. It captures the new thing happening in north India in the middle of the first millennium BCE: priests and kings, and at least one woman, arguing not about how to perform the sacrifice, but about what lies behind it, and behind the self who performs it. After the Veda The four Vedas (ch05) were collections of hymns, chants and ritual formulas for the fire sacrifice, with prose manuals, the Brāhmaṇas , explaining the rites. The Upaniṣads began as the last layers of that literature, attached to particular Vedic schools, and so were later called Vedānta , "the end of the Veda". The word upaniṣad is usually explained as "sitting down near" a teacher, or as "hidden connection", correspondence, since the texts are full of equations between ritual, cosmos and person. The oldest, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Chāndogya , are usually dated to about the seventh to sixth centuries BCE, before the Buddha; the Taittirīya , Aitareya and Kauṣītaki are also early; verse Upanishads such as the Kaṭha , Īśā , Śvetāśvatara and Muṇḍaka are later, and the brief Māṇḍūkya later still. The Indologist Patrick Olivelle warns that any dating of these texts "that attempts a precision closer than a few centuries is as stable as a house of cards". Later tradition recognizes 108 Upanishads, many of them medieval; about a dozen "principal" ones are the common core. Ātman and Brahman The Upanishads do not teach one system. They record many teachers, with different answers. But a few ideas run through them and became the foundation of much later Indian thought. Brahman. In the Vedas brahman meant the power of the sacred formula. The Upanishads use it for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything that is. Ātman. The self: at first breath or body, then the innermost, unchanging subject, the one who sees but cannot be seen. Their identity. The most famous teaching is that these two are one. In the Chāndogya, the teacher Uddālaka Āruṇi instructs his son Śvetaketu : he has him dissolve salt in water overnight, then taste the water from the top, the middle and the bottom. The salt cannot be seen, but it is everywhere. So it is with the subtle essence of all things: "that is the self, that you are " ( tat tvam asi , 6.8.7), repeated nine times. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Yājñavalkya describes the self only by…

title: Pre-Islamic Arabia
summary: Arabia before Islam, from the rocks and from the later books: Allāt, al-ʿUzzā, Manāt and the gods of the north; the Nabataean stone ‘houses of god’ at Petra and Hegra; the nomads’ prayers, sacrifices and laments in fifty thousand Safaitic inscriptions; Almaqah’s great temple at Maʾrib; the Ḥimyarite turn to ‘the Merciful’ two centuries before Muhammad, the Najrān martyrs and Abraha; and Mecca as Islamic tradition remembers it. A symbology of betyls and eye-idols, crescent and disc, the ibex and the sacred months, with the ‘moon god’ claim and the Book of Idols weighed against the inscriptions.
text: In the black basalt desert east of the Hawran, on the borderlands of what are now Syria, Jordan and Saudi Arabia, the rocks are covered with writing. Some two thousand years ago the nomads who grazed their herds there scratched their names and their fathers' names into the boulders in a script now called Safaitic , and often added a line about their lives: that they had camped here in the spring, that they were watching for rain, that they grieved for a brother killed in a raid. Then, very often, a prayer. The goddess most often called on is Allāt : asked for safety, for plunder, for rain, for a reunion with a loved one, and sometimes asked to curse whoever would deface the carving. More than fifty thousand such inscriptions are known. They are the voices of ordinary Arabians practising their own religion before Judaism, Christianity and Islam reached the desert, and they tell a different and more detailed story than the one later remembered. Two kinds of evidence The religion of Arabia before Islam is known from two very different kinds of source, and much of the history of the subject is the story of their disagreement. Islamic-era writings. The Qur'an argues against those who "associate" other beings with God ( mushrikūn ) and names three goddesses, al-Lāt , al-ʿUzzā and Manāt (53:19–20). The biographies of the Prophet and the histories describe Meccan cults, and Hishām ibn al-Kalbī (d. 819/821) wrote the Kitāb al-Aṣnām , the Book of Idols , a catalogue of the gods and sanctuaries of the "time of ignorance" ( jāhiliyya ). These texts were written a century or more after the events, by Muslims describing a past they regarded as idolatrous, and many historians treat their details with caution. Inscriptions and archaeology. Tens of thousands of inscriptions in the pre-Islamic scripts of Arabia (Safaitic, Hismaic, Dadanitic, Taymanitic, Nabataean Aramaic and the Sabaic and other languages of the south), along with temples, altars, stelae and tombs. These are contemporary and written by the worshippers themselves, but they are brief, and they come mostly from the north and the south, not from Mecca, where no pre-Islamic inscriptions or excavations of that period are known. Gods of the north In the northern half of the peninsula and its borderlands, the inscriptions name a recognizable set of deities. Allāt , "the Goddess", the most widely worshipped. The Greek historian Herodotus already knew of an Arabian goddess he called Alilat in the fifth century BCE. She had temples at Palmyra, where she was shown like Athena with a lion, and at Ṭāʾif near Mecca. al-ʿUzzā , "the Mightiest", associated with the morning or evening star (Venus), and prominent among the Nabataeans at Petra. Manāt , a goddess of fate and portion, whose shrine lay on the coast between Mecca and Medina; the Book of Idols calls her the most ancient. Ruḍā (Ruḍaw), a god known from Assyrian records of the seventh century BCE to late antiquity, in some communities the father of Allāt, in others part of an astral triad. Dushara (Dhū Sharā, "he of the Sharā mountains"), the chief god of the Nabataean kingdom, whose capital was Petra. The Nabataeans wrote dedications to "Dushara and…

title: Korea
summary: Religion in layers, all still alive: the Bronze Age dolmens and the myth of Dangun, son of heaven and of a bear; the mudang, the women shamans of musok, their spirit illness and their all-night gut for the dead; Buddhism’s arrival in the Three Kingdoms, Ichadon’s martyrdom, Seokguram and the 81,258 woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana; Joseon’s Confucian ancestor rites; a Catholic church founded by lay readers and its martyrs; Donghak and the new religions; and a South Korea where most people now claim no religion. A symbology of the taegeuk, Hangul’s heaven–earth–human vowels and the mountain god’s tiger.
text: High on the slope of Mount Toham above the old Silla capital of Gyeongju, behind a wooden gate and a pane of protective glass, a granite Buddha sits in a round chamber built of carved stone blocks. He faces east, towards the sea, where the sun rises. Around him, carved in relief on the walls, stand bodhisattvas, disciples, guardian kings and a many-headed Avalokiteśvara. The grotto of Seokguram was begun in 751 by a minister of the kingdom of Unified Silla, and finished by the royal court in 774. It is one of the masterpieces of Buddhist art in East Asia. A few kilometres away, in villages and apartment blocks of modern Korea, women called mudang still perform the ecstatic rituals of a religion far older than the Buddha's arrival, dancing, singing, and speaking in the voices of the dead. Korean religion is layered like that: shamanism at the base, Buddhism and Confucianism laid over it, then Christianity and a string of new religions, and all of them still alive. Foundations: the bear, the tiger and the son of heaven The oldest Korean religious monuments are the dolmens : stone tables of the Bronze Age (roughly 1000–300 BCE), built by the tens of thousands across the peninsula, among the densest concentrations in the world. The sites of Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa, with more than a thousand dolmens between them, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. They were tombs and perhaps markers of lineage and land; what rites were held at them is unknown. Korea's national founding myth is written down much later, in the Samguk yusa ("Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms"), compiled around 1281 by the Buddhist monk Iryeon . It tells how Hwanung , son of the heavenly lord Hwanin , descended to a sacred tree on a mountain with three thousand followers and the ministers of wind, rain and clouds. A bear and a tiger begged to become human; he gave them mugwort and garlic and told them to stay out of the sunlight for a hundred days. The tiger gave up; the bear became a woman, and her son by Hwanung was Dangun , who founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon . Tradition dates the founding to 2333 BCE , and South Korea celebrates it as National Foundation Day on 3 October. The myth is a religious charter of descent from heaven; its date and the figure of Dangun are not historical in any documentary sense. Musok: the religion of the mudang Korea's indigenous religion, usually called musok or muism , centres on the mu or mudang , ritual specialists who are almost all women . Two main types are distinguished: Spirit-descended shamans ( sinbyeong , kangshinmu ), usually from the central and northern regions, who became shamans after a "spirit illness", a crisis of physical and mental suffering that is cured only by accepting initiation. They are possessed by gods and speak in their voices. Hereditary shamans ( sesseummu ), more common in the south, who inherit the role in their families and perform rites without possession. The central ritual is the gut : an elaborate, sometimes all-night performance with drums, cymbals, costumes, food offerings and dance, in which the mudang invites gods, ancestors and spirits, lets them speak, entertains them and sends them away…

title: The Cathars & Medieval Heresy
era: High Medieval · The Cathars & Medieval Heresy
summary: The good men and good women of Languedoc: two principles, souls as fallen angels, the consolamentum with the Gospel of John laid on the head, and the few Cathar texts the inquisitors missed; the Albigensian Crusade, Béziers and the pyre at Montségur; the inquisition and the Montaillou register; and the other dissenters, Waldensians, Marguerite Porete, the Spiritual Franciscans, Wyclif and Hus. With the great historians’ quarrel over whether the Cathar church was real or built by its persecutors, and the Grail legends and ‘Cathar castles’ sorted from the record.
text: On the morning of 16 March 1244 , the defenders of Montségur , a fortress on a limestone peak in the foothills of the Pyrenees, came down the mountain. The castle had surrendered after a siege of about ten months. The garrison was allowed to go free, but the heretics among them were given a choice: renounce their faith or burn. Some two hundred men and women, led by their bishop Bertrand Marty , refused. Some of the defenders who could have left chose instead to receive the heretics' only sacrament in the last days of the truce, so that they would die with them. They were burned together in an enclosure of stakes at the foot of the mountain. The Catholic chroniclers called them Cathars , heretics who believed that the visible world was made by an evil power. They called themselves the good men and good women , or simply good Christians . Who they really were, what they believed, and how far the Church's war on them created the very enemy it fought, are among the liveliest arguments in medieval history. A century of heresy Latin Christendom had known few popular heresies for centuries when, in the early eleventh century, groups accused of heresy began to appear: at Orléans in 1022, where canons were burned; at Arras, at Monforte in Italy, and elsewhere. From the twelfth century the accusations multiply. Three broad kinds of dissent run through the High and late Middle Ages: Dualist movements, above all those later called Cathars , in southern France (Languedoc) and northern Italy. Evangelical movements of poverty and preaching, such as the Waldensians , who wanted to live like the apostles and read the Bible in their own language. Mystical and reforming movements: the beguines and the alleged " Free Spirit ", the radical Spiritual Franciscans , and later Wyclif and the Lollards in England and Jan Hus in Bohemia. The Church's response, the crusade, the inquisition and the stake, shaped Europe as much as the heresies did. The good Christians of Languedoc In the second half of the twelfth century, in the towns and castles of Languedoc , the land between Toulouse, Carcassonne and the Pyrenees, a religious movement took root that the Church called heretical. Its members did not use the name "Cathar", which was coined by a German monk, Eckbert of Schönau , in the 1160s from the Greek for "pure"; in the south they were often called Albigensians , after the town of Albi. What is known of their beliefs comes mostly from their enemies, supplemented by a few texts of their own: Two principles. The good God created the invisible, spiritual world. The visible, material world, with its bodies, lust and death, was the work of an evil principle, Satan or a fallen angel. Some Cathars held that the two principles were eternal and equal ("absolute" dualism); others, that the evil one was a creature who rebelled ("moderate" dualism). Souls as fallen angels. Human souls were spirits of heaven trapped in bodies, passing from body to body until they were freed. Christ. Christ was an angel or spirit sent to show the way home; he did not have a real material body, so he did not truly suffer or die on the cross, and the sacraments of matter, bread, wine and water, were…

title: Sabbateans, Frankists & Hasidim
summary: Messiahs and mystics in the Jewish early modern world: Luria’s shattered vessels and the catastrophe of 1648; Sabbatai Zevi, his prophet Nathan and the frenzy of 1665–66 that Glückel of Hameln remembered, ending in the Messiah’s conversion to Islam; the secret believers, the Dönme of Salonika and the amulet controversy; Jacob Frank, the burned Talmud and the mass baptisms; and, in the same borderlands, the Baal Shem Tov, the Maggid, the rebbes and their dynasties, and the fierce opposition of the Vilna Gaon. A symbology of sparks and husks, the niggun and the rebbe’s table, with hagiography and hostile sources marked as such.
text: Born in Hamburg in 1646, a Jewish woman named Glückel married at about fourteen, around 1660, into a merchant family of the town of Hameln, raised twelve children, ran a business in gold and pearls, and in her widowhood wrote her memoirs in Yiddish for her children. They are one of the great personal documents of early modern Europe. In them she remembers the winter of 1665–1666, when the news reached Hamburg that the Messiah had appeared in the Ottoman Empire. Some sold their houses and land; the Portuguese Jews of the city danced in their synagogue wearing broad green silk ribbons, the Messiah's colour. Her father-in-law in Hameln packed two great casks with linen and provisions, dried peas and beans and preserved meat, ready to set off for the Holy Land at a moment's notice, and kept them packed for years, waiting. Then word came that the Messiah had become a Muslim. That messiah was Sabbatai Zevi . The movement around him was the greatest messianic upheaval in Jewish history since antiquity, and its collapse, its underground survival and the revival of Jewish mysticism that followed it in the Polish borderlands, as Hasidism , are the subject of this chapter. The background: catastrophe and Kabbalah Two things prepared the way. The first was Lurianic Kabbalah , the mystical system taught by Isaac Luria (1534–1572) in the Galilean town of Safed and spread by his disciples in the following decades (see ch26). Luria taught that creation began with God's contraction ( tzimtzum ) to make room for the world; that the vessels meant to hold the divine light shattered ( shevirat ha-kelim ), scattering sparks of holiness into the realm of the "husks" ( kelipot ); and that the task of Israel, through the commandments and mystical intention, was repair ( tikkun ), raising the sparks and so bringing the Messiah. History itself became a drama of cosmic restoration nearing its end. The second was catastrophe . In 1648 the Cossack rising led by Bohdan Khmelnytsky against Polish rule in Ukraine brought massacres of Jewish communities. Jewish chronicles gave enormous numbers; modern estimates range from several thousand to tens of thousands of deaths, and the figures are debated . The trauma was real and lasting, and Jewish memory marked 1648 as a time of messianic "birth pangs". Sabbatai Zevi Sabbatai Zevi (1626–1676) was born in Smyrna (İzmir) in Ottoman Anatolia, a learned young man with periods of exaltation and deep depression; modern writers have often suggested a bipolar illness. In his exalted phases he performed "strange acts" ( maʿasim zarim ) that broke the law, such as pronouncing the forbidden divine name and "marrying" a Torah scroll. He was expelled from several communities. In 1665 he met Nathan of Gaza , a brilliant young kabbalist, who had a vision that Sabbatai was the Messiah. Nathan became his prophet and theologian. Sabbatai proclaimed himself in May 1665, and Nathan's letters spread the news across the Jewish world, from Yemen and Persia to Amsterdam, Hamburg and Poland. Communities fasted and did penance; some prepared to leave for the Land of Israel; rabbis who doubted were silenced. Sabbatai abolished the fasts that mourned the…

title: Secularism & the Nones
summary: The modern age’s fastest-growing ‘tradition’ is no religion: 1.9 billion people in 2020, 29% of American adults. Doubt in the ancient world, from the Cārvākas and Diagoras to Epicurus and Xunzi; the Enlightenment critics and the Festival of Reason in Notre-Dame; Comte’s Religion of Humanity, Darwin, Huxley and ‘God is dead’; the freethinkers; the grim record of state atheism in the Soviet Union, Albania and China; humanist rituals and the Sunday Assembly; and the great debate over whether modernity ends religion. A symbology of secular cults, calendars and emblems, with the question of God reported, not decided.
text: On 10 November 1793 , in the second year of the French Republic, the cathedral of Notre-Dame de Paris was given a new religion. In the nave, workmen had built a mountain of painted canvas topped by a small Greek temple inscribed " To Philosophy ", with busts of Voltaire, Rousseau and other heroes of the Enlightenment. Young women dressed in white processed around it, and from the temple came a woman, in most accounts an actress of the Opéra, playing the Goddess of Reason , while the crowd sang a hymn to Liberty. It was the Festival of Reason , the high point of the revolutionary campaign to "dechristianize" France. It did not last. Within months its promoters had gone to the guillotine, and Robespierre, who thought atheism aristocratic, replaced the Cult of Reason with a Cult of the Supreme Being . The scene is a good emblem of this chapter's subject: the attempt, in the modern age, to live without the gods, and how often that attempt has borrowed the forms of religion itself. The largest new "tradition" The fastest-growing religious category of the modern world is no religion . The Pew Research Center estimates that the number of people with no religious affiliation grew from 1.6 billion in 2010 to 1.9 billion in 2020, roughly a quarter of humanity, the largest share of them in China. In the United States, Pew's 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study found that 29% of adults are religious " nones ", atheists, agnostics or "nothing in particular", up from 16% in 2007, though the rise may have levelled off. In parts of Europe and East Asia, nones are the majority: South Korea's 2015 census counted 56% (ch71). "No religion" does not mean no belief. Pew found in 2025 that many unaffiliated people around the world still believe in God or a higher power, in spirits, or in life after death, and pray or meditate. Some call themselves " spiritual but not religious ". A minority are convinced atheists , who deny that any god exists, or agnostics , who hold that the question cannot be answered. Nonreligion is as varied as religion. Doubt in the ancient world Unbelief is not modern. Every major literate civilization has left traces of it. In India , the Cārvāka or Lokāyata school taught that only what is perceived is real, that the soul dies with the body, and that the Vedas were the invention of priests seeking a living. Their own texts are lost; they are known from their opponents' summaries (ch69). In Greece , the Sophist Protagoras (fifth century BCE) wrote that about the gods he could not know whether they exist or not; Diagoras of Melos was notorious as "the atheist" and was condemned at Athens; Democritus explained the world by atoms and the void; Epicurus taught that the gods, if they exist, take no interest in us, and that death is nothing to fear. The Roman poet Lucretius set out Epicurus's philosophy in On the Nature of Things , whose rediscovery in 1417 fed Renaissance thought. The classicist Tim Whitmarsh has argued that ancient atheism was more widespread than usually thought. In China , the Confucian Xunzi (third century BCE) argued that "Heaven" is simply nature, that rain comes whether or not one performs the rain dance, and that rites are…

title: The San & Southern African Rock Art
era: Prehistory · The San & Southern African Rock Art
summary: From the 73,000-year-old drawing at Blombos and the painted stones of Apollo 11 to the Linton panel on South Africa’s coat of arms: the rock art of the San and the rare chance to read it with the people’s own words, the 12,000 pages of |Xam testimony recorded in the 1870s. |Kaggen the mantis, the eland and its potency, the rain-animal, and the healing dance in which n|om ‘boils’ and healers bleed from the nose; the trance interpretation of the art and its critics; and the San today, from colonial violence to the Kalahari court victory and their own code of research ethics. With the ‘living fossil’ error named and set aside.
text: In 1917 a slab of sandstone about two metres long was cut out of the back wall of a rock shelter on the farm Linton , in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, and carried to the South African Museum in Cape Town, where it has been on display ever since. It is covered with paintings in red, white and black, made with a fineness that seems impossible on rock: people with arms stretched back, some bending forward, one with lines of red falling from the nose; a long, sinuous red band bordered with tiny white dots, running across the scene; fish, eels, and a scatter of other figures. The Linton panel is one of the masterpieces of the rock art of the San , the hunter-gatherers of southern Africa. Two of its figures, slightly altered, stand on South Africa's coat of arms, above a motto in the extinct |Xam San language. What the panel meant to its painters is one of the most argued questions in the study of prehistoric religion, and it is also one of the few where the people's own words can be brought to bear. The oldest continuous story Southern Africa holds some of the earliest evidence anywhere for the symbolic mind. At Blombos Cave , on the southern Cape coast, people processed ochre in shells about 100,000 years ago, engraved crosshatched designs on pieces of ochre about 75,000 years ago, and, on a flake of stone from levels about 73,000 years old, drew a crosshatched pattern with an ochre crayon: the oldest known drawing. At Apollo 11 Cave in southern Namibia, seven slabs of stone painted with animals, one perhaps a feline with human legs, were found in layers dated to roughly 30,000 years ago, among the oldest figurative art in Africa. At Tsodilo Hills in Botswana, a claim published in 2006 that a rock in "Rhino Cave" carved to resemble a python's head was the focus of a 70,000-year-old ritual was widely reported; archaeologists who excavated the site challenged it, pointing out that the dates come from deposits in front of the wall, not from the carving. It remains contested . The painted and engraved rock art of the region is much younger, mostly from the last few thousand years, and some was made within the last two centuries: paintings in the Maloti-Drakensberg mountains show horses, wagons and men with guns. Radiocarbon dating of mineral crusts over and under the paint shows that Drakensberg art goes back more than 2,000 years. There are tens of thousands of sites across southern Africa, and the uKhahlamba-Drakensberg park alone holds hundreds of shelters with many thousands of images. The makers were ancestors of the people now called San . Who the San are " San " is the collective name, originally a Khoekhoe word, for the many hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa who speak, or spoke, languages with click consonants; the older English term " Bushmen " is considered offensive by some and accepted by others, and many San prefer the names of their own groups: Ju|'hoansi , !Xun , Naro , |Xam and others. Genetic studies show that the ancestors of the Khoe-San diverged from other human populations very early, perhaps 260,000–350,000 years ago, making them carriers of some of the deepest lineages of our species. Their history since the…

title: The Olmec
summary: The first great art of Mesoamerica, c. 1600–400 BCE: offerings thrown into the sacred spring at El Manatí, with the world’s oldest rubber balls and the bones of newborn children; the colossal heads and throne-altars of San Lorenzo and La Venta; serpentine mosaics and jade figurines buried where no one would see them; the were-jaguar, the Olmec Dragon and the Maize God; rain-making in the cave of Chalcatzingo; and the earliest cacao and ballgame. With the ‘mother culture’ debate, the contested Cascajal block and the ‘African Olmec’ claim weighed against the evidence.
text: In 1987, villagers digging a fish pond at the foot of a small hill called El Manatí , in the swampy lowlands of southern Veracruz, found strange things in the mud. When archaeologists from Mexico's national institute excavated the spring there over the following years, they found that people had been throwing offerings into its water for centuries, beginning about 1700 BCE : polished stone axes set in careful clusters, jade beads, and the oldest rubber balls known anywhere in the world, some of them dated to about 1600 BCE. Later came wooden busts of people with shaven, elongated heads, wrapped in reed mats and laid in the mud with care, bones of newborn children, and more axes. Thanks to the waterlogged earth, wood and rubber survived three and a half thousand years. El Manatí is a window onto the religion of the people archaeologists call the Olmec , the makers of the earliest great art style of Mesoamerica. Who the Olmec were "Olmec" is a name borrowed from the Aztec word for the "rubber people" of the Gulf Coast; we do not know what the ancient people called themselves. Between about 1600 and 400 BCE , in the tropical lowlands of what are now Veracruz and Tabasco, they built the first large ceremonial centres in Mesoamerica: San Lorenzo (flourishing c. 1400–1000 BCE), on a vast artificial plateau above the Coatzacoalcos River; La Venta (c. 900–400 BCE), on an island in a coastal swamp, with a great earthen pyramid more than 30 metres high; Tres Zapotes , which outlived the others into the last centuries BCE. Olmec-style objects and images, jade figurines, pottery with carved motifs, rock carvings, also appear far outside the heartland, in the highlands of central Mexico, Guerrero, Oaxaca and as far as Central America. Whether this means that the Olmec were the " mother culture " from which later Mesoamerican civilizations derived, or one of several interacting " sister cultures " that shared and exchanged a common symbolism, has been one of the longest-running debates in Mesoamerican archaeology. Colossal heads and thrones The most famous Olmec monuments are the colossal heads : seventeen of them are known, ten from San Lorenzo, four from La Venta and three from the Tres Zapotes area. Carved from basalt boulders dragged from the Tuxtla mountains, some weigh more than twenty tons. Each has a distinct face and a distinct helmet-like headdress, and most archaeologists think they are portraits of individual rulers . Several were carved from older monuments, and some appear to have been deliberately damaged and buried. Alongside them stand great rectangular stone " altars ", now usually identified as thrones . The most famous, La Venta Altar 4, shows a man seated in a niche carved as the open mouth of a creature, the entrance to a cave or the underworld, holding a rope that binds figures on the sides. The ruler emerges from the earth, the place of ancestors and of water. The imagery joins kingship to the sacred landscape. Offerings buried out of sight La Venta's ceremonial centre, Complex A, north of the great pyramid, was built and rebuilt over centuries, and some of its most important religious acts left things meant never to be seen again …

title: The Etruscans
summary: The people Rome called the most devoted to religion: the ‘Etruscan discipline’ revealed by the child-sage Tages and the prophetess Vegoia; the bronze Liver of Piacenza, a sheep’s liver mapped as the sixteen regions of the sky; lightning lore and the sacred templum; Tinia, Uni and Menrva, forerunners of Rome’s Capitoline gods; the gold Pyrgi tablets that make Uni and Astarte one goddess; the linen ritual book that ended up wrapping an Egyptian mummy; painted tombs of banquets and death demons; and the ten ages allotted to their nation. With ancient DNA settling the origins debate and ‘decipherments’ weighed against the evidence.
text: On 26 September 1877 a farmer ploughing a field near Gossolengo, south of Piacenza in northern Italy, turned up a flat piece of bronze about the size of a hand. It was a model of a sheep's liver , cast in the second century BCE, its upper surface divided by incised lines into compartments, each inscribed with a name in Etruscan letters: Tin , Uni , Fufluns , Cilens , Tluscv and many more. It was a map of the heavens laid out on an organ. An Etruscan priest, the haruspex , would sacrifice a sheep, lift out its liver, and read the will of the gods from its shape, colour and marks, region by region, each region belonging to a deity. The Liver of Piacenza is the most famous object of a people whom the Romans themselves called "more devoted than any other to religious rites", and whose priests Rome went on consulting for centuries after the Etruscans had lost their independence. A people between myth and archaeology The Etruscans lived in central Italy, in the land between the Arno and the Tiber still called Tuscany, from the early Iron Age Villanovan culture of about 900 BCE until they were absorbed by Rome in the last centuries BCE. They were organized in independent city-states, traditionally a league of twelve , among them Tarquinia, Cerveteri (Caere), Veii, Vulci, Chiusi and Volsinii (Orvieto). At their height, in the seventh and sixth centuries BCE, they dominated much of Italy, traded across the Mediterranean, and gave Rome some of its early kings. Where they came from was argued about in antiquity. Herodotus said they had migrated from Lydia in Asia Minor; Dionysius of Halicarnassus said they were native to Italy. A 2021 study of ancient DNA from 82 individuals, led by Cosimo Posth , found that the Etruscans were genetically similar to their Latin neighbours, with no sign of recent migration from Anatolia: an indigenous people, despite their distinctive culture. Their language is written in an alphabet adapted from Greek, so it can be read aloud, but it is not Indo-European , unrelated to Latin or Greek, and it is still only partly understood: the meaning of many words is known from bilingual texts, glosses and context, but longer texts remain difficult. Its only relatives are the little-known Raetic of the Alps and the language of an inscription from the island of Lemnos. The discipline The Romans called Etruscan religious knowledge the Etrusca disciplina , the "Etruscan discipline". It was a body of sacred books, now lost, known from Roman writers such as Cicero , Seneca , Pliny the Elder and Censorinus . Tradition divided it into three kinds: the libri haruspicini , on divination from the entrails of sacrificed animals; the libri fulgurales , on the interpretation of lightning ; the libri rituales , on the rites for founding cities and temples, laying out boundaries, dividing time, the afterlife (the libri Acherontici ) and prodigies (the libri ostentarii ). The Etruscans said this knowledge had been revealed . Near Tarquinia, a man ploughing a field saw a child with the wisdom of an old man rise out of the furrow: Tages , who sang the rules of divination to the gathered lords of Etruria, who wrote them down, and then died or vanished.…

title: The Scythians & the Steppe
era: Axial Age · The Scythians & the Steppe
summary: The mounted nomads of the Iron Age steppe, from the Danube to the Altai: the tattooed ‘Ice Maiden’ frozen in her tomb with six horses; Herodotus’s Scythians, with their hearth-goddess Tabiti, the sword of Ares on a mountain of brushwood, willow-rod diviners and the Enarees; the royal funerals of the Dnieper kurgans, which archaeology has largely confirmed; hemp burned in felt tents, now proven by chemistry; gold stags and griffins of the animal style; horses masked as antlered beasts; and the warrior women behind the Amazon myth. With Herodotus checked against the ground, and modern ancestral claims against the evidence.
text: In the summer of 1993 , on the high, windswept Ukok plateau of the Altai mountains, where Russia meets Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China, the Russian archaeologist Natalia Polosmak and her team opened a burial mound. Under the stones, water had seeped into the log chamber more than two thousand years earlier and frozen solid, and the ice had preserved what it held. Inside a larch-wood coffin lay a young woman of the Pazyryk culture, dressed in a silk blouse and a woollen skirt, wearing a tall felt headdress decorated with carved and gilded animals. Her left shoulder and arm were tattooed with fantastic animals: a deer with a griffin's beak and antlers ending in flowers. Six horses, saddled and harnessed, had been killed and buried beside her. The " Ice Maiden ", as the press named her, was one of the peoples of the great Iron Age steppe whom the Greeks called Scythians . Their world stretched from the Danube to Mongolia, and its religion is known to us through two very different witnesses: the ground, and Herodotus . The Scythians and their cousins In the first millennium BCE, the grasslands of Eurasia were dominated by mounted nomads who spoke Iranian languages, herded horses, cattle and sheep, fought as archers on horseback, and buried their leaders under great earth mounds, kurgans . The Greeks called those north of the Black Sea Skythai ; the Persians called their eastern cousins Saka ; later came the Sarmatians and Alans . Related cultures stretched across the steppe to the Altai (the Pazyryk culture) and Tuva, where the royal kurgan of Arzhan dates to the ninth to seventh centuries BCE. Modern scholars group them as the " Scythian world " or " Scytho-Siberian " cultures, sharing a way of life, weapons, horse gear and, above all, an art of animals, while differing from region to region. The Scythians left no texts of their own. Their descendants, in a sense, survive: the Ossetians of the Caucasus speak an Iranian language descended from that of the Alans, and their Nart sagas preserve heroic legends that scholars such as Georges Dumézil traced back to the Scytho-Sarmatian world. Herodotus in Scythia The Greek historian Herodotus , writing about 430 BCE, devoted the fourth book of his Histories to the Scythians, drawing on what he learned in the Greek colonies on the Black Sea coast, perhaps at Olbia . He is our main written source, and he is a Greek describing strangers, often through Greek categories. His account includes: The origin of the Scythians. The first man, Targitaos , son of Zeus and of the daughter of the river Borysthenes (the Dnieper), had three sons. In their time four golden objects fell from the sky: a plough and yoke , a battle-axe and a cup . When the two elder brothers approached, the gold blazed with fire; when the youngest, Kolaxais , approached, it cooled, and he took it and became king. The royal Scythians kept the sacred gold and honoured it with great sacrifices every year. Dumézil read the four objects as the emblems of three social functions, farming, war and sovereignty or priesthood, the pattern he saw across Indo-European myth; that interpretation is influential and debated . The gods. Herodotus lists them…

title: The First Christian Kingdoms
summary: Three kingdoms outside Rome that made Christianity their state religion before Rome did: Armenia, where Gregory survived the pit of Khor Virap, Mesrop Mashtots invented an alphabet to carry the Bible, and Vardan died at Avarayr; Georgia, converted through the captive woman Nino and her grapevine cross; and Aksum, whose king Ezana replaced the crescent with the cross on his coins, with the shipwrecked Frumentius as first bishop. Then Ethiopia’s own Christianity: the Nine Saints, the Garima Gospels, the 81-book Bible, the tabot in every church and the Ark claimed at Aksum, and the rock-cut New Jerusalem of Lalibela.
text: The gold coins of Ezana , king of Aksum in the highlands of what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, in the mid-fourth century, show the king's crowned bust, and above it a small symbol. On his early coins, the symbol is a crescent and disc , the emblem of the old gods of South Arabia and Aksum. On his later coins, the crescent and disc are gone. In their place is a cross , one of the earliest appearances of the Christian cross on any coin in the world. Ezana's inscriptions change in the same way: the early ones thank the war god Mahrem , the later ones "the Lord of Heaven" and, in a Greek version, the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Here, in metal and stone, is the moment a kingdom changed its religion. Around the same decades, at the other end of the Christian world, in the mountains of the Caucasus, the kings of Armenia and Georgia did the same. These three kingdoms, none of them within the Roman Empire, adopted Christianity as the religion of the state before Rome itself did, and each created a Christian culture of its own that has survived for sixteen centuries. Armenia: the king, the pit and the alphabet The Armenian church traces its beginnings to the apostles Thaddeus and Bartholomew , and there were Christians in Armenia in the third century. The decisive event, in Armenian tradition, came through Gregory , later called the Illuminator (Grigor Lusavorich), a Christian of Parthian noble descent who entered the service of the Arsacid king Tiridates III (Trdat). When Gregory refused to sacrifice to the goddess Anahit , the king had him tortured and thrown into a deep pit at Khor Virap , near Mount Ararat, where he survived, the story says, for some thirteen years, fed secretly by a Christian widow. Tiridates, having martyred a group of Christian virgins led by Hripsime and Gayane , fell into madness, in legend turning into a boar. Only Gregory could heal him. The king was baptized and made Christianity the religion of his kingdom; Gregory was consecrated bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia and destroyed the temples of the old gods. The traditional date is 301 ; scholars place the conversion somewhere between about 284 and 314, and the account of the king's madness and healing is hagiography , written down in the fifth century by a writer calling himself Agathangelos. A church at Etchmiadzin , "where the Only-Begotten descended", was built on the site of Gregory's vision of Christ; the present cathedral, much rebuilt, stands on foundations of the fourth century and is the seat of the Armenian Catholicos. A century later, the monk Mesrop Mashtots , with the support of the Catholicos Sahak and King Vramshapuh , created the Armenian alphabet around 405 , in order to translate the Bible into Armenian. The first sentence translated, tradition says, was from Proverbs: "To know wisdom and instruction, to perceive the words of understanding." A golden age of translation and original writing followed, and the alphabet, 36 letters in its original form, became the bearer of Armenian identity. In 451 the Persian king Yazdegerd II , who ruled much of Armenia, ordered the Armenians to return to Zoroastrianism . The Armenian nobles under Vardan Mamikonian rose in…

title: Shi'ism
summary: The ‘party of Ali’: the succession dispute after Muhammad and the words at Ghadir Khumm; Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 and the mourning of Muharram, from passion plays to the Arba’in walk; the Imams and the branches they divided — Zaydis, Isma’ilis with the Fatimids and the Aga Khan, and Twelvers with their hidden Imam in occultation since 941; the jurists who speak in his absence; the Safavid conversion of Iran and Khomeini’s rule of the jurist. A symbology of the Five of the Cloak, Zulfiqar, the clay of Karbala and the esoteric readings of the Isma’ilis, with faith claims and sectarian myths kept apart from the record.
text: On the tenth day of the month of Muharram in the year 61 of the Islamic calendar, 10 October 680 , on the plain of Karbala by the Euphrates in Iraq, a small company of perhaps seventy men, with their women and children, faced an army of thousands. For days they had been cut off from the river. Their leader was Husayn ibn Ali , grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who had refused to swear allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid and had set out for Kufa at the invitation of its people, who did not come to his aid. By evening Husayn and nearly all the men with him were dead, among them his half-brother Abbas , killed trying to bring water, and his infant son. His head was carried to Damascus; his sister Zaynab and the surviving women and children were led as captives. Every year since, on the first ten days of Muharram, Shi'i Muslims across the world have mourned him: in processions and passion plays, in sermons and laments, in tears. Karbala made Shi'ism , the "party of Ali", into a tradition whose heart is the memory of a just man betrayed and martyred, and the hope of his descendants' vindication. Origins: who should lead? When Muhammad died in 632 , his community had to decide who would lead it. The majority accepted Abu Bakr , and then Umar , Uthman and finally Ali as caliphs; they became known as Sunnis , the people of the Prophet's custom ( sunna ) and of the community. A minority held that leadership belonged to Ali ibn Abi Talib , Muhammad's cousin and the husband of his daughter Fatima , and to their descendants. They became the shi'at Ali , the "party of Ali", or simply Shi'a . The Shi'a point above all to the event at Ghadir Khumm , an oasis on the road from Mecca, in March 632, where Muhammad, returning from his last pilgrimage, took Ali by the hand and said: " For whoever I am his mawla , Ali is his mawla . " The statement is reported in both Sunni and Shi'i collections of hadith. The meaning of mawla , a word that can mean master, patron, friend or ally, is the crux: for Shi'a it designated Ali as Muhammad's successor, and Ghadir is a festival; for Sunnis it was an expression of esteem and friendship. Ali did become the fourth caliph in 656, amid civil war, and was assassinated in 661 at Kufa; his shrine at Najaf in Iraq is one of the holiest places of Shi'ism. His son Hasan made peace with the Umayyad Mu'awiya ; his son Husayn died at Karbala. What had begun as a political question became, through suffering and memory, a religious one. The Imams For Shi'a, the rightful leaders of the community are the Imams : Ali and a line of his descendants through Fatima. They are not only political leaders but religious guides, inheritors of the Prophet's knowledge, and, in Twelver belief, sinless ( ma'sum ) and divinely appointed. Disagreements about who was the rightful Imam at each generation produced the main branches of Shi'ism: Zaydis follow Zayd ibn Ali , a grandson of Husayn, who rose in revolt in 740. They hold that any learned descendant of Ali and Fatima who rises against injustice can be Imam, and are theologically the closest of the Shi'a to Sunnis. Their Imams ruled in Yemen for over a thousand years, until 1962; the Houthi movement…

title: Tengri & the Mongols
summary: The Eternal Blue Sky of the steppe peoples: Tengri in the Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions, Chinggis Khan on Burkhan Khaldun and the shaman Kököchü, the ‘by the power of Eternal Heaven’ formula on Mongol letters and seals, and a religious policy of tolerance that was pragmatism more than creed, as William of Rubruck’s 1254 debate at Karakorum shows. Then the khanates choose: Ghazan’s Islam in 1295, Kublai and the Tibetan lama Phagpa, Altan Khan’s title ‘Dalai Lama’ in 1578; the purges of 1937–39 and the post-1990 revival and neo-Tengrism. A symbology of the ovoo, khadag, sülde banner, milk libations, scapulimancy and the soyombo, with modern revival kept distinct from the medieval record.
text: On 30 May 1254, at the camp of the Great Khan Möngke at Karakorum in Mongolia, a Flemish Franciscan friar, William of Rubruck , took part in a public debate. The khan had ordered the representatives of the religions at his court to argue their faiths before three of his secretaries, a Christian, a Muslim and a Buddhist. William, with the Nestorian Christians on his side, argued first against a Buddhist monk about whether there is one God, then against the Muslims, who, he says, agreed that there is one God and declined to argue further. At the end, nobody was converted. The Mongols, William wrote, "clapped their hands" and drank a great deal. A few days later Möngke summoned him and explained his own faith: "We Mongols believe that there is only one God, by whom we live and by whom we die, and for whom we have an upright heart. But as God gave the hand several fingers, so he has given men several ways." The God he meant was Tengri , the Eternal Heaven, in whose name the Mongols had conquered the largest land empire the world had ever seen. The sky over the steppe The peoples of the Mongolian and Central Asian steppe, Turks and Mongols alike, venerated Tengri (Mongolian Tenggeri ), the sky , as the supreme power. The word appears as the name of a god in the records of the Xiongnu , whose rulers styled themselves "sons of heaven" in the second century BCE, and it is central to the first texts written in a Turkic language, the Orkhon inscriptions , carved in 732 and 735 in the Orkhon valley of Mongolia in memory of the Göktürk prince Kül Tegin and his brother Bilge Qaghan . They speak of the ruler as "heaven-like and heaven-born", made khagan by Tengri; of Umay , the goddess of fertility and children associated with the queen; and of the sacred Earth and Water ( Yer-Sub ), the spirits of the land. When the Turks were disobedient and disunited, the inscriptions say, Tengri let them be conquered; when they were loyal, Tengri raised them up. This religion, which modern writers call Tengrism , had no scriptures, priesthood or temples in the usual sense. Its elements, reconstructed from inscriptions, Chinese, Persian and European reports, and later Mongol and Turkic folklore, included: Tengri , the Eternal Blue Sky, source of fate, life and the ruler's mandate, sometimes one supreme sky, sometimes many "tengris" (Mongol tradition later counted 99); Etügen or Itügen , the Earth, the mother; the spirits of mountains , rivers , springs and particular places, the "masters" of the land; the ancestors , above all of the ruling clan, honoured with offerings; shamans (Mongolian böö , female udagan ), who mediated with spirits, healed and divined. Genghis Khan and the mandate of heaven The Mongol conqueror Temüjin , proclaimed Chinggis (Genghis) Khan at a great assembly in 1206 , understood his mission in these terms. The Secret History of the Mongols , a Mongol chronicle of the thirteenth century, tells how the young Temüjin, fleeing enemies, hid on the sacred mountain Burkhan Khaldun in the Khentii range; afterwards he took off his hat, hung his belt around his neck, knelt nine times towards the sun and offered libations of mare's milk, and declared that he…

title: Akbar & the Mughal Synthesis
era: Early Modern · Akbar & the Mughal Synthesis
summary: The Mughal emperor Akbar’s House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri, where Sunni and Shi’i scholars, Brahmins, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and the Jesuits of 1580 debated before him; the mahzar of 1579; the small circle of disciples later called the Din-i Ilahi and the argument over whether it was a religion at all; ‘peace with all’, the divine light of kingship and the Persian Mahabharata. Then the reaction and the road not taken: Ahmad Sirhindi, Dara Shikoh’s Upanishads and his execution in 1659, and the fiercely contested reign of Aurangzeb. A symbology of light, the pun on Akbar’s coins, the jharokha window and the Buland Darwaza inscription.
text: On 28 February 1580 three Jesuit priests from Goa rode into Fatehpur Sikri , the red sandstone city the Mughal emperor Akbar had raised on a ridge west of Agra. They were Rudolf Acquaviva , Antonio de Monserrate and the interpreter Francisco Henriques , and they had been invited by the emperor himself. Among their gifts was a new Royal Polyglot Bible , printed at Antwerp by Christophe Plantin in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Aramaic and Syriac; Akbar received it with reverence and had it kept in a gold casket in his private rooms. Within weeks the priests were debating Muslim scholars before the emperor in his Ibadat Khana , the "House of Worship", on the long Thursday nights he gave to argument about God. They went home convinced he was about to be baptized. He was not. Akbar, who could not read, had built something else: an imperial court in which Sunni and Shi'i scholars, Brahmin pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and Catholic missionaries were all summoned to speak, and in which the final word on religion belonged, more and more, to the emperor. This chapter covers the religious world of the Mughal empire at its height, from Akbar (reigned 1556–1605) to the execution of his great-grandson Dara Shikoh in 1659: the debates, the translations, the imperial cult that historians call the Din-i Ilahi , the orthodox reaction, and the long argument, still fought today, over what it all meant. The emperor and his inheritance The Mughals were Central Asian Turks, descendants of Timur and, through the female line, of Chinggis Khan; Akbar's grandfather Babur had taken Delhi in 1526. Akbar was born in 1542 at Umarkot in Sindh while his father Humayun was in exile, and he came to the throne at thirteen. He ruled a Sunni Muslim dynasty over a population that was overwhelmingly Hindu, with Jain merchant communities, Shi'i nobles from Iran, Sikhs in the Punjab, Parsis on the western coast and, from 1510, a Portuguese Catholic colony at Goa. His early decisions were political as much as religious. From 1562 he married daughters of Rajput Hindu kings, beginning with the house of Amber, and the Rajputs became pillars of the empire; his Hindu wives kept their own worship in the palace. In 1564 he abolished the jizya , the poll tax on non-Muslims that Islamic law prescribed. His nobility came to include Iranians, Central Asian Turks, Indian Muslims and Rajputs serving on the same terms, as his minister and historian Abu'l-Fazl records in the Ain-i Akbari . Akbar also had a personal religious life that the sources describe as restless. He was devoted to the Chishti Sufi order. The shaikh Salim Chishti of Sikri was believed to have foretold the birth of the heir the emperor longed for; when a son was born in 1569 he was named Salim (the future emperor Jahangir), and Akbar built his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, around the shaikh's village and mosque. Sources are mixed on what Akbar could read. The chroniclers present him as unlettered, with books read aloud to him daily. Some modern writers have suggested dyslexia; that is a retrospective guess, not a diagnosis anyone can confirm. The House of Worship In 1575 Akbar ordered the Ibadat Khana built at Fatehpur Sikri…

title: Global Hinduism & the Guru Movements
era: Modern · Global Hinduism & the Guru Movements
summary: Hinduism becomes a world presence in three ways: Vivekananda’s ‘Sisters and brothers of America’ in 1893 and the reformers before him; the plantation diaspora carried to Guyana, Trinidad and Fiji in the ‘ship-bundle’ with Tulsidas’s Ramayana; and the gurus who came west — Yogananda, Prabhupada’s ISKCON, the Maharishi and the Beatles, Rajneesh and the 1984 Oregon poisoning — with the abuse reckonings, court cases and rationalist critics that followed. Then modern yoga and the argument over its age, Savarkar’s Hindutva and Ayodhya, the new diaspora temples and the 2025 Maha Kumbh. A symbology of Om, the reclaimed swastika, the maha-mantra on 108 beads, the tilak and the consecration of images.
text: On 11 September 1893 the World's Parliament of Religions opened in the hall of the new Art Institute building in Chicago, part of the World's Columbian Exposition. Late in the day a thirty-year-old Bengali monk in an ochre robe and turban, almost unknown in America, rose to speak for India and for Hinduism. His name was Swami Vivekananda . He began with five words: "Sisters and brothers of America". The audience, reported at some seven thousand, gave him a standing ovation that lasted, by the accounts, two minutes. The short speech that followed, a plea against sectarianism and fanaticism drawn from the Bhagavad Gita and the idea that all religions were paths to one truth, made him famous overnight. A year later, in November 1894, he founded the first Vedanta Society in two rented rooms on West 33rd Street in Manhattan. It was the first organized Hindu institution in the West, and Vivekananda's version of Hinduism, universal, philosophical and experiential, became for many outsiders what Hinduism simply was. The century and a quarter since has turned Hinduism, the religion of perhaps 1.2 billion people, overwhelmingly in India, into a global presence of three quite different kinds: - Diaspora Hinduism , carried by migrants from the plantations of the nineteenth century to the suburbs of the twenty-first. - Export Hinduism , the gurus, yoga and meditation movements that won Western converts and clients. - Political Hinduism , the ideology of Hindutva , which remade Indian politics and followed the diaspora abroad. This chapter covers all three, with the controversies that each has carried. Before Chicago: reformers and a new self-image Nineteenth-century Hinduism had been reshaped under British rule, in dialogue and argument with missionaries and orientalist scholars. In 1828 the Bengali scholar Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha (later Brahmo Samaj ) in Calcutta. It preached a rational monotheism grounded in the Vedas and Upanishads, and incorporated what it held to be the best teachings of other religions. On 7 April 1875 Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj . It called Hindus back to the Vedas as the source of all knowledge, and it promoted social equality and rejected image-worship. Vivekananda himself was a disciple of the Bengali mystic Ramakrishna (1836–1886), whose ecstatic devotion to the goddess Kali and experiments with other paths, including Islamic and Christian practice, Vivekananda interpreted as proof that all religions lead to the same realization. Historians describe this period as producing a "neo-Hindu" or "modern Hindu" self-image that stressed: the Upanishads and Vedanta over temple ritual; experience over caste law; universality over the local. It is this version that travelled west first. The plantation diaspora The largest Hindu migration of the nineteenth century was not to Chicago but to the sugar colonies. After the abolition of slavery in the British empire, planters imported indentured labourers from India: | Colony | First arrival | Indians arriving | |---|---|---| | Mauritius | 1834 | — | | British Guiana | 5 May 1838 | 238,909 (1838–1916) | | Trinidad | 30 May 1845, on the Fatel Razack , with 217…

title: Siberian & Arctic Shamanism
summary: The Evenki word that gave the world ‘shaman’, Witsen’s 1692 ‘Priest of the Devil’, and what the ethnographers recorded: trance, drum and iron-hung costume, the journey between upper, middle and lower worlds, the Chukchi ‘transformed’ shamans and the fly agaric of the far north-east. Across the Arctic, the Sami noaidi and their confiscated drums now coming home, and the Inuit angakkuq who combed the Sea Woman’s hair. Soviet persecution, the post-1991 revival and the jailed Sakha shaman who set out to exorcise the Kremlin. Then the big claim tested: is shamanism the first religion? Mal’ta, the earliest ‘shaman burials’ and Eliade’s thesis, with interpretation kept apart from evidence.
text: In 1692 the Amsterdam burgomaster and scholar Nicolaes Witsen published a great book on the peoples of northern and eastern Asia, Noord en Oost Tartarye . Among its pictures is a woodcut, much reproduced since, of a figure among the Tungus (Evenki) of Siberia: a man in a fringed fur costume, with an antlered headdress, beating a frame drum. The caption calls him a "Priest of the Devil" . It is one of the first European images of a shaman . The word itself came from the same people. About forty years earlier the dissident Russian archpriest Avvakum , exiled to the lands of the reindeer-herding Evenki, had met these practitioners and written about them. Through Russian travellers and scholars the Evenki word šaman entered the languages of Europe. This chapter is filed in the prehistory era for a reason that is itself the subject of the chapter. For more than a century scholars have argued that what Witsen's woodcut shows, a person who enters trance to travel among spirits on behalf of a community, is the oldest form of religion , reaching back into the Paleolithic. Some take it further, to the first religion of humanity. The evidence for that claim is thinner, and more interesting, than its popularity suggests. What follows is the documented religion of the northern peoples of Siberia and the Arctic, then the argument over whether it can be read back into the deep past. The word and the people The English word shaman comes through Russian from the Evenki šaman . The Evenki are a Tungusic-speaking people of the Siberian taiga, and Russian and Western writers long called them "Tungus". Where the Evenki word itself comes from is uncertain : It may come from a native root meaning "to know". It may be a borrowing, through Central Asian languages, from the Sanskrit śramaṇa , "ascetic", a term used for Buddhist monks. Both derivations have defenders. Other Siberian peoples had their own words for such figures: the Sakha (Yakut) oyun , the Mongolic böö , the Sami noaidi , the Inuit angakkuq . Scholars have long distinguished within Siberia a Tungus vein of shamanic practice and a Turkic vein, among peoples such as the Sakha and the Tuvans, with many local forms besides. What Siberian shamans did The ethnographic record. Most of what we know comes from observers of the seventeenth to early twentieth centuries: Russian officials and missionaries, political exiles turned ethnographers, and later Soviet and Western anthropologists. The most detailed single study of the Evenki is Sergei Shirokogoroff's Psychomental Complex of the Tungus (1935). Waldemar Bogoras and Waldemar Jochelson , exiled revolutionaries, produced classic studies of the Chukchi, Koryak and Yukaghir around 1900. The core practices. Across the region the record describes shamans as specialists who, by drumming, singing and dancing into an altered state, were believed to: Travel to other worlds. They journeyed to the upper and lower worlds to recover lost souls, escort the dead and negotiate with spirits for game or health. Take in spirits. They were believed to take helping spirits into themselves or to command them. Divine and heal. They divined and treated illness. A shaman was often…

title: The Voynich Manuscript
