Like the Mesha Stele (V22), the inscription credits a god, here Hadad, who "went before me". The same theology of divine warfare runs through the whole region. Pre-exilic Israel (ch07), Canaanite and Phoenician religion (ch58), the Mesha Stele (V22), and sacred kingship (ch49). What's well supported by the evidence - Three Old Aramaic basalt fragments found at Tel Dan in 1993–94, from a late-ninth-century BCE victory stele probably of Hazael of Damascus, mentioning a king of Israel and bytdwd. What is not supported - That the inscription proves the biblical account of David's life and empire. It attests a dynasty's name, not the stories. - That the fragments are forgeries. They were excavated in a controlled dig. What's genuinely open - The restored names (Joram and Ahaziah), and…

title: The Sudarium of Oviedo
summary: A stained linen face-cloth, venerated as the sudarium of John 20:7 and shown three times a year. Documented from the opening of the Arca Santa in 1075, radiocarbon-dated to around the seventh century, and claimed to match the Shroud.
text: Vault entry V24 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Cámara Santa, Cathedral of San Salvador, Oviedo (Spain) Three times a year the Cathedral of Oviedo shows a cloth. It is a piece of linen about 84 by 53 centimetres, stained brown and dirty, with no image on it: only blotches of what appear to be blood and fluid, in patterns that have been mapped with great care. The Gospel of John (20:6–7) says that when Peter entered the empty tomb he saw the linen cloths lying there, "and the sudarium that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths but rolled up in a place by itself". The Sudarium of Oviedo is venerated as that cloth, wrapped around the dead Jesus's face after the crucifixion. - Tradition. The cloth left Jerusalem ahead of the Persian conquest of 614, passed through North Africa, and reached Spain. It was carried north to Asturias in a chest of relics, the Arca Santa, ahead of the Muslim conquest. - Early references. A possible sixth-century mention (c. 570) by an anonymous pilgrim from Piacenza of a sudarium in Jerusalem is cited by defenders. Its link to this cloth is not demonstrable. - Oviedo. King Alfonso II of Asturias built the Cámara Santa (Holy Chamber) in the ninth century to house relics. On 14 March 1075, Alfonso VI, with Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, among the witnesses, had the Arca Santa opened and its relics listed. This is the cloth's firm documentary anchor. - Radiocarbon. Tests have repeatedly dated the linen to around the seventh century CE. They were made at Arizona (1990), Toronto (1992) and in a later test in 2007. Defenders argue that the relic was contaminated by centuries of handling and oil, which could skew the date. No independent re-test has overturned the seventh-century result. - The "match" with the Shroud. Researchers of the Spanish Centre for Sindonology have argued that the Sudarium's stain pattern and dimensions correspond to the face on the Shroud of Turin (V04), and that the blood on both is type AB. These claims are contested. The congruence studies have not been independently verified by forensic blood-pattern specialists. Blood typing of ancient, degraded material is unreliable, because AB-like reactions can come from bacterial contamination, a point made by the Shroud chemist Alan Adler. - Pollen claims of Middle Eastern origin face the same methodological problems as the Shroud pollen claims. A relic without an image. Unlike the Shroud or the Veil of Veronica (V25), the Sudarium carries no picture. Its sacredness rests entirely on contact: it is a cloth believed to have touched Christ's face. It is a clear example of the contact-relic logic central to medieval devotion. The rolled cloth. John's detail that the face-cloth was folded apart from the linen became a point of meditation on the orderliness of the resurrection. Christ was not stolen but rose, leaving the cloths set aside. The Shroud of Turin (V04), the Veil of Veronica (V25), the True Cross (V15), and Patristic and medieval Christianity (ch22, ch28). What's well supported by the evidence - A stained linen cloth (about 84 × 53 cm) kept in Oviedo, documented at the opening of the Arca Santa in 1075. It has been radiocarbon-dated to about the…

title: The Veil of Veronica
summary: The 'true image' of Christ's face that drew the crowds of the 1300 Jubilee. A legend not in the Gospels, a name with a false etymology, a relic reported lost in the Sack of Rome yet still shown each year, and a transparent veil at Manoppello claimed to be the original.
text: Vault entry V25 · Relics & Sacred Objects · A relic kept in St Peter's Basilica, Rome; a rival image at Manoppello (Abruzzo) During the first Christian Jubilee in 1300, pilgrims crowded into Old St Peter's in Rome to see one thing above all others: a cloth said to bear the face of Christ, impressed on it when a woman wiped his face on the way to Calvary. The poet Dante, who may have been among them, wrote of the pilgrim who comes from far away "to see our Veronica". The name was understood as vera icon, "true image". It became one of the great wonders of medieval Rome, and one of the most copied images in Europe. - Not in the Gospels. No Gospel mentions a woman wiping Jesus's face. The story grew from earlier legends. In the apocryphal Acts of Pilate a woman named Berenike/Veronica is identified with the woman healed of bleeding (Mark 5). Later tales describe a portrait of Christ that healed the emperor Tiberius. The wiping on the road to Calvary became the familiar form in the later Middle Ages and entered the Stations of the Cross. - "Vera icon." The popular derivation of Veronica from vera icon is a medieval folk etymology. The name is really a Latin form of the Greek Berenike. The etymology is false, but its symbolism is real: the relic was venerated as the authentic image. - A cloth identified as the Veronica was venerated at St Peter's in the twelfth century. It was shown to pilgrims at the 1300 Jubilee and in later Holy Years. - During the Sack of Rome (1527), contemporary letters report that the Veronica was stolen or destroyed. Others report that it survived. The Vatican has never declared it lost, and a relic is still kept in one of the great piers of the new St Peter's. It is shown briefly, from a distance, each year on Passion Sunday. Observers report that no image can be made out at that distance. - In the early seventeenth century the papacy restricted reproductions of the Veronica. Some historians read that restriction as a sign that the image was no longer visible, or no longer the original. That inference is debated. - In a Capuchin church at Manoppello in the Abruzzo hangs a thin, nearly transparent veil showing a man's face, eyes open, visible from both sides depending on the light. Local tradition says it arrived in the sixteenth century. - In 1999 the Jesuit art historian Heinrich Pfeiffer argued that it is the original Roman Veronica, removed from St Peter's around the time of rebuilding. Claims that the veil is woven of sea-silk (byssus) and that its image is not painted have been made by supporters. Neither claim has been published in independent, peer-reviewed analysis. - In 2006 Pope Benedict XVI visited the shrine and prayed before the image. He did not pronounce on its authenticity. The true image. Veronica relics answered the Byzantine tradition of images "not made by hands" (acheiropoieta), such as the Mandylion of Edessa. They offered the West its own authentic face of Christ as a pilgrimage goal. Their authority came from contact with the living Christ, which set them apart from ordinary art. Copies that carried power. Pilgrims bought badges and painted copies of the Veronica. Prayers said before it earned…

title: The Black Stone of the Kaaba
summary: The fragments of dark stone in a silver frame that pilgrims salute on every circuit of the Kaaba. Carried off by the Qarmatians in 930 and returned broken in 952. Its place in Islamic practice, and why no one can say what it is made of.
text: Vault entry V26 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba, the Sacred Mosque, Mecca Pilgrims circling the Kaaba during the Hajj pass one corner again and again. Set into the wall there, about a metre and a half above the ground and held in a silver frame, are the dark, polished fragments of a stone: the Black Stone (al-Ḥajar al-Aswad). Many pilgrims try to kiss or touch it as they pass, as the Prophet Muhammad is reported to have done. When the crowds make that impossible, as they usually do, pilgrims raise a hand towards it from a distance at the start of each circuit. This entry describes the stone with the restraint its sacredness asks for. It is a living object of worship for over a billion people, and it has never been scientifically examined. - Origin. Hadith and tradition describe the stone as coming from Paradise, originally white and blackened by human sins, and as set in the Kaaba by Abraham and Ishmael. These are articles of faith, not historical claims. - Muhammad and the stone. A well-known account places the Prophet at the rebuilding of the Kaaba around 605 CE, before his prophetic mission. The tribal clans quarrelled over who should have the honour of setting the stone back in place. Muhammad resolved it by placing the stone on a cloak and having a representative of each clan lift a corner, then set it in place with his own hands. - Not an object of worship. Islamic teaching insists that the stone is not worshipped, and that the Kaaba and the stone are a focus, not a god. The caliph ʿUmar is reported (in Sahih al-Bukhari) to have said to it: I know that you are a stone that can neither harm nor benefit. Had I not seen the Messenger of God kiss you, I would not have kissed you. - 930 CE. The Qarmatians, a radical Ismaili movement based in eastern Arabia, sacked Mecca during the pilgrimage season, killed pilgrims, and carried off the Black Stone to their capital. - 952 CE. The stone was returned, apparently in fragments, after more than twenty years. It had been broken, and later damage broke it further. - The fragments are held together in a silver casing, which has been renewed several times over the centuries. No one outside the tradition knows, and no sample has ever been analysed. Proposals include: - a stony meteorite, a popular idea because of the heavenly origin in tradition; - an impactite, glass formed by a meteorite striking sand. Some point to the Wabar craters in the Arabian desert; - basalt, agate or another terrestrial rock. Reported physical descriptions, for example claims that a fragment floated in water when it was recovered, are themselves traditions and cannot be tested. The question is open and likely to remain so. The hand of God. A tradition describes the stone as God's "right hand on earth", so that touching it is like pledging allegiance. This is metaphor within the tradition. It gives the gesture of touching or saluting the stone the meaning of covenant. Continuity with Abraham. Islam reads the Kaaba and its stone as restoring the monotheism of Abraham. The rites of the Hajj retrace events from the lives of Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael. The stone is part of a sacred geography that…

title: The Sacred Tooth Relic
summary: The Buddha's tooth, smuggled to Sri Lanka in a princess's hair according to the chronicle, carried in procession by elephants each year. For a thousand years it was the proof of a king's right to rule. The Portuguese claimed to have burned it in 1561.
text: Vault entry V27 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic), Kandy, Sri Lanka Every year in July or August, in the hill city of Kandy, a procession winds through the streets by night. Dozens of caparisoned elephants move among fire-dancers, drummers, whip-crackers and torch-bearers. On the back of the greatest elephant rides a casket, a replica container standing in for the relic itself, which stays in its temple. The festival is the Esala Perahera. It honours what is believed to be a tooth of the Buddha, the most sacred relic of Sri Lankan Buddhism and for centuries the sign of the right to rule the island. - Origin in tradition. Buddhist sources say that after the Buddha's cremation his relics were divided among kingdoms. A left canine tooth was kept at Kalinga in eastern India. - Arrival in Sri Lanka. According to the Pali chronicle Dāṭhāvaṃsa ("Chronicle of the Tooth") and related sources, the tooth was smuggled out of Kalinga in the fourth century CE, hidden in the hair of Princess Hemamala, who travelled with Prince Danta. It reached the capital Anuradhapura in the reign of King Kirti Sri Meghavarna. The account is traditional. Its details cannot be independently verified. - Relic and kingship. For more than a millennium the tooth moved with the royal capital. Possessing it legitimated a king. It came to Kandy with the last Sinhalese kingdom, and the present temple dates from the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries onward. - The Portuguese claim (1560–61). Portuguese chroniclers wrote that forces sent by the viceroy Constantino de Bragança captured the tooth in Jaffna in 1560 and destroyed it in Goa, grinding it and burning it publicly despite a huge ransom offer from the king of Pegu. Sinhalese tradition holds that the captured tooth was a replica, and that the true relic remained safe. Both claims come from interested parties. - 1998. Tamil Tiger (LTTE) militants detonated a truck bomb at the temple, killing sixteen or seventeen people (accounts vary) and damaging the building. The relic chamber was not reached. A relic as sovereignty. The tooth was the palladium of the kingdom: kings were expected to house it beside the palace and honour it publicly. That fusion of Buddhist devotion and royal legitimacy is documented across Sinhalese history. It persists in the relic's national importance today (ch49, Sacred Kingship). The relic that is rarely seen. The tooth itself is kept inside nested caskets shaped like stupas and is shown only rarely. What the public sees, and what the elephant carries in the Perahera, is the container. The sacred object is present but veiled, which heightens its power. Relics in Buddhism. Buddhist tradition distinguishes bodily relics (śarīra), objects used by the Buddha, and reminders such as images and texts. Venerating relics is a documented practice from the earliest centuries. It is continuous with the stupa cult described in the archive's Buddhism chapters (ch11, ch20, ch53). Buddhism (ch11, ch20), Tibetan Vajrayana (ch53), sacred kingship (ch49), and the relic traditions of the Vault: the True Cross (V15) and the Crown of Thorns (V06). What's well supported by…

title: The Birmingham Qur'an Manuscript
summary: Two parchment leaves in Hijazi script, recognised in 2015 inside a later manuscript and radiocarbon-dated to 568–645 CE. They belong with sixteen leaves in Paris. What a date for the animal's death can and cannot say about when the words were written.
text: Vault entry V28 · Manuscripts · Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham (Mingana Islamic Arabic 1572a) In 2015 a doctoral researcher, Alba Fedeli, was studying Qur'an fragments in the Mingana Collection at the University of Birmingham. She noticed that two leaves bound into one manuscript did not belong with the rest. Their script was different, and so was their parchment. They had been misbound with leaves of another early Qur'an. The university sent samples to the Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit. The answer came back 568–645 CE, at 95.4% probability. News reports around the world called them among the oldest Qur'an fragments known. - Two folios of parchment, written on both sides in Hijazi script. This early Arabic hand slopes to the right, leaves out vowel signs and marks only some of the dots that distinguish letters. - They carry parts of Sura 18 (al-Kahf, verses 17–31), the end of Sura 19 (Maryam, 91–98) and the start of Sura 20 (Ṭā Hā, 1–40). The text is in the order and wording of the standard text. - The leaves came to Birmingham with the manuscripts collected in the 1920s by Alphonse Mingana, a scholar from what is now Iraq. The collecting trips were funded by Edward Cadbury. Part of a book in Paris. Scholars soon recognised the Birmingham leaves as belonging to the same codex as sixteen leaves in Paris (Bibliothèque nationale de France, Arabe 328(c)). In December 2015 François Déroche endorsed the identification that Fedeli had proposed. The Birmingham leaves even fill a gap in the Paris text. The Paris leaves are generally held to come from the great store of old Qur'an copies at the Mosque of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ in Fustat (Old Cairo), from which a French vice-consul acquired manuscripts in the early nineteenth century. The date is real, but it measures one thing: when the animal whose skin became the parchment died. It does not say when the ink went onto the skin. Three limits follow: 1. The range is wide. 568–645 CE covers the whole traditional lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad (c. 570–632) and the years after, up to the caliphate of ʿUthmān. 2. Parchment could be stored. Writing usually followed soon after the skin was prepared, but not always. 3. Calibration has surprised before. Déroche pointed out that radiocarbon has sometimes given dates too early for Qur'an manuscripts whose dates are known from endowment notes. He also noted that the Paris leaves of the same codex had not been tested. So the result is consistent with the leaves being written within a few decades of the Prophet's death. It does not prove that they were written in his lifetime, as some headlines claimed. Nor does it show that the text existed before him, as some online arguments claimed. Islamic tradition holds that the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad and memorised and written down in his lifetime. It then holds that the third caliph, ʿUthmān (r. 644–656), had a single standard copy made and sent to the main cities. The Birmingham leaves follow that standard text, the one found in almost every Qur'an manuscript. For many Muslims they are a tangible sign of the text's preservation. For historians they are one of the early witnesses to how quickly…

title: The Sana'a Palimpsest
summary: A Qur'an codex written over an erased older Qur'an. Found in 1972 in the roof of the Great Mosque of Sana'a. The upper text follows the standard text; the lower text has different readings and a different order of suras. It is the only known witness to a non-ʿUthmānic Qur'an text, and scholars disagree about what that means.
text: Vault entry V29 · Manuscripts · Dar al-Makhtutat, Sana'a (DAM 01-27.1) In 1972 heavy rain brought down part of the Great Mosque of Sana'a, one of the oldest mosques in Yemen. Restorers working between the ceiling and the roof found a mass of old parchment and paper: thousands of fragments of worn-out Qur'an copies. They had been put there because a damaged copy of the Qur'an is not thrown away. From the 1980s a Yemeni–German project led by scholars including Gerd-R. Puin sorted and photographed the fragments. In 1981 one group of leaves was recognised as a palimpsest, a manuscript written over an earlier text that had been scraped or washed away. Under a Qur'an there was another Qur'an. - Ṣanʿāʾ 1, as scholars call it, has about 80 leaves in Sana'a, plus four leaves that left Yemen and were sold at auction in the West. - The upper text is a Qur'an that follows the standard ʿUthmānic text and the standard order of suras. - The lower text, the one erased, is also a Qur'an. It is not the standard text. Its wording often differs in small ways: different words, word order, extra or missing phrases. Its suras run in an order found in no known tradition, although the suras themselves are recognisably the same ones. - A radiocarbon test on one of the detached leaves, published by Behnam Sadeghi and Uwe Bergmann in 2010, dated its parchment, and so its lower text, to 578–669 CE at 95% probability. They reported a high probability of a date before about 646. In 2012 Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi published an edition of much of the lower text. They called it "at present the most important document for the history of the Qur'an" and argued that it is the only surviving copy of a textual tradition other than the ʿUthmānic. They linked it to the kind of Companion codices that Islamic sources say existed before ʿUthmān standardised the text, such as those attributed to Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, while noting that it matches neither exactly. Asma Hilali (2017, Oxford University Press / Institute of Ismaili Studies) published a new edition of both layers. She stressed signs that the lower text may have been a working or teaching copy rather than a finished codex. Éléonore Cellard (2021) studied how the leaves were made and assembled, and argued that the lower text was once part of a complete Qur'an codex. These readings are argued in the specialist literature and not settled. Parchment was expensive, and reusing it was common in the ancient and medieval world. Christian scribes did the same: St Catherine's Monastery, the home of the Codex Sinaiticus (V18), also yielded the famous Syriac Sinaiticus, a Gospel text under a later one. Scribes may have erased the lower text because it no longer matched the standard text that had become authoritative. They may simply have needed the parchment. The manuscript itself does not tell us which. Layers as history. A palimpsest is a physical record of change: one text, then another. Here the change runs from a non-standard to the standard text, the direction Islamic tradition describes when it tells of ʿUthmān's recension and the retirement of other copies. The paper grave. Worn copies of the Qur'an are not discarded.…

title: The Diamond Sutra of Dunhuang
summary: A five-metre scroll printed from woodblocks, found in a sealed cave library on the Silk Road and dated by its maker to 868. It is the oldest complete printed book that carries a date. Its text teaches that all conditioned things are like a dream.
text: Vault entry V30 · Manuscripts · British Library, London (Or.8210/P.2) Around 1900, a Daoist monk named Wang Yuanlu, who had made himself caretaker of the Mogao caves near Dunhuang, found a sealed doorway behind a painted wall. Behind it was a small chamber, now called Cave 17 or the Library Cave, packed from floor to ceiling with tens of thousands of manuscripts, paintings and prints. It had been walled up around the year 1000, and the reason is unknown. In 1907 the archaeologist Aurel Stein bought a large share of the collection from Wang. Among the rolls he took to London was a scroll about five metres long, printed from carved wooden blocks. At its end it gives the day it was made: 11 May 868. - Seven sheets of paper, printed from woodblocks and pasted into a scroll, with a frontispiece: the Buddha preaching to his elderly disciple Subhūti, surrounded by monks, attendants, guardians and two lions. - The text is the Diamond Sutra (Sanskrit Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā, "the Perfection of Wisdom that cuts like a thunderbolt/diamond"), in the Chinese translation by Kumārajīva (c. 402 CE). - The colophon reads: "Reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents on the 15th day of the 4th month of the 9th year of Xiantong." - It is not the oldest printing known. Printed charms and short texts survive from earlier, and a Buddhist dhāraṇī from Korea may be older. It is the oldest complete printed book that is dated, and its quality shows that printing was already a mature craft by 868. The Diamond Sutra is one of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) scriptures of Mahāyāna Buddhism. It is a dialogue in which the Buddha teaches Subhūti that a bodhisattva must work to free all beings while not holding on to any idea of self, of beings or of liberation. Its paradoxical sayings (a thing is taught to be "not X, therefore it is called X") train the reader to see that all phenomena are empty (śūnya) of fixed identity. Its closing verse, shown on the scroll above, compares all conditioned things to a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew and lightning. In East Asia it became one of the most recited and copied sutras, above all in Chan/Zen Buddhism. Tradition says the sixth patriarch Huineng was awakened on hearing a line of it. Wang Jie's colophon explains why the book was printed. In Mahāyāna Buddhism, copying, reciting and spreading a sutra earns great merit, and the Diamond Sutra itself says so. Merit could be dedicated to others, living or dead. Printing let one pious act make many copies, each "for universal free distribution". It was a devotional technology before it was a commercial one. Many of the Library Cave's manuscripts are sutra copies dedicated in the same way. The diamond (vajra). The vajra, both "diamond" and "thunderbolt", stands for wisdom that is indestructible and cuts through illusion. The same word names the ritual implement of Vajrayāna Buddhism. The frontispiece as teaching scene. The picture sets out the scene that opens the sutra, Subhūti kneeling before the Buddha, so that the reader enters the text as a member of the assembly. Emptiness in images. The dream, illusion, bubble…

title: The Dresden Codex
summary: The finest of the four Maya books that survived the Spanish conquest: a folding screen of bark paper, bought in Vienna in 1739 and damaged by water in 1945. Its tables track Venus, predict eclipse seasons, and bind both to the sacred 260-day count.
text: Vault entry V31 · Manuscripts · SLUB Dresden, Mscr.Dresd.R.310 In 1739 Johann Christian Götze, director of the Royal Library in Dresden, bought from a private owner in Vienna a folded strip of painted bark-paper, covered in pictures and signs no one in Europe could read. Nobody knows how it reached Vienna, though a gift sent to the Habsburg court after the conquest of Mexico is one guess. In February 1945, in the firebombing of Dresden, the vault where it was kept was flooded, and some pages were water-damaged. It survived. It is the finest of the four Maya books known to have outlasted the Spanish conquest, when friars burned such books as works of idolatry. - A screenfold: a long strip of fig-bark paper (huun) coated with fine lime plaster, folded like a fan into 39 leaves painted on both sides. It is about 3.5 metres long when unfolded. - Painted in red, black, blue and other colours by several scribes, in Maya hieroglyphs with bar-and-dot numerals and pictures of the gods. - Usually dated between the 11th and 14th centuries. It may be a copy of older material, and its date is debated. - The other three: the Madrid and Paris codices, and the Maya Codex of Mexico (formerly the Grolier Codex), whose authenticity was long disputed and was confirmed by Mexican authorities in 2018. - Almanacs for the 260-day ritual count (tzolkʼin), giving the gods and omens for days, in fields such as medicine, farming, weaving and marriage. - The Venus table (pages 24 and 46–50). It follows the 584-day cycle of Venus through five appearances, which add up to eight 365-day years. It repeats until the three counts, of Venus, the 260-day count and the 365-day year, all come back into step after 104 years. The table divides each cycle into 236 days as morning star, 90 hidden, 250 as evening star and 8 hidden. These are canonical numbers, chosen to make the calendar work, not direct observations. - The eclipse table (pages 51–58). It lists 405 lunar months, about 33 years, grouped to mark the seasons when eclipses were possible. - Rain and the Chaak gods, new-year ceremonies, and a closing page showing a flood pouring from the sky and from the mouth of a celestial caiman. It has been read as a world-destruction scene, and that reading is debated. The German librarian Ernst Förstemann worked out in the 1880s how the codex's numbers and calendars ran, and identified the Venus table, decades before the glyphs themselves could be read. The decipherment of Maya writing as a logo-syllabic script, largely after the 1950s, now lets most of its texts be read. The Venus pages do more than count. Each first rising of Venus as morning star is paired with a picture of an armed god spearing a victim, such as a jaguar or the maize god. Maya belief held that the planet's heliacal rising was dangerous, and the table told priests when to expect the danger and whom it would strike. It is astronomy in the service of divination, as it was across the ancient world. Bar, dot and shell. Maya numbers are written with dots for one, bars for five and a shell for zero, stacked in places of increasing value. In calendar counts the third place is worth 360 instead of 400, to approach the solar…

title: The Popol Vuh Manuscript
summary: The K'iche' Maya book of creation, the Hero Twins and the lords of Xibalba, which survives only because a Dominican friar in Chichicastenango copied it around 1701, K'iche' beside Spanish. The alphabetic original, written by K'iche' nobles after the conquest, is lost.
text: Vault entry V32 · Manuscripts · The Newberry Library, Chicago (Ayer MS 1515) Around 1701, a Dominican friar named Francisco Ximénez (born 1666) was parish priest of Santo Tomás Chichicastenango in the Guatemalan highlands. There he saw a book written in K'iche', the Maya language of his parishioners, in the Latin alphabet. He copied it in two columns, K'iche' on the left and Spanish on the right, into a volume of his own writings on the language and on Christian doctrine. The book he copied is lost. His copy is now in Chicago, and it is the only reason the K'iche' creation epic survives. - Ximénez's copy, made between about 1700 and 1715, bound with his K'iche'–Kaqchikel–Tz'utujil grammar and other works. It is catalogued as Ayer MS 1515 at the Newberry Library. - The lost original was written in the mid-sixteenth century, commonly dated c. 1554–1558, by K'iche' nobles of the old capital Q'umarkaj, after the Spanish conquest of 1524. They say why: they are writing now "amid the preaching of God, in Christendom", because the ancient book can no longer be seen. The phrasing here follows the sense of the standard English translations. - They also say there had been an older book (popol wuj, "council book"). Whether it was a hieroglyphic codex like the Dresden Codex (V31) or a tradition in painted and spoken form is not known. - The manuscript was found in the library of the University of San Carlos in Guatemala City by the Austrian Carl Scherzer, who published it in 1857. The French abbé Brasseur de Bourbourg published it with a French translation in 1861 and took the manuscript to France. It passed through the collector Alphonse Pinart to Edward E. Ayer, who gave his collection to the Newberry. The making of the world. In the beginning there is only sea and sky, still and silent. The creator gods, Tepew and Q'ukumatz (the "Sovereign Plumed Serpent") with Juraqan ("Heart of Sky"), bring forth the earth by speaking: "Earth", they say, and it arises. Three failed peoples. The gods want beings who will speak their names and keep their days. They make animals, which can only howl. They make people of mud, who dissolve. They make people of wood, who speak but have no hearts or memory of their makers; these are destroyed by a flood and a rain of resin, and their survivors become the monkeys. The Hero Twins. Before the dawn of the present world, the twins Junajpu (Hunahpu) and Xb'alanke (Xbalanque) defeat the vain bird-god Seven Macaw and his sons. They are summoned to Xib'alb'a, the underworld, as their father and uncle were before them. They pass the lords' trials of the Dark House, the Razor House, the Cold House, the Jaguar House, the Fire House and the Bat House, play the ballgame against death, allow themselves to be burned and ground to powder, return as wandering performers and defeat the lords of death. They rise as the sun and moon. People of maize. At last the gods grind yellow and white maize and make the first four men from it. These people see and understand too much, so the gods cloud their sight "as breath clouds a mirror". The book ends with the history of the K'iche' lineages down to the time of writing. Maize as flesh. Human bodies…

title: The Kartarpur Bir
summary: The volume that Sikh tradition holds is the first Adi Granth, compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 with Bhai Gurdas as scribe. It was kept by a rival claimant to the Guruship, and scholars have seldom been allowed to see it. Its authority is revered, and its text history is debated.
text: Vault entry V33 · Manuscripts · The Sodhi family, Kartarpur, Punjab In 1604, Sikh tradition holds, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, completed a great anthology of hymns. It gathered the compositions of the first five Gurus with those of Hindu and Muslim devotional poets such as Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and the Sufi Shaikh Farid. The scribe was the Guru's relative and follower Bhai Gurdas. The volume, the Adi Granth, was installed in the newly built Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar. A century later the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, ended the line of human Gurus and declared the scripture, as Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru for all time. A manuscript that Sikh tradition identifies as that first 1604 volume is kept today, privately, in the town of Kartarpur. It is the Kartarpur Bir. - After Guru Arjan, the volume passed to the family of Dhir Mal, a grandson of the sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind. Dhir Mal claimed the Guruship himself and held the book as a sign of his claim. - Sikh sources tell that followers of the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, seized it, and that the Guru ordered it returned. It stayed with Dhir Mal's Sodhi descendants at Kartarpur. - It later passed to Maharaja Ranjit Singh (d. 1839), who kept it at Lahore. After the British annexation of the Punjab it was returned in 1850 to Sodhi Sadhu Singh of Kartarpur on his petition, and it has stayed with the family. - It is shown to the public on special occasions. Scholarly access has been rare: the most famous examination was by Bhai Jodh Singh, who described it page by page in Sri Kartarpuri Bir de Darshan (1968). The Adi Granth did not arise from nothing. The Goindval pothis (also called the Mohan pothis), compiled under the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, in the 1570s, already collected hymns of the Gurus and the bhagats, and scholars such as Gurinder Singh Mann have shown how Guru Arjan built on them. The Kartarpur Bir is the key witness to the 1604 stage. The text that Sikhs use today follows the Damdami Bir, the recension traditionally associated with Guru Gobind Singh at Damdama Sahib (c. 1706). That recension adds the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Other early manuscripts, such as the Banno Bir, differ at points, and their relationship to the Kartarpur volume has been argued for more than a century. In 1991 Pashaura Singh submitted a doctoral thesis at the University of Toronto, The Text and Meaning of the Adi Granth, supervised by W. H. McLeod. It compared early manuscripts to trace how Guru Arjan edited the text. Some Sikh critics read the work as questioning the scripture's integrity. In 1994 Pashaura Singh was summoned before the Akal Takht, the highest seat of Sikh religious authority, where he submitted a statement and undertook to revise his work. The affair became a lasting debate about academic study of a living scripture and about who has the authority to examine it. The Kartarpur Bir itself is at the centre of this. Its supporters regard it as the authentic original written under the Guru's supervision. Critics and some historians have asked how the text of the Kartarpur volume relates to the Banno Bir and other copies, and whether the whole of it dates from 1604. The debate is limited by…

title: The Pyramid Texts of Unas
summary: The oldest large body of religious writing in the world: 283 spells carved and painted blue on the walls of a king's burial chambers under a ceiling of stars. They were meant for no living reader, and were found in 1881. They include the notorious 'Cannibal Hymn'.
text: Vault entry V34 · Texts & Tablets · In place: the Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara In 1880 workmen of Egypt's Antiquities Service broke into a ruined pyramid at Saqqara, the pyramid of the Sixth-Dynasty king Pepi I. They found its inner walls covered in columns of hieroglyphs. Auguste Mariette, the head of the service, was dying and doubted the report: no Old Kingdom pyramid had ever been found inscribed. His successor, Gaston Maspero, pressed on. In 1881 he entered the smaller, older pyramid of Unas, last king of the Fifth Dynasty (c. 2350 BCE). From floor to ceiling its chambers were carved with spells, the signs filled with blue pigment. Above them, on the gabled ceiling, were carved stars. It is the oldest large body of religious writing known from anywhere in the world. - 283 spells (called utterances in older scholarship) in the pyramid of Unas. Later pyramids of the Sixth Dynasty kings and some queens add others, giving a corpus of about 800. - They cover the burial chamber, the antechamber and the corridor: the route the king's spirit (ba) was believed to take from the sarcophagus out towards the sky. - They were written for no living reader: sealed inside the pyramid, they worked by being there, in the belief that written words, like spoken ones, acted. - They were published by Maspero from 1882 and edited by Kurt Sethe (1908–1922), whose spell numbers are still used. Standard English translations are by R. O. Faulkner (1969) and James P. Allen (2005). Deny death. "You have not gone away dead: you have gone away alive" (Utterance 213) opens the burial-chamber texts. The king becomes Osiris, the god who died and lives again, and at the same time joins the sun-god Ra in his daily journey. Feed the dead. An offering ritual lists bread, beer, linen and ointment with a spoken formula for each, so that the king would be provided for for ever, even if the priests stopped coming. Protect. Among the oldest spells are short charms against snakes, scorpions and other dangers, some in language that was already archaic. Ascend. The king climbs to the sky by a ladder, rises on smoke, or flies up on wings as a bird, to join the "imperishable stars", the circumpolar stars that never set. The "Cannibal Hymn." In Utterances 273–274 the sky is darkened and the stars tremble as the king appears as a hunter who catches, cooks and eats the gods, "their magic in his belly", and so takes in their power. It shocked early Egyptologists. It is now read as a ritual image of royal supremacy, drawing on the language of sacrifice and butchery, not as evidence of real cannibalism. Writing that could hurt. In some Pyramid Texts, hieroglyphs of dangerous creatures, such as snakes, scorpions and lions, are cut in half or drawn without legs, so that the signs themselves could not come alive and harm the king. This is some of the clearest evidence for the belief that hieroglyphs were living images (see Egypt, ch02). Blue and stars. The signs were filled with blue, the colour of the sky and of the waters of creation, and the ceilings were carved with five-pointed stars, making the burial chamber an image of the night sky the king would enter. The cartouche. The king's name Unas…

title: The Cyrus Cylinder
summary: A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. It praises Cyrus as Marduk's chosen king and records the return of gods and peoples to their homes. It is often called the first charter of human rights, which it is not, and it is read beside the Bible's decree of Cyrus.
text: Vault entry V35 · Texts & Tablets · British Museum, London (BM 90920) In 1879 the archaeologist Hormuzd Rassam, digging for the British Museum at Babylon, recovered a barrel-shaped cylinder of baked clay about 23 centimetres long, broken and incomplete. It was covered in Babylonian cuneiform. It came from the ruins of Marduk's great temple, the Esagila, and was made as a foundation deposit: Mesopotamian kings buried building inscriptions for the gods and for future rulers to find. Its speaker was Cyrus the Great, the Persian king who had taken Babylon in 539 BCE. The text is written in Akkadian in the traditional style of Babylonian royal inscriptions, by Babylonian scribes and for a Babylonian audience. - The fall of Nabonidus. It opens by condemning Nabonidus, the last native king of Babylon, for neglecting the worship of Marduk, the city's god, and for oppressing its people. - Marduk chooses Cyrus. Marduk searches the lands for a just ruler, takes Cyrus by the hand, calls his name, and sends him to Babylon, which he enters "without battle". - "I am Cyrus." In line 20 Cyrus speaks in the first person, with the traditional titles of Mesopotamian kingship: king of the universe, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters. He traces his descent from his forefathers, kings of Anshan. - The return of gods and peoples. Cyrus says he returned the statues of gods to their sanctuaries in several cities, and gathered their people and returned them to their homes. - Building work. It ends with Cyrus's repair of Babylon's walls and a mention that he saw an inscription of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, an earlier restorer. It is not unique. In 2010 Irving Finkel of the British Museum identified two fragments of clay tablets in the museum's collection carrying parts of the same text. The proclamation was copied and circulated, not only buried. The Hebrew Bible remembers Cyrus warmly. Ezra 1:1–4 and 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 quote a decree allowing the exiled Judeans to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple. Isaiah 44:28–45:1 calls Cyrus the Lord's "anointed" (mashiach), the only non-Israelite given that title. The cylinder does not mention Judah, Jerusalem or the Jews. What it shows is a policy: a new king presenting himself as the restorer of local gods and displaced peoples. The biblical decree fits that policy, and many historians think the return of Judean exiles was part of it. The cylinder does not confirm the biblical decree as written, and it does not contradict it. In 1971 the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, celebrated 2,500 years of Persian monarchy and promoted the cylinder as the first declaration of human rights. A replica was presented to the United Nations, where it stands at the headquarters in New York. Invented "translations" circulate online, with articles on freedom of religion, abolition of slavery and choice of occupation that appear nowhere on the cylinder. Historians agree that the cylinder is royal propaganda in a Mesopotamian tradition. Its claims of restoration are the claims earlier Assyrian and Babylonian kings made about themselves. Calling it a human-rights charter is anachronistic: the…

title: The Rök Runestone
summary: A granite slab carrying the longest runic inscription in the world, some 760 runes, raised by a father for his dead son. It is full of riddles and written partly in cipher, and it names Theodoric the Great. No two scholars read it quite the same way.
text: Vault entry V36 · Texts & Tablets · Rök, Östergötland, Sweden (Ög 136) For centuries the stone lay built into the wall of a storehouse beside the church at Rök, in the plains of Östergötland in southern Sweden, its carved faces partly hidden. In 1843 workers found carving on more sides than the one they could see; in 1862 it was taken out of the wall and set up in the churchyard. It is a granite slab about 2.4 metres high, covered on five faces with some 760 runes. It is the longest runic inscription in the world. Carved in the early ninth century, it begins plainly: In memory of Vámóðr stand these runes. And Varinn coloured them, the father, in memory of his dead son. What follows is anything but plain. After the dedication the inscription turns to a series of questions and answers, framed with the formula sagum mogminni, roughly "I tell the folk-memory" or "I say to the young men". It asks which "two war-booties" were taken twelve times, and who died among whom. It names heroes of legend, including a stanza on Theodoric: Theodoric the bold, chief of sea-warriors, ruled over the shores of the Hreiðsea. Now he sits armed on his Gothic horse, his shield strapped, the prince of the Mærings. Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths in Italy (d. 526), had lived three centuries before the stone. A famous equestrian statue of him, taken from Ravenna to Aachen by Charlemagne in 801, may be the image behind "sits armed on his Gothic horse". This is a proposal, not a certainty. The stanza is in fornyrðislag, the metre of Old Norse eddic poetry, so it is also among the earliest recorded Scandinavian verse. Parts of the inscription are written in cryptographic runes. Among them: - Substitution: each rune is replaced by the next rune in the futhark. - Coordinate (cipher) runes: a rune's position is given as "family" and number within the three groups (ættir) of the futhark, marked as strokes on the branches of a stem. - Older runes: some passages are written in the elder futhark, already archaic by the ninth century. The ciphers are deciphered, and there is broad agreement on which rune is which. The difficulty is what the text means and in what order to read it. For much of the twentieth century the dominant reading, following Elias Wessén, saw the stone as a heroic memorial full of legendary lore, meant to inspire vengeance for the dead son. In 2020, Per Holmberg, Bo Gräslund, Olof Sundqvist and Henrik Williams published a new interpretation in Futhark, "The Rök Runestone and the End of the World". They read the riddles as being about the sun and a great cold, and linked them to fear of a climate catastrophe like the dark years after the volcanic eruptions of 536 CE, remembered as a "Fimbulwinter". In their reading the grieving father finds hope that his son will fight beside Odin at Ragnarök, after which the light returns. The interpretation drew wide attention and criticism, and runologists continue to debate it. Colouring the runes. Varinn says he "coloured" (fāði) the runes. Runestones were painted, often in red and black, and traces of paint survive on some stones. Runes and secrecy. The word rún also means "secret" or "mystery" in Germanic…

title: The Gundestrup Cauldron
summary: Nine kilograms of gilded silver, taken apart and laid in a Danish bog. Its plates show an antlered figure holding a torc and a serpent, a giant dipping a man into a vat, and a bull sacrifice. Probably made far to the south-east. Celtic gods, Thracian silversmiths, or both?
text: Vault entry V37 · Relics & Objects · National Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen On 28 May 1891 peat-cutters in a small bog called Rævemose, near Gundestrup in the north of Jutland, struck metal. Under the peat lay a great silver bowl, and stacked inside it a set of silver plates crowded with gods, beasts and warriors. Someone had taken the cauldron apart before it was laid in the bog, placing the rim and the decorated plates in the bottom of the bowl. It is the largest known piece of European Iron Age silverwork. - About 69 cm across and 42 cm high, weighing almost 9 kg, of silver, gilded in places. It is made of 13 plates: five inner plates, seven outer plates (an eighth is missing), and a round base medallion, fitted to a plain curved bowl. - It was made by several silversmiths, working by repoussé (hammering from behind). The busts' eyes once held glass. - Most specialists date it between about 150 BCE and the early first century CE, the pre-Roman Iron Age. Inside are the famous scenes. An antlered figure sits cross-legged holding a torc and a ram-horned serpent, among stags and other animals. A bearded god holds a wheel. A goddess appears between wheels, with elephants and griffins. Three bulls face men with swords. On the most discussed plate, foot-soldiers with long carnyx war-horns march in one direction while horsemen ride above them in the other, and a giant figure holds a man head-down over a vat. Outside, great busts of gods and goddesses grasp smaller human figures and animals. At the bottom of the bowl, a bull collapses beneath a figure with a sword. Almost everything about the cauldron's origin is argued. - Celtic elements: the torcs, the carnyx horns, the helmets and the shield types match finds from the Celtic world. The antlered figure closely resembles the god named Cernunnos on a Gaulish monument from Paris, the Pillar of the Boatmen. Scholars such as Garrett Olmsted read the scenes as Gaulish myth. - Thracian workmanship: the silversmithing techniques, the style of the animals, and the elephants and griffins point to the lower Danube, in modern Bulgaria and Romania, where Thracian silverwork flourished. Timothy Taylor and others argued that Thracian smiths made it, perhaps for Celtic patrons. - How it reached Denmark is unknown: as booty, a gift, a trade good, or carried by migrating peoples such as the Cimbri, who came from Jutland and raided southwards in the late second century BCE. Most scholars now see it as the product of contact, a Thracian-style object bearing Celtic imagery, and do not think it has to be one or the other. The antlered god. The seated figure with antlers is the best-known image of what is called Cernunnos. The name comes from one damaged inscription, and whether the cauldron's figure bore it is not known. The torc and serpent recur with antlered figures in Gaulish art. The vat. The scene of a man held over a vat has been read as human sacrifice by drowning, which a later Roman scholium on Lucan links to the god Teutates. It has also been read as a cauldron of rebirth, like the one in the Welsh Mabinogion that brings dead warriors back to life. Both are modern readings of an image without text.…

title: The Aleppo Codex
summary: The 'Crown of Aleppo': the model Hebrew Bible whose vowels and accents were added by the master Masorete Aaron ben Asher, and which Maimonides called the text everyone relied on. Kept for six centuries in Aleppo's great synagogue, damaged in the riots of 1947, and brought to Israel with about 40% of its leaves missing, most of the Torah among them.
text: Vault entry V38 · Manuscripts · The Israel Museum, Jerusalem In December 1947, days after the United Nations voted to partition Palestine, rioters in Aleppo set fire to the city's ancient Central Synagogue. In a locked iron chest in a side chamber lay the community's greatest treasure, a Bible its keepers called Keter Aram Tsova, the Crown of Aleppo. When the fires died down, the manuscript had survived, but scattered and damaged. For ten years it was hidden. In 1958 it was smuggled to Jerusalem. By then about 40% of its leaves were missing, among them almost all of the Torah. Only a few stray leaves have come to light since. - A parchment codex written around 930 CE in Tiberias, then the centre of Hebrew textual scholarship. It is not a scroll: it has pages, as a study book, not for reading in synagogue. - The consonantal text was copied by the scribe Shlomo ben Buya'a. The vowel signs, cantillation accents and marginal notes (the Masorah) were added by Aaron ben Asher, the most renowned of the Masoretes, the families of scholars who fixed the pronunciation and reading of the Bible. - Originally about 480 leaves; about 295 survive. The surviving text begins in Deuteronomy 28. - Its journey: from Tiberias to Jerusalem, where the Karaite community held it. It was taken in the Crusader capture of 1099 and ransomed. It went to Cairo, and by the late fourteenth century to Aleppo, where it stayed for some 600 years. In the twelfth century Moses Maimonides, in Egypt, used a Bible "known in Egypt" corrected by Ben Asher, which "everyone relied upon", to set the rules for how a Torah scroll's open and closed sections should be laid out. Most scholars identify that book with the Aleppo Codex. That endorsement made it the model for the Masoretic text. It is why the loss of its Torah pages is felt so keenly: they would have shown exactly the text that Maimonides saw. What happened to the missing 40% is still argued over. Some leaves were surely burned in 1947. But a few leaves and fragments have surfaced in private hands, and journalists and scholars have asked whether the damage was all from the fire, or whether pages were taken in the years of hiding and transit. The book's own custody, from the Aleppo community to the Ben-Zvi Institute in Jerusalem, led to a legal dispute over ownership and, decades later, to investigative reporting. The facts about who held which pages, and when, remain disputed. Signs added to a fixed text. The Hebrew Bible was written in consonants only. The Masoretes did not change a letter. They added dots and dashes above and below the letters for vowels, and accent marks that show how each verse is chanted and where it breaks. The interactive text above lets you remove the vowel signs to see the consonantal text they were fitted around. The Masorah as guardian. In the margins, tiny notes count words and letters and flag unusual spellings: "this form occurs three times". They are a checksum in manuscript form, meant to stop copyists from introducing errors. The "Crown". Calling the manuscript a keter, a crown, marked it as the community's glory. The community believed that its presence protected Aleppo's Jews and that curses…

title: The Derveni Papyrus
summary: A papyrus roll half-burned on a funeral pyre near Thessaloniki, the oldest surviving book in Europe. It is a philosopher's allegorical commentary on a secret Orphic poem about the birth of the gods, which opens by telling the uninitiated to shut the doors.
text: Vault entry V39 · Manuscripts · Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki On 15 January 1962, road-workers widening the highway from Thessaloniki to Kavala uncovered a group of rich Macedonian cist tombs at Derveni, about 10 km north of the city. On the covering slabs of the tomb labelled A lay the remains of a funeral pyre, and in the ash a charred lump of papyrus. Papyrus does not survive in Greece's damp soil. This roll survived because the fire had turned it to carbon without consuming it. It is the oldest surviving book in Europe. - Only the upper part survives, the rest burned away. Conservators separated the lump into 266 fragments, which scholars have arranged into 26 columns. - The roll itself is dated to c. 340–320 BCE, in the time of Philip II and Alexander. The text it carries was composed earlier, around 400 BCE. - The official edition appeared only in 2006 (Kouremenos, Parássoglou and Tsantsanoglou), 44 years after the find. New readings, many from multispectral imaging, have continued since. - In 2015 it became the first Greek item on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. The author is unknown. Proposals include Euthyphron, Prodicus and Diagoras, and none is accepted. He writes in the tradition of the natural philosophers, especially Anaxagoras, and his book has two parts: 1. Columns I–VI discuss ritual: the Erinyes (Furies), the souls of the dead, daimones, and offerings made by magoi and initiates, including libations and birds. 2. Columns VII–XXVI are a line-by-line allegorical commentary on a theogony attributed to Orpheus. In the poem, Night advises, Kronos acts, Zeus swallows the phallus (or, in some readings, the body) of Ouranos, becomes the beginning, middle and end of all things, and then brings the world forth again. The commentator insists that the poem's shocking images are riddles for physics: "Zeus" is air or Mind, and the swallowing is a cosmic process. He also quotes Heraclitus ("the sun, the breadth of a human foot"), the oldest surviving copy of that philosopher's words. "Orphic" writings claimed the authority of the mythical singer Orpheus. They were used by wandering initiators who promised purification and a better lot after death. The Derveni author criticises people who undergo initiation without understanding it. His book shows that by c. 400 BCE Orphic poetry was already being read allegorically, like a scripture needing interpretation. The gold tablets found in graves from southern Italy to Thessaly, which instruct the dead soul on the path in the underworld, belong to the same religious world. "Shut the doors, you uninitiated." The poem opened with a formula of secrecy, known from later writers and partly preserved here. Sacred words were for those "for whom it is lawful". Ironically, the only reason we have them is that someone burned the book at a funeral. Allegory as decoding. The commentator treats the poem as a code: every god-name and act stands for something physical. It is one of the earliest surviving examples of allegorical interpretation of a sacred text, the method later used on Homer, on the Bible by Philo, and by Christian and Jewish exegetes. Burned for the dead. Why was a book burned on…

title: The Gospel of Judas (Codex Tchacos)
summary: A Gnostic gospel that the church father Irenaeus denounced around 180 and that was then lost for 1,700 years. It surfaced in a Coptic papyrus codex dug up in Middle Egypt, which rotted for years in a New York bank vault. Unveiled in 2006 as the story of a heroic Judas, a reading many specialists quickly disputed.
text: Vault entry V40 · Manuscripts · Coptic Museum, Cairo (Codex Tchacos) Around 180 CE, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, listed the books of groups he called heretics. One group, he wrote, honoured Cain and the men of Sodom, and "they produce a fictitious history of this kind, which they style the Gospel of Judas." For 1,800 years that one sentence was all that was known of it. Then, in the 1970s, a leather-bound papyrus codex in Coptic was found, probably in a burial cave near al-Minya in Middle Egypt. On its pages, after a letter of Peter and a text about James, was a work ending with the words "The Gospel of Judas." - Dealers took it out of Egypt. Offered for sale in 1983 for a huge price and unsold, it spent sixteen years in a safe-deposit box in Hicksville, New York, where damp and heat crumbled it. - In 2000 the Zurich dealer Frieda Tchacos Nussberger bought it and named it Codex Tchacos after her father. After another failed sale it was placed with the Maecenas Foundation, which partnered with the National Geographic Society to conserve and publish it. The codex was to be returned to Egypt, and is now in the Coptic Museum. - Restorers reassembled about a thousand fragments. Radiocarbon dating by the University of Arizona placed the codex between 220 and 340 CE. Ink analysis was consistent with antiquity. - The Gospel is a Coptic translation of a Greek original, most likely the one Irenaeus knew, so written before c. 180. The text is a dialogue. Over a week before Passover, Jesus laughs at the disciples' piety, telling them they worship a lesser god. He takes Judas aside and reveals the mysteries of the kingdom: an unseen realm, a great invisible Spirit, luminous aeons, and below them rulers such as Nebro/Yaldabaoth and Saklas who made this world. It is the cosmology of Sethian Gnosticism. It ends abruptly with Judas taking money and handing Jesus over. On 6 April 2006 National Geographic unveiled the text, in a television documentary and a book, as the story of a good Judas, the only disciple who understood Jesus, acting on his instructions in betraying him. Almost at once specialists challenged it. April DeConick of Rice University, in The Thirteenth Apostle (2007) and in The New York Times, argued that the team had made crucial choices in the most flattering direction: - daimōn, which in early Christian texts normally means demon, was rendered "spirit", so "thirteenth demon" became "thirteenth spirit". - A line saying Judas would not ascend to the holy generation was read as saying he would. - "You will exceed them all" was read as praise. DeConick and others read it as saying Judas would do the worst deed of all. Other scholars, including members of the original team, defended parts of their reading. A newly surfaced fragment later helped settle some readings and not others. Most specialists now see Judas in this text as a tragic or demonic figure, not a hero, although the question remains debated. Thirteen. Judas is the thirteenth, set apart from the Twelve. In Sethian cosmology the thirteenth aeon is the realm of the lower ruler, so the number may place Judas with the world-maker, not with the divine. Laughter. Jesus' laughter, a motif in…

title: The Codex Borgia
summary: A painted screenfold of deerskin from the Puebla–Tlaxcala region of Mexico, among the very few divinatory books to survive the conquest. It is a manual of the 260-day count, with gods, omens, a Venus almanac and a mysterious central section that may describe a journey through the night.
text: Vault entry V41 · Manuscripts · Vatican Apostolic Library (Borg.mess.1) In 1805 the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, in Rome, examined the collections of the late Cardinal Stefano Borgia, a passionate collector of antiquities from every continent. Among them was a long strip of deerskin, folded like a screen and painted on both sides with gods, day-signs, numbers and brilliantly coloured scenes. How it came to Italy from Mexico is unknown. Humboldt published pages from it. When the cardinal's collection went to the Vatican, the book went with it and took his name. It is one of the very few religious books from central Mexico to survive the Spanish conquest. - A screenfold of fourteen pieces of deerskin joined into a strip over 10 metres long, coated with white gesso and folded into 39 leaves. It is painted on both sides, making 76 pages (the end panels are unpainted). - Painted with mineral and plant colours in the Mixteca-Puebla style, probably in the Puebla–Tlaxcala region. - Dated to the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century, most likely just before the conquest. - It belongs to the Borgia Group, a set of related divinatory books that also includes the Codex Vaticanus B, the Codex Cospi, the Codex Fejérváry-Mayer and the Codex Laud. The book is built on the tonalpohualli, "the count of days": 260 days, made by combining the numbers 1 to 13 with twenty named day-signs, from Crocodile to Flower. Priest-diviners (tonalpouhque) used books like this to read a person's fate from their birth-day, and to choose good days for marriages, journeys, planting and war. The Borgia sets out the count in many ways: - The twenty trecenas (thirteen-day periods), each with its presiding gods. - The days divided among the four directions and the world-trees. - The nine Lords of the Night and the thirteen birds. - A Venus almanac (pages 53–54) on the dangerous first appearance of the morning star, the same concern as the Dresden Codex (V31). Pages 29–46 break the pattern. They show a continuous series of scenes that are not a calendar table: dark, night-time spaces, the wind god Quetzalcoatl-Ehecatl, deities emerging from a body of night, fire, sacrifice and rebirth. Interpretations include: - a ritual journey of a priest or a god through the underworld and the night sky; - an account of Venus in its hidden phase; - a sequence of temple ceremonies in the order they were performed. These are serious proposals, and none is proven. The section is often called the most enigmatic group of pages in Mesoamerican art. Signs as beings. Each day-sign (Crocodile, Wind, House, Lizard, Serpent, Death and the rest) is a living power with its own gods, directions and colours. A day's name is its character. The body and the calendar. One page sets the twenty day-signs on the body of a god, each sign tied to a part of the body. It shows that time, the cosmos and the person were read as one system. Colour and direction. Red, black, yellow, blue-green and white are tied to the four directions and the centre, a cosmic map painted in pigment. The Aztec (ch43), the Maya (ch29), Creation & the First Order (ch46) and Sacrifice & the Scapegoat (ch51). Compare the Dresden Codex…

title: The Lindisfarne Gospels
summary: The four Gospels made on Holy Island in honour of St Cuthbert, probably by one man, Bishop Eadfrith. Two centuries later the priest Aldred wrote a word-by-word Old English translation between the lines, the oldest surviving English version of the Gospels, and a colophon naming the book's makers.
text: Vault entry V42 · Manuscripts · British Library, London (Cotton MS Nero D IV) In 687 Cuthbert, monk, hermit and bishop, died on the rocky islet of Inner Farne. He was buried at the monastery of Lindisfarne, the Holy Island off the Northumbrian coast. In 698 his coffin was opened and his body was found, it was said, incorrupt, and his cult took hold. Around the same years, a monk of Lindisfarne began one of the most ambitious books ever made in early medieval Europe: the four Gospels, written and painted in honour of God and St Cuthbert. Two hundred and fifty years later another member of the community wrote in the back of the book who had made it. - 259 leaves of vellum, made around 715–720, containing the four Gospels in Latin (Jerome's Vulgate), with prefaces and canon tables, the concordance of parallel passages. - Each Gospel opens with an evangelist portrait, a carpet page of pure ornament built on a cross, and a great decorated initial page. Matthew's account of Christ's birth has a Chi-Rho page. - It was probably written and painted by one person, a feat of concentration that took years. That person is traditionally Eadfrith, bishop of Lindisfarne (698–721). - Its pigments came from local minerals and plants, with some that may have been traded from afar. Modern analysis has argued that fewer exotic imports were used than once thought. In the mid-tenth century the community, driven from Lindisfarne by Viking raids, was settled at Chester-le-Street, carrying Cuthbert's body and the book. There a priest named Aldred did two things: 1. He wrote an interlinear gloss: an Old English translation of the Latin, word by word, in small letters between the lines. It is the oldest surviving English version of the Gospels, and a major source for the Northumbrian dialect of Old English. 2. He added a colophon naming the book's makers: Eadfrith wrote it, Æthelwald bound it, Billfrith the anchorite made its jewelled cover, and Aldred glossed it. Aldred wrote about 250 years after the book was made, and scholars take his colophon seriously but not as certain. It may record community tradition rather than documents. The book travelled with Cuthbert's relics to Chester-le-Street and then to Durham. It was removed from Durham at the dissolution of the monasteries in the sixteenth century, its jewelled cover lost, and entered the collection of Sir Robert Cotton, which passed to the nation and then to the British Library. In the north-east of England there have been repeated calls for its return, and it has gone back to Durham and Newcastle for exhibitions. The carpet page as cross. Each carpet page hides a cross within dense interlace. The eye has to find the cross in the knotwork, an act often compared to prayer or meditation. The evangelists' symbols. A man (angel) for Matthew, a lion for Mark, an ox (calf) for Luke, an eagle for John, from Ezekiel and Revelation. Matthew's portrait is labelled in Greek letters, O AGIOS MATHEUS, "Saint Matthew", a mark of learned devotion. The book as relic. Made for Cuthbert and kept with his body, the Gospels were a contact relic and a treasure of the saint's shrine as well as a text. Early Christianity (ch16)…

title: The Merneptah Stele
summary: A pharaoh's granite hymn of victory, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896. Of its 28 lines, one names Israel, about 3,200 years ago, the earliest certain mention of Israel anywhere. The hieroglyphs say something precise about what Israel was.
text: Vault entry V43 · Texts & Tablets · Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 31408) In 1896 Flinders Petrie was digging in the ruined mortuary temple of the pharaoh Merneptah at Thebes. He found a black granite stele over three metres tall, lying face-down. One side carried an inscription of the earlier king Amenhotep III. Merneptah, the thirteenth son and successor of Ramesses II, had taken the stone and carved his own text on the back. An epigrapher, Wilhelm Spiegelberg, read it for Petrie on the spot. Near the end he came to a name he did not expect. Petrie is said to have told his colleagues that evening that this stele would be better known than anything else he had found. The name was Israel. - 28 lines in hieroglyphs, dated to Merneptah's fifth year, about 1208 BCE. - Almost all of it celebrates his victory over the Libyans and their allies, the "Sea Peoples", who invaded Egypt's western Delta. - The last lines turn to Canaan: "Canaan is plundered… Ashkelon is carried off; Gezer is seized; Yenoam is made as though it never was; Israel is laid waste, his seed is not; Kharu has become a widow for Egypt." - "His seed is not" is standard Egyptian boasting. It may mean offspring or grain, and it claims destruction, not a fact of extinction. Egyptian writing adds determinatives: silent signs that say what kind of thing a word is. Canaan, Ashkelon, Gezer and Yenoam are written with the sign for a foreign land or city. Israel is written instead with the signs for a people: a throw-stick, a man and a woman, and plural strokes. Most scholars read this to mean that around 1208 BCE "Israel" was a group of people in Canaan, significant enough for Pharaoh to name, but not a state with a fixed territory or city. This fits the archaeology of the central highlands, where small villages multiply from about 1200 BCE. How far the scribes' use of determinatives can be pressed is itself debated. It is the earliest certain mention of Israel in any source. It shows a people called Israel in Canaan before the monarchy described in the Bible, and it predates the Mesha (V22) and Tel Dan (V23) stelae by over three centuries. It says nothing about the Exodus, Moses, or where Israel came from. It is sometimes used on both sides of the Exodus debate, but it only shows Israel already present in Canaan by c. 1208. A minority of scholars have questioned the reading "Israel" (for instance proposing Jezreel), but the majority reading stands. Some scholars have also connected the stele with battle reliefs at Karnak that may show Merneptah's Canaan campaign, including a group sometimes identified as Israel; that identification is disputed. The king who restores order. Egyptian victory texts present the king as upholding Ma'at, cosmic order, against chaos. Foreign enemies are chaos personified, and their destruction is a ritual necessity as much as a military claim. The Nine Bows. Egypt's traditional enemies were symbolised as nine bows under the king's feet. The stele names them as crushed. The formula made every victory an act in a cosmic drama. Reused stone. Carving over an earlier king's stele was common. It borrowed the monument's sanctity while claiming it for the new king. Egypt…

title: The Pilate Stone
summary: A broken limestone block from Caesarea, reused as a step in the Roman theatre, which names Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea. Found in 1961, it is the only inscription from Pilate's lifetime that names him, and it corrected the title later Roman writers gave him.
text: Vault entry V44 · Texts & Tablets · The Israel Museum, Jerusalem In June 1961 an Italian team led by Antonio Frova was excavating the Roman theatre at Caesarea Maritima, the port city Herod the Great had built on the coast of Judaea. The archaeologist Maria Teresa Fortuna Canivet turned over a limestone block that had been used as a step in a later rebuilding of the theatre. Its underside carried four broken lines of Latin, and in the second line was a name known from every Christian creed: PILATVS. - A limestone block about 82 × 65 cm, cut down when it was reused, so that the left side of every line is missing. - The surviving text, with standard restorations in brackets: [ . . . ]S TIBERIEVM [ . . . PO]NTIVS PILATVS [ . . . PRAEF]ECTVS IVDA[EA]E [ . . . FE]CIT D[E . . . ] - It records that Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judaea, built or dedicated a Tiberieum, a structure named in honour of the emperor Tiberius. - Pilate governed Judaea from 26 to 36 CE, so the stone dates from those years. The original is in the Israel Museum; a replica stands at Caesarea. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing around 116, calls Pilate a procurator. So does most later tradition. The stone shows that in his own time Pilate's title was praefectus, a military rank. The governors of Judaea became procurators under Claudius, after Pilate's day. Tacitus used the title of his own time. The Gospels simply call him "governor" (Greek hēgemōn). The first line is the most uncertain. Proposals include: - a temple for the cult of the emperor, which Pilate, as a loyal official, would promote; - the epigrapher Géza Alföldy's restoration [Nautis] Tiberieum, "a Tiberieum for sailors": a lighthouse or harbour structure at Caesarea's port. Neither restoration can be proven from the surviving letters. Pilate appears in the four Gospels, in Josephus and Philo, who describe him as provocative and harsh, and in Tacitus, who notes that Christ "suffered the extreme penalty" under him. The stone adds no new events. What it gives is independent, contemporary confirmation of his office and name. A copper ring found at Herodium, inscribed "of Pilatus" and read with new imaging in 2018, may also be connected with him, although Pilatus was not a unique name. Honouring the emperor. Naming a building after Tiberius was a political and religious act. In the Roman world, loyalty to the emperor was expressed through cult. In Judaea this collided with Jewish law against images, and Josephus and Philo record Pilate provoking protests by bringing military standards and gilded shields into Jerusalem. Reuse as erasure. Cutting a governor's dedication down to serve as a stair shows how quickly monuments to officials lost their meaning. It also shows that the stone survived only by accident. Rome (ch13), Early Christianity (ch16) and Second Temple Judaism (ch10). Compare the James Ossuary (V16) for inscriptions naming New Testament figures and how they are tested, and the True Cross (V15). What's well supported by the evidence - A Latin dedication found at Caesarea in 1961 naming Pontius Pilate as praefectus of Judaea and a Tiberieum. It is authentic, from an excavated context, and dates to 26–36 CE. - It…

title: The Nebra Sky Disc
summary: A bronze disc 30 cm across with a gold sun or full moon, a crescent and 32 stars, among them a cluster read as the Pleiades. It was dug up by looters in 1999, recovered in a Swiss police sting in 2002, and altered at least four times in antiquity. It may be the oldest known concrete depiction of the sky.
text: Vault entry V45 · Relics & Objects · State Museum of Prehistory, Halle (Saale) In July 1999 two men with metal detectors, working illegally, dug into the summit of the Mittelberg, a hill near Nebra in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. They found a hoard: two bronze swords, two axes, a chisel, fragments of spiral bracelets, and a round green plate of bronze inlaid with gold. They sold it on, damaging it in the process. In February 2002, in a hotel in Basel, a buyer who said he represented a museum met the dealers. He was Harald Meller, the state archaeologist, working with the Swiss police. The disc was seized. The looters were later convicted, and one led archaeologists to the find spot. - A bronze disc about 30 cm across and about 2 kg, now green with corrosion, originally perhaps a dark brown or black-violet. - Inlaid with gold: a large circle (sun or full moon), a crescent, and 32 small circles read as stars, among them a tight group of seven, usually identified as the Pleiades. - Analysis of the metals suggests the copper came from the eastern Alps and the gold, at least in part, from Cornwall. That provenance has been debated but is widely accepted. - It went on the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2013. Close study shows the disc was altered several times. The interactive object steps through the stages: 1. Sun, moon and 32 stars. 2. Two horizon arcs are added at the edges; to fit them, one star is covered and two are moved. Each arc spans about 82°, close to the angle between the solstice sunsets (and sunrises) on the horizon at this latitude. 3. A curved band is added at the bottom, often read as a sun-boat. 4. About 39 holes are punched around the rim. 5. One arc is lost, and the disc is buried with the weapons and tools, around 1600 BCE. The hoard's swords and axes date the burial to the end of the Early Bronze Age, c. 1600 BCE, in the Únětice culture. In 2020, Rupert Gebhard and Rüdiger Krause argued that the looters' account of the find spot was unreliable, that the disc might not belong with the hoard, and that its style fits the Iron Age, a thousand years later. In 2021 Ernst Pernicka, Harald Meller and colleagues replied with soil, corrosion and metal analyses linking the disc to the hoard and the site. Most specialists accept the Bronze Age date, and the Iron Age proposal has few supporters. - A calendar? The horizon arcs track the sun between midsummer and midwinter. It has been proposed (notably by Rahlf Hansen) that the crescent and Pleiades together encode a rule for adding a leap month to keep lunar and solar years aligned. Such a rule is known from much later Babylonian texts. The idea is striking and debated. - A religious object? The boat, the sky and the burial with weapons suggest a sacred object, perhaps used by a ruler or priest, then deposited as an offering. - Both. In the Bronze Age, reading the sky and serving the gods were not separate. The sun-boat. The idea that the sun crosses the sky or the underworld in a boat is known from Egypt and from later Nordic Bronze Age rock carvings and razors. The band on the disc may be its earliest appearance in central Europe. Changing the sky. The alterations show that the…

title: The Piprahwa Relics
summary: Bone fragments, a soapstone urn and some 1,800 gems dug from a stupa in 1898 by a British estate manager. The urn's inscription says the shrine holds relics of the Buddha, or of the Buddha's kinsmen, depending on how it is read. In 2025 India halted a Sotheby's sale of the gems.
text: Vault entry V46 · Relics & Objects · Indian Museum, Kolkata; National Museum, New Delhi In January 1898 William Claxton Peppé, an English estate manager in the Terai of northern India, near the Nepal border, had his workmen dig into a large brick mound on his land at Piprahwa. It was an ancient stupa. About 18 feet down they reached a massive sandstone coffer. Inside were five small vessels: urns and caskets of soapstone and crystal, holding bone fragments, ash, and some 1,800 tiny offerings: pearls, gems, gold leaf and stars, beads and shells. Around the lid of one urn ran a line of writing in the Brahmi script. It seemed to say that these were relics of the Buddha, enshrined by his own people, the Sakyas. The words are in a Prakrit language, and each can be glossed in the interactive object above. The standard reading: This deposit of relics of the Blessed One, the Buddha, is (the gift) of the Sakyas, the brothers of Sukiti, with their sisters, sons and wives. The grammar is ambiguous. The genitives can be arranged in more than one way. Soon after the find, the epigrapher J. F. Fleet argued that it could mean the relics of the Sakyas, the kinsmen of the Buddha. On that reading the bones are those of the Buddha's relatives, perhaps victims of the massacre of the Sakyas recorded in Buddhist tradition, and not the Buddha's own. Most scholars since have preferred the reading "relics of the Buddha", while accepting that the text can be taken both ways.
