The find came in the same years that a German archaeologist, Alois Führer, was exposed as a forger of Buddhist inscriptions and relics in the same region. Suspicion inevitably fell on Piprahwa. Investigations, including the historian Charles Allen's study (2008), concluded that Peppé's find was genuine and that Führer did not have the opportunity to plant it. Some doubts about the inscription's date have been raised, but most epigraphers accept it as ancient. In 1971–1973 the archaeologist K. M. Srivastava excavated deeper at Piprahwa and found earlier caskets with bone, and at the nearby monastery sealings reading "Kapilavastu", the name of the Buddha's home town. He argued that Piprahwa was Kapilavastu. Nepal identifies Kapilavastu with Tilaurakot, across the border, and the question remains disputed between the two countries. The British government kept most of the gems and gave the bone relics to King Chulalongkorn of Siam, who shared them among Buddhist communities in Asia. Much of the jewellery went to the Indian Museum in Calcutta (Kolkata). Peppé's family kept a share of the gems. In May 2025 Sotheby's in Hong Kong offered the family's gems for sale. The Indian government objected that they were sacred relics and national heritage. Buddhist leaders protested, and the sale was postponed. In July 2025 they were bought by the Godrej group and returned to India, where they are to be displayed. Relics and the stupa. Buddhist tradition says the Buddha's remains were divided into eight portions after his cremation, one of them to the Sakyas of Kapilavastu, each enshrined in a stupa. The stupa became the central monument of Buddhism, a mound whose relic core made the Buddha present. Jewels as…

title: The Kensington Runestone
summary: A greywacke slab a Swedish immigrant farmer said he found under the roots of a tree in Minnesota in 1898, telling of Norse explorers killed in 1362. Scholars rejected it within months, and its runes and language point to the nineteenth century. It remains a beloved local symbol and a case study in how claims are tested.
text: Vault entry V47 · Texts & Tablets · Runestone Museum, Alexandria, Minnesota In November 1898 Olof Öhman, a Swedish immigrant farmer near Kensington, Minnesota, was clearing trees on his land. According to his account, he pulled up an aspen and found a flat grey slab gripped in its roots. It weighed about 90 kg and was carved on its face and one edge with runes. Translated, they told of 8 Goths and 22 Norwegians on a journey of exploration from Vinland, of ten men found "red with blood and dead", a prayer to the Virgin, and a year: 1362. If genuine, Scandinavians had reached the middle of North America 130 years before Columbus. - In 1899 the stone was examined by Olaus Breda at the University of Minnesota and by scholars at the university in Christiania (Oslo). They declared it a modern forgery. - The objections were linguistic. The language is close to nineteenth-century Swedish, not fourteenth-century Norse. Some words and forms did not exist in 1362. Several runes are unusual or invented, and some match nineteenth-century runic alphabets in books a Swede of the period could own. - Hjalmar Holand, a writer and local historian, bought the stone in 1907 and spent half a century defending it. It was exhibited at the Smithsonian in 1948–49. - In 1967 two children of Öhman's neighbour John Gran said in a recorded interview that their father had made the stone with Öhman as a hoax. This is hearsay, and supporters reject it. From the 1980s the geologist Scott Wolter and the researcher Richard Nielsen argued that the carving's weathering implied great age, and that some runic forms, such as a dotted R, appear in medieval Scandinavian sources, including a manuscript from Gotland. Runologists such as Henrik Williams have answered that weathering estimates are unreliable for a stone of unknown history and that the language as a whole, not single letters, points to the nineteenth century. The overwhelming scholarly consensus is that the stone is a nineteenth-century creation. It remains a proud local symbol, standing at the Runestone Museum in Alexandria beside a giant statue of a Viking. The Vault includes objects whose claims are disproved as well as those that are proved or open. The Kensington stone is a clear case of how claims about ancient inscriptions are tested: by language, by script, by provenance and by weathering. It also shows how identity and pride keep a claim alive after the scholarly case has closed. Compare the Rök Runestone (V36), a genuine ninth-century inscription. "AVM, save from evil." The stone's one religious line invokes the Virgin Mary (AVM = Ave Maria). This is plausible in form for a medieval Catholic party. Critics note that such formulas were well known in the nineteenth century as well. Runes as heritage. For Scandinavian Americans in 1898, runes were a powerful symbol of ancestry. The late nineteenth century's romantic revival of the Viking past explains both why a forger might carve such a stone and why so many people wanted it to be true. Norse Paganism (ch23) and Native North American (ch62), whose lands are the setting of the claim. Compare the Rök Runestone (V36) and the Gospel of Jesus's Wife (V17), another…

title: The Great Isaiah Scroll
summary: The only complete book of the Hebrew Bible among the Dead Sea Scrolls: all 66 chapters of Isaiah in 54 columns on a scroll 7.34 metres long, copied about a thousand years before the oldest complete medieval Hebrew Bibles, and remarkably close to them.
text: Vault entry V48 · Manuscripts · The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (1QIsaᵃ) In 1947 Bedouin shepherds took a handful of leather scrolls from a cave above the Dead Sea (V02). One of them, when unrolled, turned out to be a complete book of the Bible: the prophet Isaiah, all 66 chapters, in 54 columns on seventeen sheets of parchment sewn end to end. It is 7.34 metres long. Before 1947 the oldest complete manuscripts of Isaiah in Hebrew were medieval, from around 1000 CE. This scroll was about a thousand years older. - Known as 1QIsaᵃ ("Cave 1, Isaiah, copy a"). It is one of the seven original Dead Sea Scrolls, bought in 1947 by the Syrian Orthodox Metropolitan Athanasius Yeshue Samuel and acquired for Israel in 1954. - Palaeography dates it to about 150–100 BCE. Radiocarbon tests have given ranges reaching back into the fourth to second centuries BCE. It is the best preserved of the biblical scrolls. - It is displayed, in facsimile, around the central drum of the Shrine of the Book; the original is shown only rarely, to protect it. This is what made the scroll famous. Compared with the Masoretic text of the medieval codices, such as the Aleppo Codex (V38): - The wording is overwhelmingly the same. Most differences are in spelling: the scroll often writes vowel letters that the later text leaves out, for example לוא for לא. - There are also real variants, a few thousand in all counting spelling, including changed words, added or missing phrases and scribal corrections. Most are small; a handful affect meaning. - A second Isaiah scroll from the same cave, 1QIsaᵇ, is closer still to the Masoretic text. So the scroll shows both remarkable stability over a thousand years of copying and that the text was not yet fixed letter by letter in the second century BCE. Believers and sceptics sometimes each quote only half of this. The divine name. Scribes treated the name of God with special care. In some Qumran scrolls it is written in palaeo-Hebrew letters (see V02); in this scroll it appears in square script, and in places a scribe's corrections show hesitation over how to write divine titles. Marks in the margins. The scroll carries marginal signs whose meaning is not certain: some may mark passages of special interest to the community, others may be reading aids. A book in two halves. The scribe left three blank lines after chapter 33, and the second half was written differently. Scholars have linked this to how Isaiah was copied, and it connects with the long-standing view that the book grew in stages ("First", "Second" and "Third" Isaiah), although the gap falls at chapter 33, not at chapter 40 where that scholarly division usually begins. Second Temple Judaism (ch10) and Pre-exilic Israel (ch07), where the prophet Isaiah belongs. Compare the Dead Sea Scrolls (V02), the Copper Scroll (V10) and the Aleppo Codex (V38). What's well supported by the evidence - A complete Hebrew scroll of Isaiah, 7.34 m, 54 columns, from Qumran Cave 1, dated by palaeography to c. 150–100 BCE. - Its text is very close to the medieval Masoretic text, with frequent spelling differences and a smaller number of genuine variants. What is not supported - That it shows the biblical text…

title: The Book of Enoch
summary: The book of the Watchers, the fallen angels who taught forbidden arts, and of Enoch's journeys through the heavens. Quoted in the New Testament's Letter of Jude, dropped by most churches, and preserved whole only in Ethiopia, where it is Scripture.
text: Vault entry V49 · Manuscripts · Ge'ez manuscripts in Ethiopia and Europe; Aramaic fragments from Qumran Genesis says only this of Enoch, seventh from Adam: he "walked with God; and he was not, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). From that one strange line grew an entire literature. By the third century BCE, Jewish writers were composing books in Enoch's name: visions of heaven, a history of the fallen angels, the secrets of the calendar, the end of days. The Letter of Jude in the New Testament quotes one of them as prophecy. Then, in most of the Christian world, the book disappeared. In 1773 the Scottish traveller James Bruce came home from Ethiopia with three manuscripts of it, written in Ge'ez, the classical language of the Ethiopian church, where it had been read as Scripture all along. What we call 1 Enoch is really five books gathered into one. The interactive codex above lists them: 1. The Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36). 2. The Parables or Similitudes (37–71). 3. The Astronomical Book (72–82). 4. The Dream Visions (83–90). 5. The Epistle of Enoch (91–108). The evidence comes in three languages: - Aramaic: fragments of eleven manuscripts from Qumran Cave 4 (4Q201–212), the earliest from around 200 BCE. They cover every part except the Parables, perhaps a fifth of the whole text. - Greek: substantial parts, including a sixth-century codex from Akhmim in Egypt. - Ge'ez: the only complete text, translated in late antiquity. The surviving manuscripts date from the fourteenth or fifteenth century onwards, and there are many of them. Richard Laurence published the first English translation from Bruce's manuscripts in 1821. The book's most influential story expands Genesis 6:1–4, where "the sons of God" take human wives and "the Nephilim" are on the earth. In Enoch the sons of God are angels called Watchers, led by Shemihazah and Asael (Azazel). They descend on Mount Hermon, father giants, and teach humanity metallurgy, weapons, cosmetics, sorcery and astrology. The earth fills with violence; the Flood is God's answer. This became the root of Jewish and Christian ideas of fallen angels and demons as the spirits of the dead giants. - Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9, and 2 Peter 2:4 alludes to its angels in chains. Several early Christian writers, such as Tertullian, valued it. - By the fourth century most churches had rejected it. It is not in the Jewish Bible or in Catholic, Orthodox or Protestant Bibles. - The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean church include it in their canon, and the Beta Israel (Ethiopian Jews) also revered it. 364 days. The Astronomical Book describes a 364-day solar year: exactly 52 weeks, so that every festival falls on the same weekday each year. The Qumran community followed this calendar, in conflict with the Temple's lunar calendar. Forbidden knowledge. The Watchers' teaching links technology and secret arts with corruption. The theme runs through later ideas of illicit magic and of knowledge as temptation. The Son of Man. The Parables speak of a pre-existent heavenly judge called the Son of Man and the Chosen One. How this relates to the Gospels' use of the phrase for Jesus is a major, unresolved…

title: The Vienna Dioscurides
summary: A great illustrated herbal made in Constantinople around 512 for the princess Anicia Juliana, with hundreds of full-page paintings of plants. It passed through Byzantine, Arab, Jewish and Ottoman hands before an emperor's envoy bought it in 1569. In it the mandrake is shown as medicine and as legend.
text: Vault entry V50 · Manuscripts · Austrian National Library, Vienna (Cod. med. gr. 1) Around 512 the people of the Constantinople suburb of Honoratae wanted to thank a patron. Anicia Juliana, daughter of a western emperor and one of the richest women of the Roman world, had paid for a new church there. Their gift was a book: a luxurious copy of the most famous work of ancient medicine, Dioscorides' De materia medica, with a painting of every plant. On one of its first pages Juliana sits enthroned, flanked by personified virtues. It is one of the greatest books to survive from late antiquity, and it has been in constant use ever since. - About 491 leaves of parchment, with 383 surviving full-page paintings of plants out of an original 435 or so. - The main text is De materia medica, written by the Greek physician Pedanius Dioscorides in the first century CE, the standard reference on medicinal plants for fifteen hundred years. The volume also contains poems and paraphrases on plants, snakes and poisons, birds and fish. - The plant paintings are unusually naturalistic; many were copied from older illustrated herbals now lost. - On UNESCO's Memory of the World register since 1997. The book stayed in Constantinople for a thousand years. Readers wrote in its margins: plant names in Greek minuscule, and later in Arabic, Hebrew, Turkish and Latin. It was rebound and repaired in the fifteenth century. After the Ottoman conquest it belonged, by tradition, to the physician of Suleiman the Magnificent's court. In 1569, on the advice of the Habsburg envoy Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, who had seen it in Constantinople, it was bought for the emperor Maximilian II and carried to Vienna. In the ancient and medieval world, medicine and religion were not separate. Healing plants were linked to gods and saints, collected at particular times with prayers or charms, and some plants carried legends of power. The Vienna Dioscurides shows the most famous: The mandrake. Its forked root looks like a human figure. Legend said it shrieked when pulled up and killed whoever pulled it, so a dog must be tied to it and made to draw it out. One of the book's frontispieces shows the personification of Discovery (Heuresis) handing a mandrake to Dioscorides, with the dead dog at her feet. The mandrake was used as a sedative and anaesthetic, and it became central to later European folk magic and to accusations of witchcraft. The patron as virtue. Juliana's portrait places her among personified virtues, a Christian-imperial image of the donor as a model of generosity. An inscription in the frame praises her building of churches. Authority in a circle. Two pages show famous physicians gathered as a learned assembly, among them Galen and the centaur Chiron, who in myth taught medicine to Asclepius. Pagan and Christian authority sit together. Plants as creation. For Christian readers, the ordered catalogue of plants and their powers could be read as a book of creation, showing the gifts God placed in nature. Eastern Orthodoxy & Byzantium (ch60), with Classical Greece (ch15) and Rome (ch13) for the medicine it preserves, and The Witch Trials (ch32) for the later afterlife of mandrake…

title: The Codex Mendoza
summary: Painted by Nahua artists for the first viceroy of New Spain, with Spanish notes: the founding of Tenochtitlan, the tribute of the empire, and an Aztec life from birth to old age. Bound for the emperor Charles V, it was seized by French privateers and ended up in Oxford.
text: Vault entry V51 · Manuscripts · Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS. Arch. Selden. A. 1) Around 1541, twenty years after the fall of Tenochtitlan, the first viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, commissioned a book for the emperor Charles V. Indigenous tlacuiloque, painter-scribes trained in the old way, painted its pages in the pictorial script of central Mexico. A Spanish interpreter added notes and a commentary. It was meant to explain to the king the empire he now ruled: how it began, what it collected, and how its people lived. The ship carrying it across the Atlantic was taken by French privateers. The book survived, travelled through the hands of scholars in France and England, and has been in Oxford since 1659. - 71 leaves of European paper, painted and annotated in Spanish. - Made c. 1541, and in any case before 1553, when it belonged to the French royal cosmographer André Thevet, whose name is written on its pages. - In England it passed from Richard Hakluyt to Samuel Purchas, who published woodcuts of it in 1625, and then to the jurist John Selden. It reached the Bodleian Library in 1659. 1. History. The founding of Tenochtitlan in 1325 (the year 2 House), and the conquests of each Mexica ruler, each town shown with a burning temple, the sign of conquest. 2. Tribute. Town by town, what the provinces sent to Motecuhzoma: cloaks, warriors' suits, feathers, jade, cacao, maize. It was probably copied from an older, pre-conquest tribute record. 3. A life. From birth and naming through education, punishments, training for war or for the priesthood, marriage and old age. The first page shows the story that stands at the heart of Mexica religion and identity. Guided by their god Huitzilopochtli, the wandering Mexica were to settle where they saw an eagle on a cactus growing from a rock. On the frontispiece the eagle perches on the nopal in the middle of a lake divided by canals into four parts, surrounded by the ten founding leaders, with Tenoch seated among them. The same emblem is on the flag of Mexico today. Pictorial writing. Aztec writing combined pictures, place-name glyphs built from recognisable images (a hill, a stone, a cactus) and number signs: dots for ones, flags for twenties, feathers for four hundreds. The tribute pages use them throughout. The four quarters. The lake divided into four by blue canals represents the four quarters of Tenochtitlan and the four directions of the cosmos, with the eagle and cactus at the centre. The priests' school. Part III shows the calmecac, the school where young nobles trained for the priesthood with night vigils, penance and study of the sacred books, and the telpochcalli for warriors. The Aztec (ch43). Compare the Codex Borgia (V41), a pre-conquest divinatory book, and the Tilma of Guadalupe (V13), made in the same decades of colonial Mexico. What's well supported by the evidence - A colonial Mexican pictorial manuscript made c. 1541–1553 for Viceroy Mendoza, with Spanish glosses, in the Bodleian since 1659. - Its founding image, tribute lists and life-cycle pages are major sources for the Aztec world. What is not supported - Treating it as a neutral record. It was made after the conquest for…

title: The Ishtar Gate
summary: Babylon's northern gate, faced with glazed blue bricks and rows of bulls and dragons, the beasts of the storm god and of Marduk. Through it ran the Processional Way of the New Year festival. Excavated by Robert Koldewey's German expedition in the early 1900s and rebuilt in Berlin.
text: Vault entry V52 · Relics & Objects · Pergamonmuseum, Berlin (reconstruction) Each spring, at the New Year festival (Akitu), the statues of Babylon's gods were carried in procession along a broad road lined with walls of blue glazed brick, where lions strode in yellow and white relief. The road ran through a double gate faced with the same shining blue, set with row after row of bulls and dragons. The king who built it, Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605–562 BCE), set a plaque in it: I placed wild bulls and ferocious dragons in the gateways and thus adorned them with luxurious splendour so that people might gaze on them in wonder. This was the Babylon of the Judean exile. Many of the exiles taken there after 597 and 586 BCE will have seen it. - The eighth gate of the inner city of Babylon, on its north side, dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. It was built around 575 BCE, in several phases, over earlier gates. - Faced with glazed bricks in deep blue, with moulded relief animals in yellow, white and brown: rows of aurochs (wild bulls) and mušḫuššu (dragons). - The Processional Way leading to it was lined with about 120 lions, animals of Ishtar. A German expedition under Robert Koldewey excavated Babylon from 1899 to 1917 and uncovered the gate's foundations and tens of thousands of glazed brick fragments. The fragments were shipped to Berlin, sorted and reassembled over years, and the front gate and part of the Processional Way were rebuilt in the Pergamonmuseum in the 1930s. The much larger rear gate was not rebuilt. Lions and other panels are also in museums in Istanbul, Paris, New York, Chicago and elsewhere. Iraq has called for the return of Babylonian antiquities, and parts of the gate's foundations still stand at the site of Babylon, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019. Beasts as gods. Each animal stands for a god: the dragon (mušḫuššu) for Marduk, Babylon's supreme god, and his son Nabu; the bull for the storm god Adad; the lion for Ishtar. A worshipper walking the Processional Way passed between the gods' own emblems. Blue as the sacred. The deep blue glaze imitated lapis lazuli, the precious stone of the gods, brought from Afghanistan. The gate announced the city as a dwelling of gods. The procession. At the Akitu festival Marduk's statue left his temple, the Esagila, and the king "took the hand of Bel [Marduk]", renewing his right to rule. The gate framed that renewal. Mesopotamia (ch03) and Second Temple Judaism (ch10), whose exiles lived in this city. Compare the Cyrus Cylinder (V35), found in the ruins of the Esagila, and the Behistun Inscription (V54). What's well supported by the evidence - A glazed-brick gate built by Nebuchadnezzar II c. 575 BCE, decorated with bulls and dragons, with a Processional Way of lions, excavated by Koldewey and rebuilt in Berlin from original bricks. What is not supported - That the Berlin gate is the whole structure. It is the smaller front gate, reconstructed with many modern bricks alongside the original ones. What's genuinely open - How the phases of construction relate to each other, and the precise original arrangement of the animal rows. - The future of calls for restitution. The gate - "Ishtar Gate"…

title: The Rosetta Stone
summary: A priestly decree honouring the boy-king Ptolemy V, carved in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Found by French soldiers in 1799, taken by the British in 1801, and used by Thomas Young and Jean-François Champollion to crack the Egyptian script. Egypt asks for its return.
text: Vault entry V53 · Texts & Tablets · British Museum, London (EA 24) In July 1799, French soldiers of Napoleon's expedition to Egypt were rebuilding an old fort near the Nile port of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. The engineer officer Pierre-François Bouchard noticed a slab of dark granodiorite built into a wall. It carried three bands of writing: hieroglyphs at the top, broken; a flowing Egyptian script in the middle; and Greek at the bottom. The scholars with the army understood at once that if the three said the same thing, the Greek might unlock the other two. When the French surrendered Egypt in 1801, the stone was handed to the British under the Treaty of Alexandria. It has been in the British Museum since 1802. The text is a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BCE by a council of Egyptian priests, honouring the young king Ptolemy V Epiphanes on the anniversary of his coronation. It lists his good deeds, such as tax remissions, gifts to temples and the restoration of order, and in return grants him divine honours: statues in every temple and festivals on his birthday. It ends by ordering the decree to be set up in sacred (hieroglyphic), native (Demotic) and Greek letters. Copies stood in temples across Egypt; the Rosetta Stone is one of them. Knowledge of hieroglyphs had been lost since late antiquity. Scholars had long thought them pure symbols of mystical ideas. - Thomas Young, an English physicist, showed from 1814 that the cartouches (ovals) enclosed royal names, and worked out the sound values of several signs in the name of Ptolemy. But he thought phonetic signs were used only for foreign names. - Jean-François Champollion compared the Ptolemy cartouche with a Cleopatra cartouche on an obelisk from Philae, brought to England by William Bankes. The shared signs for p, t, o and l confirmed the readings. He then showed that the system was used for Egyptian words too, a mixture of sound signs and meaning signs. He announced this in his Lettre à M. Dacier on 27 September 1822, the date often given for the birth of Egyptology. The interactive object above lets you follow the first step: the name Ptolemy, sign by sign. The stone was taken as a spoil of war. Egyptian scholars and officials, including Zahi Hawass, have repeatedly called for its return, and a 2022 petition gathered wide support. The British Museum's position has been that it is legally part of its collection. The question is open and actively contested. Three scripts, three audiences. Hieroglyphs were the "words of the gods", carved on temples. Demotic was the everyday script of Egyptian administration. Greek was the language of the Ptolemaic court. The decree speaks to gods, Egyptians and rulers at once. The cartouche. The oval ring round a royal name is a rope loop symbolising all that the sun encircles: the king as ruler of the world (see the Pyramid Texts, V34). The king as god. The decree turns political gratitude into cult: the Macedonian king becomes an Egyptian god in temple worship, the same pattern as Egypt's ancient sacred kingship. Egypt (ch02) and Sacred Kingship (ch49). Compare the Behistun Inscription (V54), which did for cuneiform what the Rosetta Stone…

title: The Behistun Inscription
summary: Darius the Great's account of how he seized the Persian throne, carved about 60 metres up a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, beneath a relief of the king and the winged symbol of Ahuramazda. Copied at great risk by Henry Rawlinson, it opened cuneiform to modern reading.
text: Vault entry V54 · Texts & Tablets · Mount Bisotun, Kermanshah, Iran On the old royal road from Babylon to Ecbatana, a limestone cliff rises from the plain at Bisotun in western Iran. High on its face, far out of reach, a relief shows a king with his foot on a fallen man. Nine bound captives stand before him, roped together at the neck. Above them floats a figure in a winged disc. Around the relief run columns of cuneiform in three languages. In the 1830s and 1840s a young British officer, Henry Rawlinson, climbed ladders and ropes to copy them, and at the most dangerous spot a local boy swung across on ropes to take paper casts. The text he brought down became the key that opened cuneiform, the writing of ancient Mesopotamia. - Carved at the command of Darius I around 520 BCE, soon after he took the Persian throne in 522. - The same text in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian (Akkadian), the longest trilingual cuneiform inscription known. - It tells how, after the death of Cambyses, a magus named Gaumata seized the throne claiming to be Cambyses' brother Bardiya, and how Darius and six nobles killed him and Darius then crushed a series of rebellions in a single year. - Copies were sent around the empire: a fragment of an Akkadian version was found at Babylon, and an Aramaic version on papyrus at Elephantine in Egypt. Darius's account is the official version. Several historians, beginning in the nineteenth century, have suspected that the "false Bardiya" was the real Bardiya, and that Darius, from a side branch of the royal family, was the usurper who then wrote the story. Others accept Darius's account. Herodotus tells a similar story, perhaps from Persian sources that go back to Darius's own propaganda. The question is genuinely open. "By the favour of Ahuramazda." The phrase recurs again and again: Darius rules and wins by the will of Ahuramazda, the Wise Lord, the supreme god of Zoroastrian religion. The rebels, in turn, are driven by "the Lie" (drauga), the opposite of truth and order (arta). Whether Darius was a Zoroastrian in the full sense is debated, but the religious language of truth against the Lie is unmistakably Iranian (see Zoroaster, ch06). The winged figure. The figure in the winged disc above the relief is often identified as Ahuramazda; others read it as the royal fortune or glory (farnah), or a guardian spirit (fravashi). The identification is disputed. A new script for a king. Old Persian cuneiform may have been invented for Darius for inscriptions like this one; Darius himself claims to have made a new form of writing. It was never an everyday script. Zoroaster (ch06) and Sacred Kingship (ch49), with Mesopotamia (ch03) for the Babylonian version. Compare the Cyrus Cylinder (V35), the Rosetta Stone (V53) and the Ishtar Gate (V52). What's well supported by the evidence - A trilingual royal inscription and relief of Darius I, c. 520 BCE, at Bisotun, copied by Rawlinson (1835–1847) and central to the decipherment of cuneiform. - It invokes Ahuramazda and the struggle of truth against the Lie. What is not supported - Reading the inscription as a neutral history. It is the victor's account. What's genuinely open - Whether…

title: The Oracle Bones of Anyang
era: The Vault · The Early Iron Age
summary: Turtle shells and cattle shoulder-blades that Shang kings had cracked in fire to put questions to their ancestors, then had the questions and answers carved beside the cracks. Sold as 'dragon bones' for medicine until 1899, they are the oldest body of Chinese writing.
text: Vault entry V55 · Texts & Tablets · Academia Sinica, Taipei; institutions in China and worldwide In Chinese pharmacies of the late nineteenth century one could buy "dragon bones", fragments of old bone and shell ground into medicine. In 1899 the scholar Wang Yirong noticed that some of them bore carved signs that looked like a very ancient form of Chinese writing. Collectors traced the bones to farmland near Anyang in Henan. From 1928 archaeologists excavating there found the royal capital of the late Shang dynasty, called Yinxu, "the ruins of Yin". They found the palaces and tombs of kings, and pits holding tens of thousands of inscribed turtle shells and cattle shoulder-blades. They are the earliest substantial body of Chinese writing, and they are almost all records of divination. The interactive object above follows the steps: 1. A turtle plastron (the flat under-shell) or an ox scapula was cleaned, polished and cut with rows of hollows on the back. 2. The diviner spoke the charge, a statement put to the spirits, often in paired forms: "we will receive harvest" / "we may not receive harvest". 3. A hot brand was pressed into a hollow. The bone cracked on the front in a ⊢ shape, the origin of the character 卜 (bu), "to divine". 4. The king read the cracks. 5. Engravers carved the date, diviner's name and charge beside the crack, sometimes the king's prognostication, and occasionally the verification: what actually happened. Around 150,000 pieces are known, most from the reigns of about nine kings, especially Wu Ding (c. 1250–1192 BCE). They asked about: - Sacrifices to the royal ancestors, and to the high god Di: which ancestor, how many cattle, sheep or human victims. - Harvests, rain and weather. - War, hunting and travel. - Illness, dreams and childbirth, including dozens of divinations about the consort Fu Hao, whose unlooted tomb was found at Yinxu in 1976. The world they reveal is one where the living king mediated between the people and powerful, sometimes dangerous ancestors, who had to be fed and consulted. Writing born in ritual. The oracle bones show Chinese writing already developed, with thousands of distinct characters, used in a religious setting: communication with the spirits. Many characters can be traced directly to their modern forms. The crack as answer. The spirits answered not in words but in cracks. The character 卜 draws the crack itself, and 占 (zhan, "to prognosticate") adds a mouth: speaking the reading of the crack. Pairs and balance. Posing each question in positive and negative forms reflects a way of thinking in complementary pairs, sometimes compared with later yin–yang thought. That link is interpretive. Early China (ch09) and Sacred Kingship (ch49), with Confucianism & Daoism (ch12) for later ancestor rites. Compare the Diamond Sutra (V30), from the same written tradition two thousand years later. What's well supported by the evidence - Inscribed turtle plastrons and cattle scapulae from Yinxu (Anyang), c. 1250–1050 BCE, recording royal pyromantic divination, identified as writing in 1899 and excavated from 1928. - They are the oldest large corpus of Chinese writing and show a religion centred on royal…

title: The Phaistos Disc
summary: A fired clay disc about 16 cm across, found in the Minoan palace of Phaistos in 1908, with 45 different signs pressed into it by stamps in a spiral on both sides: printing, in a sense, three thousand years early. It is unread, and probably unreadable unless more text turns up.
text: Vault entry V56 · Relics & Objects · Heraklion Archaeological Museum, Crete On 3 July 1908 the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier was excavating the Minoan palace of Phaistos in southern Crete. In a room of the palace complex he found a small disc of fired clay, about 16 centimetres across. Both faces were covered with a spiral of little pictures: a walking man, a head with a plumed crest, a fish, a bird, a ship, a flower. Each sign had been pressed into the wet clay with a stamp, so that every occurrence of a sign is identical. It is the earliest known text made with something like movable type, and it has never been deciphered. - 241 or 242 stamped signs (the count depends on one uncertain sign) of 45 distinct types, arranged in 61 groups separated by incised lines: 31 on side A, 30 on side B. - The text runs in a spiral, most scholars think from the rim inwards. - Usually dated to the Middle Minoan period, c. 1850–1600 BCE, from its find context, although the context has been questioned. - It is unique. No other text uses the same signs, except for a single possible parallel sign on a sealing found in 1955. Decipherments need enough text and ideally a bilingual or known names. The Rosetta Stone (V53) had both; Linear B had thousands of tablets. The Phaistos Disc has fewer than 250 signs, no parallel texts and no known language. Statistical analysis suggests the 45 sign types fit a syllabary (signs for syllables) better than an alphabet or a word-script, but that does not tell us the language. Most specialists agree that no proposed decipherment can be verified unless new texts are found. The interactive cards above list the main kinds of claimed reading, from Greek and Luwian to calendars and hymns. There have been dozens more. In 2008, for the centenary of the find, the antiquities specialist Jerome Eisenberg argued that the disc was a forgery made or commissioned by Pernier, pointing to its uniqueness, its crisp firing and unusual find circumstances. Most archaeologists reject this. They point to the excavation records, to the 1955 sealing and to features a forger of 1908 would not have known. A thermoluminescence test, which could date the firing, has not been permitted by the museum. Its authenticity is widely accepted but not proven by testing. Pictures that are signs. The signs are pictures, but as in all early scripts they probably stood for sounds. Reading the pictures as symbols of their objects is the most common mistake in amateur decipherments. Stamps and repetition. Making stamps for 45 signs suggests the maker expected to produce more than one text. None has been found. The spiral. A spiral text had to be turned as it was read, perhaps suiting a ritual use such as a hymn or prayer. This is a suggestion, not evidence. Early Greece (ch08), where Minoan Crete is discussed. Compare the Voynich Manuscript (V01) and the Rohonc Codex (V11) for other unread texts, and the Rosetta Stone (V53) for what a decipherment needs. What's well supported by the evidence - A stamped clay disc found at Phaistos in 1908, with 45 sign types in 61 groups, undeciphered. - Its authenticity is accepted by most archaeologists. What is not supported -…

title: The Holy Mandylion
summary: The Image of Edessa: a cloth said to bear Christ's face, not made by human hands, sent to King Abgar of Edessa. The first of the 'true images', carried in triumph to Constantinople in 944 and lost from view after 1204. Two cloths claim to be it, and one theory says it was the Shroud.
text: Vault entry V57 · Relics & Objects · Claimed by Genoa and the Vatican On 16 August 944, the city of Constantinople turned out for a procession. The Byzantine army had besieged Edessa (modern Şanlıurfa in Turkey), then under Muslim rule, and had lifted the siege in exchange for the city's most sacred treasure: a cloth said to bear the face of Christ, imprinted not by any artist but by Christ himself. The emperor received it and placed it in the palace chapel of the Pharos among the empire's holiest relics. The Byzantines called it the Mandylion, "the little cloth". Its story had begun centuries earlier, with a king who wrote to Jesus. - c. 325. The church historian Eusebius says that he found in the archives of Edessa letters between King Abgar V, who was ill, and Jesus, who promised to send a disciple to heal him. No image is mentioned. - c. 400. The Syriac Doctrine of Addai adds that Abgar's envoy painted a portrait of Jesus and brought it home. - c. 593. Evagrius Scholasticus writes that during the Persian siege of Edessa in 544, an image "made by God" (theoteuktos) saved the city. This is the first record of the image as miraculous. - Later legend. Jesus pressed a cloth to his wet face, leaving his likeness, and sent it to Abgar. The image was said to have been hidden in the city wall, rediscovered, and even to have printed copies of itself on tiles. When crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, the Pharos chapel's relics were scattered; some reached Paris, where the Crown of Thorns (V06) went. The Mandylion's fate is undocumented. Two images each claim to be it: - The Holy Face of Genoa, kept in the church of San Bartolomeo degli Armeni, said to have come to Genoa in the fourteenth century. - The Mandylion of Rome, long kept at San Silvestro in Capite and now in the Vatican. Both are faces painted on cloth mounted on board in later frames. Neither has been scientifically dated, and art historians generally date both to the Middle Ages. In 1978 the writer Ian Wilson argued that the Mandylion was actually the Shroud of Turin (V04), folded so that only the face showed. This would give the Shroud a history before its first appearance in France around 1354. The theory is attractive to Shroud supporters, but most historians find it unproven: the Mandylion was consistently described as a face on a small cloth, and the 1988 radiocarbon dating of the Shroud (itself contested) places it in the Middle Ages. Acheiropoieta. The Mandylion is the model of the acheiropoieton, an image "not made by hands". Such images answered a theological question: if Christ himself made his image, then images of him could be holy, not idols. This mattered greatly in the Iconoclast controversy of the eighth and ninth centuries. The icon of the Holy Face. In Orthodox art the Mandylion became a standard icon: Christ's face on a white cloth, often held by angels, placed over church doors and on battle standards. A city's protector. At Edessa and later at Constantinople the image was a palladium, a sacred object that protected the city, like the Ark of the Covenant (V07) in Israel's wars. Eastern Orthodoxy & Byzantium (ch60) and Patristic Christianity (ch22). Compare the…

title: The Lion Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel
summary: A figure 31 cm tall, carved from mammoth ivory, with a cave lion's head on an upright body. Found smashed in a German cave a week before the Second World War and pieced together over seventy years, it is among the oldest known figurative sculptures, and among the oldest images of a being that does not exist in nature.
text: Vault entry V58 · Relics & Objects · Museum Ulm, Germany On 25 August 1939, in the last days of an excavation in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in the Lone valley of southern Germany, the geologist Otto Völzing recovered a mass of broken mammoth ivory from the back of the cave. The dig, led by the anatomist Robert Wetzel, was closed a week later when the Second World War began, and the fragments went into storage in Ulm unrecognised. Thirty years later they were found to belong to a single figure: a standing body with a lion's head. It is one of the oldest known sculptures in the world, and one of the oldest images of something no one has ever seen: a being that is part human, part animal. - About 31 centimetres tall, carved from a mammoth tusk, using the tusk's curve for the body. - It stands upright on two legs, arms at its sides, with the head, ears and muzzle of a cave lion. Carved lines cross its left arm. - The find layer belongs to the Aurignacian, the culture of the first modern humans in Europe, and is dated by radiocarbon to roughly 41,000–35,000 years ago. - An experiment by the archaeologist and craftsman Wulf Hein, working with stone tools on fresh ivory, suggested that carving it took a very long time, perhaps hundreds of hours. The interactive timeline above follows the reconstruction. Joachim Hahn assembled more than 200 fragments into a figure in 1969. More pieces were added in the 1980s, when Elisabeth Schmid also suggested the figure might be female. Between 2009 and 2012 excavators returned to the cave, led by Claus-Joachim Kind, and sifted the old spoil heaps, recovering hundreds more fragments. After a full restoration in 2013 the figure was shown in its most complete form. In 2017 the cave became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura. The new excavations found that the figure had lain in a chamber at the back of the cave, away from the living area, together with pierced animal teeth and ornaments. This suggests a special place, though what was done there is not known. A being between kinds. A human body with an animal head is called a therianthrope. Such beings appear in the religious art of many later cultures, from the animal-headed gods of Egypt (ch02) to shamanic masks. The Lion Man shows that imagining them is extremely old. Whether it was a god, a spirit, a shaman in costume, a character in a story or something else cannot be known. The lion. The cave lion was the most powerful predator of Ice Age Europe. Choosing it may have meant strength or danger, but that is interpretation. Male or female? The figure was long called the "Lion Man". Some researchers have read it as female ("Lion Woman"); others see no clear sex. The question is open. Palaeolithic Prehistory (ch41). Compare the Venus of Willendorf (V59), a little younger, and Göbekli Tepe (V60), where carved animals and human figures appear again some 25,000 years later. What's well supported by the evidence - A mammoth-ivory figure with a lion's head on an upright body, found at Hohlenstein-Stadel in 1939 and reassembled from hundreds of fragments between 1969 and 2013. - An Aurignacian date of roughly 40,000 years…

title: The Venus of Willendorf
summary: An 11-centimetre limestone figure of a woman with no face, found beside the Danube in 1908. She is perhaps the most famous image of the Ice Age. The name 'Venus' is a modern joke, and her meaning is unknown. A 2022 scan traced her stone to northern Italy.
text: Vault entry V59 · Relics & Objects · Natural History Museum, Vienna On 7 August 1908, at a railway cutting beside the Danube near the village of Willendorf in Austria, a workman named Josef Veram was digging in an excavation directed by Josef Szombathy, Hugo Obermaier and Josef Bayer. From the loess he lifted a small stone figure, about 11 centimetres tall: a woman with heavy breasts, a rounded belly and wide hips, her thin arms resting on her breasts. Her head has no face. Instead it is covered with rows of carved bands, perhaps braided hair or a woven cap. She has become the most famous image of the Ice Age. - Carved from oolitic limestone, a stone not found at Willendorf, and once coloured with red ochre, traces of which survive. - Dated to the Gravettian period, roughly 30,000–25,000 years ago; a revised study of the site in 2015 placed the find layer at around 30,000 years. - It is one of more than a hundred small female figures made across Europe and into Siberia in the Upper Palaeolithic. The earliest known, the Venus of Hohle Fels, is about 40,000 years old. In 2022 a team at the Natural History Museum Vienna and the University of Vienna (Weber, Lukeneder, Harzhauser and colleagues) scanned the figure by micro-CT, comparing the grains and tiny fossils inside the stone with samples from across Europe. The closest match came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy, some 700 km away. If this is correct, the stone, or the figure, travelled a long way. The authors note that a match from eastern Ukraine could not be excluded, and the conclusion is probable, not certain. The name. Nineteenth-century archaeologists called such figures "Venus" figures after the Roman goddess of love, partly as a joke. The name carries no evidence about their meaning. A body without a face. The carver took great care over the body and the hair but gave no features to the face. Readings include anonymity, a type rather than a person, or a figure meant to be held and seen from above. None can be tested. Red ochre. Red pigment appears in many Palaeolithic burials and objects, and is often read as blood or life. Again, this is interpretation. The interactive cards above set out the main readings of the figure and the evidence for and against each. Palaeolithic Prehistory (ch41) and The Great Goddess (ch48), which discusses the rise and decline of the theory of a prehistoric goddess religion. Compare the Lion Man (V58). What's well supported by the evidence - An 11 cm limestone figure of a woman, found at Willendorf in 1908, made about 30,000 years ago, with traces of red ochre. - Its stone is not local; the 2022 study points to northern Italy. What is not supported - That it represents a goddess, or that a single "Mother Goddess" religion spanned Ice Age Europe. What's genuinely open - What it meant to the people who made it, and how it was used. - Whether the stone's origin near Lake Garda is confirmed by further work. The figure - Natural History Museum Vienna, "Venus of Willendorf", - "Venus of Willendorf", - Smarthistory, "Nude woman (Venus of Willendorf)", Studies - G. W. Weber, A. Lukeneder, M. Harzhauser et al., "The microstructure and the origin of the Venus…

title: Göbekli Tepe's Pillars
summary: Round enclosures of carved T-shaped pillars, some 5 metres tall, raised by people who had not yet begun to farm. Their foxes, snakes, vultures and belted human figures were hailed as the world's first temple. New work shows people also lived there, and claims about comets and lost civilisations are not supported.
text: Vault entry V60 · Relics & Objects · In place: Göbekli Tepe, Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey On a limestone ridge above the Harran plain in south-eastern Turkey, excavators have uncovered circles of great stone pillars, each shaped like a T, standing inside rough stone walls. The largest are over 5 metres tall. On their sides are carved foxes, boars, snakes, vultures, scorpions and cranes, and on two central pillars, arms that reach around from the back and hands that meet above a belt: the pillars are people, or beings. They were raised some 11,500 years ago, by people who hunted and gathered, before pottery, before metal and, it seemed at first, before farming. - The mound was recorded in a survey in 1963, but its broken slabs were taken for a medieval cemetery. - From 1995 Klaus Schmidt of the German Archaeological Institute (DAI) excavated it with the Şanlıurfa Museum, until his death in 2014. Excavation continues. - Four large enclosures (A–D) belong to the oldest layer, dated to about 9500–8000 BCE, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. Geophysical survey shows many more still buried. - It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018. Schmidt argued that Göbekli Tepe was a sanctuary, "the first temple", visited by hunter-gatherers who gathered there for feasts and ritual, and that the need to feed these gatherings helped drive the invention of farming. He also held that the enclosures were deliberately buried. More recent work by the excavation team has revised this picture. They have found cisterns, huge numbers of grinding stones, and domestic buildings, which suggest that people lived at the site. The enclosures may have been filled by slope slides rather than deliberate burial. Similar sites nearby, such as Karahan Tepe, show that Göbekli Tepe was part of a wider regional culture. Most archaeologists still see the enclosures as special, probably ritual buildings, but "temple" is now used with more caution. Pillars as persons. The T-shaped top is a head seen from the side; carved arms, hands, belts and loincloths make the pillars stylised human or superhuman beings. The two great central pillars of each enclosure may have been ancestors, spirits or gods. Nobody knows. Dangerous animals. The animals carved are overwhelmingly wild and often dangerous: predators, venomous creatures and carrion birds. Many readings link them to death or to the spirit world, especially the vultures. Carved skulls. Fragments of human skulls with carved grooves were found at the site (Gresky and colleagues, 2017), suggesting a skull cult, as known from other Neolithic sites in the region. The "Vulture Stone" and the comet. In 2017 two engineers, Martin Sweatman and Dimitrios Tsikritsis, read Pillar 43 as a star map recording a comet impact around 10,950 BCE. The excavators rejected this, pointing out that the carvings do not match the proposed constellations and that the pillar is later than the supposed event. Claims that Göbekli Tepe was built by a lost advanced civilisation have no archaeological support. The interactive plan above shows the layout of an enclosure. Touch a pillar to read about it. Neolithic Prehistory (ch42) and Palaeolithic Prehistory (ch41). Compare…

title: The Kojiki: the Shinpukuji Manuscript
summary: The 'Record of Ancient Matters', presented to the Japanese court in 712: the birth of the gods, Izanagi and Izanami, the sun goddess Amaterasu, and the descent of the emperors. Its oldest surviving copy was made by a monk of Shinpukuji in 1371–72 and is a National Treasure of Japan.
text: Vault entry V61 · Manuscripts · Ōsu Kannon (Shinpukuji), Nagoya, Japan In 1371 and 1372, a monk named Ken'yu at the Buddhist temple of Shinpukuji in Owari province copied out, in three volumes, a Japanese book that was already more than six hundred years old. It began: "At the time when heaven and earth first opened..." His copy is the oldest surviving manuscript of the Kojiki, the "Record of Ancient Matters", Japan's oldest surviving book. It is kept today at the temple of Ōsu Kannon in Nagoya and is a National Treasure of Japan. - According to its preface, the Emperor Tenmu (r. 673–686) ordered the old genealogies and legends to be corrected. A court attendant, Hieda no Are, memorised them. - Years later the courtier Ō no Yasumaro wrote down what Hieda no Are recited, and presented the book to Empress Genmei in 712. - Three volumes: the Age of the Gods; the legendary early emperors; and the emperors down to Empress Suiko (d. 628). - Written in Chinese characters, some used for their meaning in Chinese style, some for their sound to spell Japanese words, names and songs. - Eight years later, in 720, the court produced a second, longer history in formal Chinese, the Nihon Shoki, which tells many of the same myths in variant forms. - The first deities appear alone in the Plain of High Heaven and hide themselves. - The divine pair Izanagi and Izanami stir the ocean with a jewelled spear and create the islands of Japan and many gods. Izanami dies giving birth to fire; Izanagi follows her to the land of the dead, Yomi, and flees in horror. - Washing himself, Izanagi gives birth to the sun goddess Amaterasu, the moon god Tsukuyomi and the storm god Susanoo. Offended by Susanoo, Amaterasu hides in a cave and the world goes dark until the gods lure her out. - Amaterasu's grandson Ninigi descends to earth, and his great-grandson becomes Jimmu, the first emperor. The interactive scroll above gives the opening words in the book's own characters. For centuries the Kojiki was less read than the Nihon Shoki. The scholar Motoori Norinaga devoted over thirty years to its study, completing his Kojiki-den in 1798; he treated it as the pure record of ancient Japan. From 1868 the Meiji state used its account of the divine descent of the emperors in State Shinto. After 1945 the emperor renounced claims to divinity, and scholars read the Kojiki as a political and literary work of the early court, as well as a treasury of myth. Writing sounds with meanings. The Kojiki's mixed script, using Chinese characters for sound (the system later called man'yōgana), is the root of Japanese writing. The names of the gods are often long compounds whose parts carry meaning, such as Ame-no-minakanushi, "Lord of the Centre of Heaven". The imperial regalia. The myths explain the three sacred treasures of the emperor: the mirror used to lure Amaterasu from the cave, the jewels, and the sword Susanoo took from the tail of an eight-headed serpent. They are still kept at shrines and in the palace and are not shown to the public. Purity and pollution. Izanagi's washing after returning from Yomi is the mythic model of purification (misogi), central to Shinto ritual. Shinto (ch25) and…

title: The Inca Khipu
summary: Bundles of knotted cords that ran the largest empire of the Americas without an alphabet: census counts, tribute, calendars, and, the Spanish said, histories. The numbers were cracked in 1912. Whether some khipus also recorded words remains one of the great open questions of decipherment.
text: Vault entry V62 · Texts & Tablets · About 1,000 or more in museums worldwide In 1583, the Third Council of Lima, the Catholic bishops of Spanish Peru, ordered that the Indigenous peoples' khipus be taken and burned, because they were used to record "idolatry" and to confess sins in the old way. The khipu was the knotted cord of the Andes: a main cord from which hung dozens or hundreds of coloured pendant cords, knotted in patterns. With them the Inca, who ruled the largest state in the Americas, counted people, llamas, tribute and time. The Spanish chroniclers said that the khipu specialists, the khipukamayuq, could also read out histories, laws and songs from them. Whether that is true is still unknown. In 1912 the American historian Leland Locke showed how the numbers worked. Each pendant cord holds a number in base ten: clusters of single knots mark hundreds and tens, and the units position uses a long knot of 2 to 9 turns, or a figure-eight knot for one. An empty position means zero. Some khipus have a top cord recording the sum of a group of pendants, and it was these sums that proved the knots were numbers. Later work by Marcia and Robert Ascher (1981) documented how khipus were structured, with colour, cord order and subsidiary cords carrying further information. The interactive khipu above follows Locke's rules. It is illustrative, not a copy of a surviving khipu. Many khipus do not follow the numerical rules. That, with the chroniclers' reports, suggests that some khipus recorded words, names or narrative. - Gary Urton (2003) proposed that khipus encode information in binary choices: cord material, direction of spin, knot direction. - In 2016, a Harvard student, Manuel Medrano, working with Urton, matched six khipus to a Spanish census of the 1670s, and found that cord features might mark names. - In 2017 Sabine Hyland studied two khipus kept by the village of Collata in Peru, said by villagers to be letters written in a rebellion. They use 95 distinct combinations of colour and fibre, enough for a logosyllabic system, and she proposed that the final cords spell family names. None of these is an accepted decipherment. The question of narrative khipus remains open. Knots in a sacred landscape. Around Cusco, the Inca organised the valley's shrines (huacas) along some 41 lines, the ceques, radiating from the Temple of the Sun. The anthropologist R. T. Zuidema compared the ceque system to a khipu laid on the landscape; the comparison is influential but interpretive. Colour. Cord colours were meaningful, possibly marking categories such as types of tribute or social groups. What each colour meant is mostly unknown. Religious use and suppression. Chroniclers report khipus used to record sacrifices, the calendar of festivals, and confessions. Hence the Church's decree of 1583. Some Andean villages, however, kept khipus in ritual use into modern times. The Inca (ch44). Compare the Dresden Codex (V31) and the Codex Mendoza (V51), a record of Aztec tribute, for other record systems of the Americas, and the Phaistos Disc (V56) for an undeciphered text. What's well supported by the evidence - Khipus used by the Inca (and earlier by the Wari) to…

title: The Kalpa Sutra Manuscripts
summary: The Shvetambara Jain scripture of the lives of the Jinas, read aloud each year at Paryushana. From the 14th century it was copied on paper in western India with brilliant miniatures in red, blue and gold, above all the fourteen dreams of Queen Trishala before the birth of Mahavira.
text: Vault entry V63 · Manuscripts · Jain temple libraries (bhandars) in India; museums worldwide Each year at the end of summer, during the eight-day festival of Paryushana, Shvetambara Jain monks in western India read aloud from a book that the community holds among its most sacred: the Kalpa Sutra. On the fifth day the reading reaches the birth of Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Jina. Before his birth his mother, Queen Trishala, dreamed fourteen dreams, and in temples silver replicas of the dreams are shown to the congregation and families make offerings to honour them. For centuries the book was copied by hand and illustrated, in brilliant red, blue and gold, and gifting a copy to a temple library was an act of religious merit. - Tradition attributes it to the teacher Bhadrabahu, traditionally of the fourth century BCE; the text was fixed, with the rest of the Shvetambara canon, at the Council of Valabhi in the fifth century CE. - Three parts: the lives of the Jinas (above all Mahavira, then Parshva, Nemi and Rishabha); a list of the elders who handed on the teaching; and rules for monks during the rainy-season retreat. - The Kalpa Sutra is a Shvetambara text. The Digambara Jains do not accept it, and their tradition counts sixteen dreams, not fourteen. - The oldest copies are on palm leaf. From the late fourteenth century Jain scribes in Gujarat and Rajasthan began to use paper, and the number of illustrated copies grew rapidly. - The pages are long and narrow, imitating palm leaves, often with a painted dot or hole where a string once passed through. - The paintings are in the Western Indian style: flat red grounds, figures in profile with a projecting far eye, and lavish use of gold and ultramarine. Wealthy merchants commissioned them. - Thousands survive in the temple libraries, the bhandars, and in museums worldwide. The fourteen dreams. An elephant, a bull, a lion, the goddess Shri, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a vase, a lotus lake, the ocean, a celestial palace, a heap of jewels and a smokeless fire. Interpreters told the king that they announced the birth of a universal ruler or a Jina. The interactive cards above show all fourteen. The transfer of the embryo. In the Kalpa Sutra, Mahavira was first conceived by a Brahmin woman, Devananda, and the god Harinaigamesin moved the embryo to the womb of the Kshatriya queen Trishala. The episode is often painted. The Digambaras reject it. Books as objects of worship. Jains honour knowledge as sacred: on the festival of Jnana Panchami manuscripts are cleaned and venerated. Copying and donating books earned merit, which is why so many were made and preserved. Jainism (ch52). Compare the Diamond Sutra (V30) for a Buddhist book, and the Book of Kells (V21) for another tradition of sacred illumination. What's well supported by the evidence - A Shvetambara Jain scripture, read at Paryushana, containing the lives of the Jinas and the fourteen dreams of Trishala. - A large tradition of illustrated paper manuscripts from western India, mostly from the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries. What is not supported - That the text in its present form goes back unchanged to Bhadrabahu. It was transmitted…

title: The Benin Bronzes
summary: Thousands of cast brass plaques, heads and ivory carvings from the royal court of Benin, made for the altars of the Oba's ancestors and for the palace. The British army looted them in 1897 and sold them to museums around the world. Their return is one of the defining restitution cases of our time.
text: Vault entry V64 · Relics & Objects · Dispersed since 1897; returns to Nigeria under way since 2022 In February 1897, a British force of about 1,200 men under Admiral Harry Rawson marched on Benin City, capital of the kingdom of Benin in what is now southern Nigeria (not the modern Republic of Benin). The attack followed the killing, in January, of a British party that had tried to reach the city during a sacred royal festival. The city was taken and burned, and the Oba, Ovonramwen, was sent into exile. From the royal palace and its altars the soldiers carried away thousands of objects in brass, ivory and wood. They were auctioned to pay for the expedition and scattered to museums across Europe and North America. The world came to know them as the Benin Bronzes. - Commemorative heads of past Obas and Queen Mothers, placed on the ancestral altars of the palace, often holding a carved ivory tusk. - Hundreds of rectangular plaques that once clad the palace pillars, showing the Oba, chiefs, warriors, musicians, rituals and Portuguese traders. Most date from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. - Figures, bells, altar pieces, and carved ivory, including the famous ivory mask of Queen Mother Idia, adopted as the emblem of FESTAC 77, the 1977 Festival of Black and African Arts and Culture in Lagos. - Most are of brass or bronze, cast by the lost-wax method by the royal guild of casters, the Igun Eronmwon, which still works in Benin City today. - Much of the metal came from brass bracelets, manillas, brought by European traders. A 2023 chemical study traced many manillas to the Rhineland in Germany. The Digital Benin project (2022) recorded more than 5,000 objects in more than 130 institutions in 20 countries. The largest holding, about 900 objects, is in the British Museum, which is forbidden by law from permanently giving up objects in its collection. The interactive timeline above follows the objects' history. From 2021 several institutions agreed to return them: - Germany and Nigeria signed a joint declaration in July 2022, and German museums transferred ownership of more than 1,000 objects; the first 22 were handed over in December 2022. - The Horniman Museum in London transferred ownership of 72 objects in 2022; the Smithsonian returned 29 the same year. - In March 2023 a Nigerian presidential declaration recognised the Oba of Benin as the owner of returned objects. This led to debate, including in Germany, about where and how they would be displayed, and between the Oba's palace and plans for a new museum in Benin City. The Oba between worlds. The Oba was a sacred king, the link between the living and the royal ancestors. Heads on the altars honoured past kings and were the focus of ritual; they were not simply portraits. The head (uhunmwun) was the seat of a person's destiny and judgement. Mudfish and leopards. The Oba is often shown with legs in the form of mudfish, creatures that live in water and on land, linking him with Olokun, god of the sea and wealth. Leopards were royal animals, symbols of the Oba's power over the wild. Coral. The Oba's regalia of coral beads, shown on the heads and figures, carried spiritual power and were…

title: The Staff God of Tiwanaku
summary: A monolithic gateway of andesite at Tiwanaku, carved with a frontal figure holding two staffs, its head ringed with rays, flanked by rows of winged attendants. The figure belongs to a 'Staff God' tradition running through Andean art for two thousand years. Later writers linked it to the Inca creator Viracocha.
text: Vault entry V65 · Relics & Objects · In place: Tiwanaku, Bolivia At almost 3,850 metres above sea level, on the high plain near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia, a single block of andesite stands in the ruins of Tiwanaku. It is a gateway about 3 metres high and 4 metres wide, cut from one stone, cracked through the top. Above the doorway, in the centre of a carved frieze, a figure faces the viewer. It stands on a stepped platform and holds a staff in each hand, and its head is ringed with rays ending in animal heads. On both sides, rows of smaller winged figures turn toward it. The Spanish and later travellers called it the Puerta del Sol, the Gateway of the Sun. Its builders' name for it, and for the figure, is lost. - A great city and ceremonial centre that flourished from about 500 to 1000 CE, with monumental platforms and sunken courts, and influence across the southern Andes. - The gateway stands in the Kalasasaya, a large walled platform, but it was found broken and is probably not in its original position. It was later re-erected. - Tiwanaku declined around 1000–1100 CE, perhaps with drought. By the time of the Inca, centuries later, it was already an ancient ruin, and the Inca treated it as a sacred place of origin. - It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. The Staff God. A frontal figure holding two staffs appears across Andean art for two thousand years: on the Raimondi Stela of Chavín de Huántar in Peru, many centuries earlier; at Tiwanaku; and in Wari art. Scholars call this the Staff God or "Staff Deity". It seems to have been a major deity or a model of divine power, but its names and myths in each culture are unknown. Viracocha. The figure is popularly called Viracocha, the creator of Inca religion, whose myths say he rose from Lake Titicaca and created the sun and the peoples of the world at Tiwanaku. The link is attractive but late: the Inca myths were recorded by the Spanish, a thousand years after the gateway was carved. The rays and attendants. The head rays, the condor and puma heads, and the 48 winged attendants (in three rows of eight on each side) form a symmetrical composition. Its meaning is uncertain. The "calendar". The engineer Arthur Posnansky, in the early twentieth century, read the frieze as a calendar, and claimed that Tiwanaku was built more than 15,000 years ago on astronomical grounds. Archaeological dating shows the city is of the first millennium CE, and his calendar reading is not accepted. The interactive cards above summarise these readings. The Inca (ch44), for Viracocha and the later sacred status of Tiwanaku. Compare the Inca Khipu (V62) and the Codex Borgia (V41), from the religious art of Mesoamerica. What's well supported by the evidence - A monolithic gateway at Tiwanaku, carved with a frontal Staff God and winged attendants, from the city's florescence c. 500–1000 CE. - The Staff God as a long-lived Andean motif, from Chavín to Wari and Tiwanaku. What is not supported - That Tiwanaku is tens of thousands of years old, or that the frieze is a proven calendar. - That the figure is Viracocha as the Inca understood him. That identification is later. What's genuinely open -…

title: The Kebra Nagast
summary: Ethiopia's 'Glory of the Kings': how the Queen of Sheba visited Solomon, bore his son Menelik, and how Menelik brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. It gave the Solomonic dynasty its legitimacy for 650 years, and it is revered by Rastafari. A copy looted from Magdala was returned to Ethiopia in 1872.
text: Vault entry V66 · Manuscripts · Many Ge'ez manuscripts in Ethiopia and in European libraries In August 1872, the British Museum sent a manuscript back to Ethiopia. Four years earlier, a British army under Sir Robert Napier had stormed the mountain fortress of Magdala, where the Emperor Tewodros II took his own life, and carried away hundreds of manuscripts from his library and the churches. The new emperor, Yohannes IV, wrote to the British government asking for one book in particular: the Kebra Nagast, the "Glory of the Kings". Without it, he wrote, his people would not obey him. A copy was returned. The book told how Ethiopia's kings descended from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, and how the Ark of the Covenant came to Ethiopia. - Written in Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia, in 117 chapters. - According to its colophon, it was translated from Arabic (itself from Coptic) by a churchman named Yeshaq of Aksum, in the reign of the Solomonic dynasty's early kings; it is usually dated to about 1314–1322. Many scholars think it was largely composed in Ethiopia, drawing on older material, and that the translation claim adds authority. This is debated. - It is framed as a discussion among the 318 Orthodox fathers of the Council of Nicaea about where the true glory of kings lies. - Makeda, Queen of Sheba, visits Solomon in Jerusalem, learns his wisdom and turns to the God of Israel (expanding 1 Kings 10). - She bears Solomon's son, Menelik, who grows up in Ethiopia and later visits his father. - Menelik returns with the firstborn sons of Israel's nobles, who secretly take the Ark of the Covenant with them. The glory of Zion passes from Israel to Ethiopia, the new chosen people. The interactive book above follows the story and the book's own history. In 1270 a new dynasty took the Ethiopian throne claiming descent from Solomon. The Kebra Nagast gave this Solomonic dynasty its charter, and it ruled until 1974. Haile Selassie's 1955 constitution declared the emperor a descendant of Menelik. In the twentieth century the Kebra Nagast became important to Rastafari, who revere Haile Selassie as a descendant of Solomon and, for many, as divine. The Ark and the tabot. Ethiopian tradition holds that the Ark rests in the chapel of St Mary of Zion at Aksum, guarded by a single monk and shown to no one (see V07). Every Ethiopian Orthodox church keeps a tabot, a consecrated tablet representing the Ark, without which a church cannot be consecrated. At the feast of Timkat the tabots are carried in procession, wrapped in cloth. Zion. The book calls the Ark "Zion", and treats Ethiopia as the new Israel, a theme still central to Ethiopian Orthodox identity. Sheba. The Queen of Sheba appears in the Bible, the Qur'an (as the Queen of Saba, later named Bilqis) and Jewish legend. The Kebra Nagast gives her a name and a son. Where Sheba was, in Arabia or Africa, is debated. Eastern Orthodoxy (ch60), for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church; Diaspora Religions (ch40), for Rastafari; Sacred Kingship (ch49). Compare the Ark of the Covenant (V07), and the Benin Bronzes (V64) for another restitution. What's well supported by the evidence - A Ge'ez work compiled in the early…

title: The Aramaic Incantation Bowls
summary: Clay bowls written with spells in a spiral, sometimes around a drawing of a chained demon, and buried upside down under houses to trap evil. Made for Jewish, Christian, Mandaean and pagan clients in Babylonia, they are the everyday magic of the world that produced the Babylonian Talmud.
text: Vault entry V67 · Texts & Tablets · About 2,000 or more in museums and private collections Between 1888 and 1900, excavators from the University of Pennsylvania at Nippur in southern Iraq kept turning up ordinary clay bowls, the kind used for food, buried upside down under the floors of houses. Inside, written in ink, were spells that spiralled from the rim to the centre. Many had a drawing in the middle: a figure with wild hair, its hands and feet bound in chains. The spells were written for named clients, to protect their homes, wives, children and cattle from demons, the evil eye and curses. In 1913 James Montgomery published forty of them as Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur. Today some 2,000 or more are known. - Made in Mesopotamia under the Sasanian Persian empire, mostly in the 5th to 7th centuries CE, and continuing a little after the Islamic conquest. - Written in several scripts and dialects: Jewish Babylonian Aramaic (the largest group), Syriac, Mandaic, and a few in Middle Persian. Some are written in pseudo-script, imitation writing by scribes who could not write, or for clients who could not read. - Clients included Jews, Christians, Mandaeans, Zoroastrians and pagans, and a single scribe might write for clients of different faiths. - Many bowls have come from Nippur and other excavations; many more came onto the market after the 1990s from unrecorded sources in Iraq, raising questions about looting and ownership. - Many begin with a formula such as "Healing from heaven for..." followed by the client's name. Clients are named by their mothers' names ("N son of N"), as in many Jewish prayers for the sick. - They bind, seal and adjure demons, often in the name of God, angels and holy names. - Some are divorce writs (get) against the demoness Lilith, modelled on Jewish law: the demon is formally divorced from the household and must leave. Several invoke the sage Joshua bar Perahia, who appears in the Babylonian Talmud, as having sent such a writ. - Some quote biblical verses and use formulae also known from Jewish mystical texts. The spiral. The text coils around the bowl, sometimes from the rim inward, sometimes from the centre outward. The spiral may have been meant to confuse or trap demons, but this is an interpretation. Turned over. Buried face down at a threshold or in the corners of a room, the bowl became a trap or a dome over the demon. Some bowls were found in pairs, rim to rim, sealed together. The bound figure. The drawing in the centre often shows a demon or Lilith in chains, making the spell's binding visible. Holy names. The spells use divine names, including forms of the Tetragrammaton, and strings of letters and names whose meaning is uncertain, a form of sacred encoding shared with Jewish amulets and later Kabbalistic magic. The interactive bowl above shows the opening formula as a spiral. Turn it over to see how it was buried. Rabbinic Judaism (ch19), since the bowls come from the same time and place as the Babylonian Talmud; Mandaeans, Yazidis and Druze (ch56). Compare the Ketef Hinnom Silver Scrolls (V12), much earlier Jewish amulets. What's well supported by the evidence - Clay bowls with Aramaic spells…

title: The Tjurunga of Central Australia
summary: Sacred boards and stones of the Arrernte and their neighbours, which embody ancestral beings of the Dreaming and are seen only by those entitled to see them. Collectors took thousands into museums, and European thinkers built theories of religion on them. This entry tells their history but shows none of them.
text: Vault entry V68 · Relics & Objects · Held by their custodians; many in museums under restricted access In 1896, at the telegraph station in Alice Springs, Arrernte men held a long cycle of ceremonies in front of two outsiders: the biologist Baldwin Spencer and the telegraph master Francis Gillen. Among the things the men revealed were flat, oval boards of wood and stone, carved with circles, lines and arcs. They called them tjurunga (in older spelling, churinga). Three years later Spencer and Gillen published photographs of them. Today those photographs are treated as something that should never have been printed, and this entry does not reproduce any. - Sacred objects of the Arrernte and neighbouring peoples of Central Australia, made of wood or stone, usually oval and incised with designs. - In Arrernte belief they are bound to ancestral beings of the Altyerre, the Dreaming, and to particular places, songs and ceremonies. A tjurunga can be spoken of as the body or the spirit of an ancestor. - They are secret-sacred: held by men of the right kin and country, stored hidden, and shown only in ceremony to those entitled to see them. Seeing them without that right, or showing them to others, is a serious offence in Arrernte law. Spencer and Gillen's The Native Tribes of Central Australia (1899) and the missionary Carl Strehlow's studies made the Arrernte one of the most discussed peoples in the history of anthropology. In 1912 the French sociologist Émile Durkheim built much of The Elementary Forms of Religious Life on their evidence: the tjurunga became his model of the sacred, set apart from the everyday. Sigmund Freud's Totem and Taboo (1913) also drew on this literature. Few of these theorists ever met an Arrernte person. Tjurunga were sold, traded and taken into museums and private collections throughout the twentieth century. The largest single collection was made by Carl Strehlow's son, the linguist T. G. H. Strehlow, who from the 1930s recorded songs and ceremonies and received many objects from senior men who, he said, entrusted them to him for safekeeping. After his death in 1978 the collection became the subject of a long and bitter dispute. It is now held by the Strehlow Research Centre in Alice Springs, whose board controls access, and Arrernte people work with the Centre on how the objects should be cared for. Museums in Australia and overseas are returning secret-sacred objects to their communities. A map in a design. The circles, lines and tracks cut into a tjurunga are said to record an ancestor's journey and the places it made, a kind of sacred map that can be read only by those who know the story. This entry does not describe any particular design. Secrecy as part of the meaning. For a tjurunga, being hidden is not incidental: its power depends on being seen only by the right people at the right time. That is why this archive treats the refusal to show them as part of the record, not a gap in it. Aboriginal Australian Dreaming (ch61). Compare the Benin Bronzes (V64) for another history of taking and returning sacred objects. What's well supported by the evidence - Tjurunga are secret-sacred objects of the Arrernte and…

title: The Kumulipo
summary: A Hawaiian creation chant of 2,102 lines in sixteen ages, from the first night and the birth of the coral polyp to the gods and the chiefs. Composed in honour of an 18th-century chief, printed by King Kalākaua in 1889, and translated by the deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani while she was held prisoner.
