text: Vault entry V69 · Texts & Tablets · Printed 1889; translated 1897 In 1895, after a failed rising to restore her to the throne, Queen Liliʻuokalani, the last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, was held prisoner in a room of ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu. She spent part of her confinement translating a chant her brother, King Kalākaua, had printed in 1889: the Kumulipo, the genealogy of her line from the beginning of the world. Her English version was published in 1897. It begins in heat and darkness: "At the time when the earth became hot, at the time when the heavens turned about..." - A genealogical chant (koʻihonua) of 2,102 lines, divided into sixteen wā, "ages" or "eras". - It was composed in the eighteenth century in honour of the chief Kalaninuiamamao and handed down orally in his family, which led to Kalākaua and Liliʻuokalani. - The first seven wā belong to pō, the night: out of darkness are born, in order, the coral polyp, the creatures of the sea, the plants of the land, insects, birds and animals, each paired with its counterpart. - With the eighth wā comes ao, daylight: the first humans and the gods. The later wā trace generations of chiefs, ending with the line of Kalaninuiamamao. The interactive scroll above gives the opening lines in Hawaiian with Liliʻuokalani's translation. Printing the Kumulipo was political. Kalākaua, whose family was not of the old royal line, published it to show his descent from the gods and the first chiefs, at a time when American business interests were pressing on his kingdom. Liliʻuokalani's translation, made in captivity after the monarchy was overthrown in 1893, presented her people's learning to the outside world. Later translations include those of Martha Beckwith (1951) and the scholarship of Hawaiian writers since. Creation as genealogy. In the Kumulipo the world is not made; it is born. Every creature is a relative, and the chief at the end of the chant is kin to the coral, the fish and the stars. Reciting the genealogy was a way of affirming that kinship and that rank. Night and day. The division between pō (night) and ao (day) organises the whole chant: the long darkness of growth, then the light of gods and people. Paired births. Each creature of the sea is born alongside a creature of the land that shares part of its name, for example sea and land plants. Scholars read this pairing as a way of ordering nature through language. Evolution? Because the chant moves from simple sea life to complex land life, some writers have compared it with evolution. The comparison is a modern reading; the chant's own logic is genealogy. Oceania (ch63) and Creation & the First Order (ch46). Compare the Kojiki (V61), another creation account that ends in a royal line, and the Popol Vuh (V32). What's well supported by the evidence - A 2,102-line genealogical chant in sixteen wā, printed by Kalākaua in 1889 and translated by Liliʻuokalani, published 1897. - Its association with the chief Kalaninuiamamao and the royal line. What is not supported - That the chant is an early statement of scientific evolution. The resemblance is a modern comparison. What's genuinely open - How much the chant changed in oral…

title: The Pictish Stones
summary: Standing stones of the Picts of early medieval Scotland, carved with a small set of symbols repeated across the country: crescents crossed by broken rods, double discs, combs and mirrors, and a strange beast no one can identify. Later stones add the Christian cross. What the symbols mean, and whether they are writing, is unknown.
text: Vault entry V70 · Relics & Objects · About 350 stones and objects, mostly in north-east Scotland In the churchyard and by the roadside at Aberlemno in Angus, Scotland, great slabs of stone stand in the open. On one, above a hunting scene, are two strange signs: a crescent crossed by a rod bent in a V, and a double disc crossed by a rod bent in a Z. On another, the back of a Christian cross-slab shows warriors fighting, sometimes read as the battle of Nechtansmere (685). The same signs appear on stones across the north and east of Scotland. They were carved by the Picts, a people who left almost no writing of their own, and nobody knows what they mean. - Some 350 carved stones and objects bear the symbols, most in north-east Scotland. - Some thirty to fifty different symbols are recognised, depending on how variants are counted, some abstract (crescent and V-rod, double disc and Z-rod, "tuning fork", rectangle), some animals (the Pictish Beast, wolf, bull, eagle, salmon, snake), and some objects (mirror and comb). - They usually appear in pairs, sometimes with the mirror and comb added below. - In 1903 J. Romilly Allen and Joseph Anderson sorted the stones into Class I (symbols on rough stones), Class II (symbols with a relief Christian cross on shaped slabs) and Class III (crosses without symbols). The classes broadly follow the Picts' conversion to Christianity from the sixth century. Theories include names of people or families, marks of rank or lineage, records of marriage alliances, memorials, or boundary markers. In 2010 Rob Lee, Philip Jonathan and Pauline Ziman argued from a statistical measure, Shannon entropy, that the symbol pairs behave like a written language. The computational linguist Richard Sproat and others replied that such statistics cannot distinguish writing from other symbol systems. The question is open. Pagan or Christian? The Class I stones are often assumed to be pre-Christian, but no one knows whether the symbols had any religious meaning. On Class II stones they sit comfortably beside the cross, which suggests they meant something the Church could accept, such as names or ranks. The Pictish Beast. The most distinctive animal, with a long snout, a crest and scrolled feet, is drawn so consistently that it must have had a fixed meaning. Suggestions include a dolphin, a water-horse (kelpie) or a mythical creature. Ogham beside the symbols. Some Pictish stones also carry inscriptions in ogham, the Irish stroke alphabet, which are themselves largely unreadable because the Pictish language is poorly known. Celtic & Germanic (ch14) and Patristic Christianity (ch22), for the conversion. Compare the Phaistos Disc (V56) and the Rohonc Codex (V11) for other symbol systems no one can read, and the Book of Kells (V21), from the same Insular art world. What's well supported by the evidence - About 350 Pictish carved stones and objects with a shared set of some thirty to fifty symbols, mostly from the sixth to ninth centuries, and the Class I–III sequence into Christian cross-slabs. What is not supported - Any decipherment of the symbols, or any proven religious meaning. What's genuinely open - Whether the symbols are writing, and…

title: The Stećci: Medieval Tombstones of Bosnia
summary: Great carved gravestones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbours, shaped as slabs, chests and gabled houses, carved with spirals, crescents, hunts, circle dances and a man with a raised hand. Long called the tombstones of the dualist Bogomil heretics, they were in fact raised by Catholic, Orthodox and Bosnian Church Christians alike.
text: Vault entry V71 · Relics & Objects · In place across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia On a hillside at Radimlja, near Stolac in Herzegovina, about 130 great blocks of limestone lie in rows beside the road. Some are flat slabs, some chests, some shaped like little houses with gabled roofs. Their sides are carved with spirals, vines, crescents, horsemen hunting deer, and a line of dancers holding hands. On one, a man stands with his right hand raised and open, the hand carved larger than life. These are stećci (singular stećak), the medieval tombstones of Bosnia and its neighbours, and for a century and a half they were wrongly known as the graves of heretics. - About 70,000 stećci are recorded at some 3,300 sites, most in Bosnia and Herzegovina, others in Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia. - They date from the twelfth to the sixteenth centuries, most from the fourteenth and fifteenth. - Most are undecorated; a minority carry carved ornament or figures, and a smaller number inscriptions in bosančica, the Bosnian form of Cyrillic. - In 2016, 28 of the sites, with some 4,000 stones, were inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the nineteenth century, scholars linked the stećci to the Bogomils, a dualist movement of the medieval Balkans that taught that the material world was the work of an evil power (see Gnosticism, ch17, and Manichaeism, ch55). Medieval Bosnia had its own church, the Bosnian Church, which its Catholic and Orthodox opponents accused of that heresy. The idea that the stećci were "Bogomil tombstones" became popular and is still repeated. Modern historians and archaeologists reject it. Stećci are found in areas that were Catholic and Orthodox as well as in the lands of the Bosnian Church; some bear crosses and Christian inscriptions; and they were used by all three communities, as UNESCO's description states. Whether the Bosnian Church itself was dualist is also debated. The raised hand. The best-known figure has been read as a greeting, an oath, a gesture of prayer, or a sign of rank. There is no medieval explanation. Sky signs. Crescents, stars and discs are common. Because the crescent later became associated with Islam, some have read them as Muslim, but they appear on stones made before the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia in 1463, and were part of older Christian and folk symbolism. Life carved in stone. Hunting scenes, tournaments and the kolo, the circle dance still danced in the region, may show the life of the dead person, a funeral rite, or both. House-shaped tombs. Gabled stećci resemble houses, echoing the widespread idea of the grave as the home of the dead. The interactive cards above set out the main motifs. Eastern Orthodoxy & Byzantium (ch60), and Gnosticism (ch17) and Manichaeism (ch55) for the Bogomils. Compare the Pictish Stones (V70), another set of carved stones whose symbols are unexplained. What's well supported by the evidence - About 70,000 medieval tombstones from the 12th to 16th centuries, at some 3,300 sites in four modern countries, 28 of them a UNESCO site since 2016. - Their use by Catholic, Orthodox and Bosnian Church communities. What is not supported - That they are…

title: The Book of Shadows
summary: The handwritten ritual book of Gerald Gardner's witchcraft, copied by each new initiate, and the founding scripture of Wicca. Gardner presented its rites as those of a surviving ancient witch cult; historians have traced them to twentieth-century sources, from Crowley to folklore, and to Doreen Valiente's poetry.
text: Vault entry V72 · Manuscripts · Gerald Gardner's manuscripts in private hands; copied by initiates Some time in the late 1940s, a retired British customs officer named Gerald Gardner began filling a leather-bound notebook with rituals, charms and invocations, written in mock-archaic spelling: Ye Bok of ye Art Magical. Gardner said he had been initiated in 1939 into a coven of hereditary witches in the New Forest, the survivors of an ancient pagan religion. His notebook, renamed the Book of Shadows, became the ritual book of the religion he launched, Wicca. Every new initiate was expected to copy it out by hand. - A working ritual manual: the casting of the circle, the calling of the quarters, initiation rites for three degrees, seasonal festivals, and the Charge of the Goddess. - It changed constantly. Gardner revised it through the 1950s, and his students adapted it; there was never one fixed text. - It is oath-bound: in traditional (Gardnerian and Alexandrian) covens, its contents are kept secret. Versions have been published, and they differ. In 1953 Doreen Valiente was initiated into Gardner's coven. She saw that much of the book came from the writings of Aleister Crowley (see V73) and from ceremonial magic, and she feared this would discredit the Craft. Gardner invited her to rewrite. Her poetic version of the Charge of the Goddess, in which the Goddess speaks to her worshippers, is now one of the best-known texts of modern Paganism. In 1964 she gave the first known public form of the Wiccan Rede: "Eight words the Wiccan Rede fulfil: an it harm none, do what ye will." Gardner presented the rites as ancient. Historians, above all Ronald Hutton in The Triumph of the Moon (1999), have traced them to sources of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries: Crowley, the Golden Dawn, Charles Leland's Aradia (1899), Freemasonry, folklore, and Margaret Murray's theory of a surviving witch cult, which historians of the witch trials reject (see The Witch Trials, ch32). Whether Gardner met any real group of practising witches before he wrote is uncertain; some researchers have argued for a New Forest group of some kind, but no evidence shows it continued an ancient religion. The circle and the pentacle. The rites centre on the magic circle, cast to make a sacred space, and the pentacle, a disc marked with a five-pointed star and other signs, taken from ceremonial magic. A copied book. The instruction to copy the book by hand made each initiate's copy a record of their own lineage, and handwriting itself part of the tradition. The Goddess and the God. The book gave form to Wicca's pair of deities, the Goddess and the Horned God (see the Pantheon). Wicca & Modern Paganism (ch38), with The Witch Trials (ch32) for the history Gardner claimed. Compare the Book of the Law (V73), from which some of its words came. What's well supported by the evidence - A ritual manual begun by Gerald Gardner in the late 1940s, revised with Doreen Valiente in the 1950s, and the foundation of Wicca. - Its borrowings from Crowley, ceremonial magic, Leland and folklore. What is not supported - That its rites preserve an ancient pagan witch religion. What's genuinely open - Whether…

title: The Book of the Law
summary: Sixty-five handwritten pages that Aleister Crowley said were dictated to him in a Cairo hotel in April 1904 by a being called Aiwass, and the scripture of his religion, Thelema: 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law.' The manuscript was lost and found again five years later in his attic, behind a pair of skis.
text: Vault entry V73 · Manuscripts · Manuscript in private hands; facsimiles published In March 1904, in Cairo, Rose Kelly, the wife of the English occultist Aleister Crowley, fell into what he called a trance and told him that the god Horus was waiting for him. To test her, he took her to the museum and asked her to find Horus. She walked past several images and stopped at a small painted wooden stele of a priest named Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu standing before the falcon-headed god. Its museum number was 666, the number of the Beast of Revelation, which Crowley had taken as his own. On 8, 9 and 10 April, at noon, Crowley sat at a desk in their rooms and, he said, wrote down the words of a voice that spoke from behind him. The result was Liber AL vel Legis, the Book of the Law. - Three chapters, one for each day, written in an hour each, on 65 sheets of paper. - Chapter I speaks as Nuit, the goddess of the night sky; chapter II as Hadit, the point at her centre; chapter III as Ra-Hoor-Khuit, a warlike form of Horus. - Crowley named the speaker Aiwass, a "praeterhuman intelligence", and regarded the book as a revelation announcing a new age, the Aeon of Horus. - Its key sayings: "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law" (I:40), "Love is the law, love under will" (I:57), and "Every man and every woman is a star" (I:3). In Thelema, "will" means one's true purpose, not whim. Crowley was at first reluctant to follow the book. The manuscript was mislaid, and in 1909 he found it in the attic of his house, Boleskine, on Loch Ness, while looking for a pair of skis. He took this as a sign and published the text that year. The book forbids any change to its text, and printed editions have since included a facsimile of the handwriting, errors and corrections included. Numbers and letters. Crowley used gematria constantly, and the book itself invites it: it says a later "child" will find its key, and verses such as II:76 give strings of letters and numbers never explained. Its number, 220, is the count of its verses. The stele. The Stele of Revealing (Cairo Museum, A 9422) is a genuine funerary stele of the 25th–26th Dynasty, about the seventh century BCE, showing the priest before Ra-Horakhty under the arching sky goddess Nut. Crowley had its texts translated and worked them into the book. The 666 is its inventory number in the museum's old Bulaq register, a coincidence that Crowley read as a sign. The unicursal hexagram. Thelema's emblem, a six-pointed star drawn in a single line, was popularised by Crowley; its earlier history is unclear. Theosophy & the Occult Revival (ch37). Compare the Book of Shadows (V72), which borrowed from it, the Emerald Tablet (V03) for another text claimed as revelation, and the Papyrus of Ani (V20) for the Egypt it drew on. What's well supported by the evidence - A handwritten text produced by Crowley in Cairo on 8–10 April 1904, published from 1909, and the scripture of Thelema. - The stele is a real Egyptian object with museum number 666. What is not supported - That the text was dictated by a non-human being. That is Crowley's account and a matter of faith; no outside evidence can test it. What's genuinely open - How much…

title: The Satanic Bible
summary: Anton LaVey's book of 1969, the founding text of the Church of Satan: an atheist philosophy of self-interest, indulgence and personal responsibility, in which Satan is a symbol, not a being. It borrows heavily from an 1896 tract and from John Dee's Enochian calls, and it remains in print.
text: Vault entry V74 · Texts & Tablets · Published by Avon Books, 1969 On Walpurgisnacht, 30 April 1966, in a black-painted Victorian house on California Street in San Francisco, a former carnival organist and occult lecturer named Anton Szandor LaVey shaved his head and declared the founding of the Church of Satan. Three years later, in December 1969, the paperback house Avon Books published his Satanic Bible. Its cover carried a goat's head inside an inverted five-pointed star: the Sigil of Baphomet. The book has never gone out of print, and it remains the core text of the Church of Satan. It is divided into four "books", each linked to an element and a figure of hell: - The Book of Satan (fire): a furious attack on conventional morality and "the Golden Rule". - The Book of Lucifer (air): LaVey's essays on human nature, sex, love and hate, and the Church's philosophy. - The Book of Belial (earth): ritual and "greater magic", which LaVey presents as a psychological technique. - The Book of Leviathan (water): invocations and the nineteen Enochian calls. It opens with the Nine Satanic Statements, beginning "Satan represents indulgence instead of abstinence!" LaVey did not believe in a literal devil or God. In the book Satan is a symbol of human nature, pride, carnal desire and rebellion against religious restraint; the Church of Satan describes itself as atheistic. Its ethic combines individualism, self-interest and responsibility to those who deserve it. It rejects the crimes attributed to "Satanists" by Christian polemic (see The Witch Trials, ch32). - The Book of Satan is largely adapted from Might Is Right (1896), a social-Darwinist tract published under the name "Ragnar Redbeard", usually identified as the New Zealander Arthur Desmond. LaVey named Redbeard among the book's dedicatees but did not mark the borrowing. The text was out of copyright; critics call it plagiarism, and the Church of Satan disputes the charge. - The Enochian calls are those of the Elizabethan magus John Dee and Edward Kelley, taken from the version printed by Aleister Crowley and rewritten with Satanic wording. The Sigil of Baphomet. The goat's head in an inverted pentagram, with the Hebrew letters of Leviathan (לויתן) around it, combines Éliphas Lévi's Baphomet and a design from Stanislas de Guaita's La Clef de la magie noire (1897). The Church of Satan adopted it as its emblem. Inversion. Much of the book's imagery reverses Christian symbols (the inverted star, the black mass), used as theatre and psychodrama, not worship. The elements. Assigning the four books to fire, air, earth and water borrows the structure of Western ceremonial magic. Satanism (ch39), and Theosophy & the Occult Revival (ch37) for Lévi and Crowley. Compare the Book of the Law (V73) and the Codex Gigas (V09), the "Devil's Bible" of an earlier age. What's well supported by the evidence - A book by Anton LaVey, published in 1969, the founding text of the Church of Satan (founded 1966), which describes itself as atheistic. - Its extensive borrowing from Might Is Right and its adaptation of Dee's Enochian calls. What is not supported - That the book teaches the worship of a literal devil, or the…

title: The Golden Plates
summary: Metal plates engraved in 'reformed Egyptian' that Joseph Smith said an angel led him to in a hill in western New York, and from which he dictated the Book of Mormon, published in 1830. Eleven witnesses signed statements that they had seen them. No one else has, and their existence and nature are matters of faith and debate.
text: Vault entry V75 · Relics & Objects · Not held: returned, by Joseph Smith's account, to an angel Before dawn on 22 September 1827, Joseph Smith, a twenty-one-year-old farmer's son of Manchester, near Palmyra in western New York, went up a hill near his family's farm. He said that an angel named Moroni had shown him a stone box buried in its side four years earlier, and that this night, at last, he was permitted to take what was in it: a book of thin metal plates that looked like gold, bound with three rings and engraved in an unknown script. From them, over the next two years, he dictated the Book of Mormon, the founding scripture of the Latter Day Saint movement. The plates themselves, he said, were then taken back by the angel. - 1823: Moroni first appears to Smith and tells him of the buried record. - 1827: Smith receives the plates, with two seer stones set in a frame, the "interpreters". He keeps them covered and says he is forbidden to show them. - 1828: Martin Harris, a farmer who financed the book, takes a sheet of characters copied from the plates to the classicist Charles Anthon in New York. Harris said Anthon confirmed them; Anthon later wrote that he had told Harris they were a hoax. That summer the first 116 pages of the dictated translation, lent to Harris, are lost. - 1829: With Oliver Cowdery as scribe, Smith dictates most of the text in about three months. Three Witnesses sign a statement that an angel showed them the plates; Eight Witnesses that Smith showed them and they "did handle with our hands". - 1830: The Book of Mormon is printed at Palmyra by E. B. Grandin. Smith said the plates recorded, in "reformed Egyptian", the history of peoples who came from the Near East to the Americas, above all the Nephites and Lamanites, and the visit of the risen Christ to them. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and other Latter Day Saint churches hold it to be scripture alongside the Bible. About 28 per cent of the original dictated manuscript survives, damaged by years in the cornerstone of the Nauvoo House; the printer's manuscript copied from it is nearly complete. In 2017 the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints bought the printer's manuscript from the Community of Christ for $35 million, the highest price then paid for a manuscript. A sheet of characters, the "Caractors" document, also survives. Reformed Egyptian. The characters on the Caractors document do not match any known writing system. Latter-day Saint scholars have compared them with Egyptian scripts; Egyptologists and linguists have not accepted any match. Seer stones. Witnesses described Smith dictating with his face in a hat, looking at a seer stone. The Church has published photographs of one such stone. The witnesses' statements. Printed in every edition, the eleven testimonies are the book's own evidence for the plates. Latter-day Saint historians point out that none of the witnesses formally withdrew his testimony, though several later broke with Smith. What they experienced is debated. New Religious Movements (ch35). Compare the Book of the Law (V73), another nineteenth- and twentieth-century scripture presented as revealed, and the Emerald…

title: The Báb's Star Tablet
summary: A tablet in the Báb's own hand, its lines of Arabic writing laid out as a five-pointed star, the haykal or 'temple', whose points stand for the head, hands and feet of the human body. The Báb, the forerunner of the Bahá'í Faith, wrote such stars as talismans, full of letter-numbers and derivatives of the word Bahá, 'glory'.
text: Vault entry V76 · Manuscripts · British Library, London (Or. 6887) In 2019, to mark two hundred years since the birth of the Báb, the British Library put on display a sheet of paper covered in fine Arabic script. The lines of writing were not laid out in rows. They formed a five-pointed star, each of its five strokes made of words, the whole in the Báb's own hand. The Báb called such a figure a haykal, a "temple", and he wrote many of them: prayers, talismans and letters in the shape of the human body. - Siyyid ʻAlí-Muḥammad Shírází (1819–1850), a merchant of Shiraz, declared in 1844 that he was the Báb, the "Gate", and later that he was the promised Qāʼim of Shiʻi Islam, the bearer of a new revelation. - His movement spread rapidly in Iran and was violently suppressed. He was imprisoned in the fortresses of Mākū and Chihrīq and executed by firing squad in Tabriz in 1850; thousands of his followers were killed. - He foretold "Him whom God shall make manifest". Most Bábís came to recognise that figure in Baháʼu'lláh, whose followers founded the Baháʼí Faith. The Báb is revered by Baháʼís as a Manifestation of God and the forerunner of their faith. In his book the Persian Bayán, the Báb gave instructions for writing a haykal. Its five lines frame the star, and he wrote verses into them, often made up of derivatives of a single word. One famous tablet, addressed to Baháʼu'lláh, consists of 360 derivatives of the word Bahá, "glory" or "splendour", the root of Baháʼu'lláh's title. The Báb said men should carry such a star as a talisman; for women he prescribed a design of concentric circles. The interactive star above is schematic: its lines repeat an invocation and derivatives of Bahá in the manner of the star tablets, and it can show the human form the star stands for and the numbers inside it. The body as temple. The five points of the haykal are the head, two hands and two feet. In the Báb's writings the human being is a temple of God, and the star makes the text into a body. Abjad numbers. In the abjad system each Arabic letter has a number, and the Báb used it constantly. The haykal's five lines give the letter hāʼ (ه = 5) and its six chambers the letter wāw (و = 6), which together spell huwa (هو), "He", a name for God in Islamic mysticism. The Báb also organised his calendar and writings around 19, the value of wāḥid, "one": the Badíʻ calendar has 19 months of 19 days. Bahá. The name Bahá has the abjad value 9, which is why nine became a symbol of the Baháʼí Faith, and the source of its nine-pointed star. No image of the Báb. Baháʼís treat photographs and portraits of the Báb and Baháʼu'lláh with great reverence and do not display them publicly, so this entry shows none. Baháʼí & New Faiths (ch65), with Islam (ch21) and Sufism (ch27) for the Shiʻi and mystical background. Compare the Sana'a Palimpsest (V29) and the Birmingham Qur'an (V28) for other Arabic sacred manuscripts, and the Kartarpur Bir (V33) for a founder's scripture. What's well supported by the evidence - The Báb (1819–1850) wrote tablets in the form of a five-pointed star, including one held by the British Library (Or. 6887) and displayed in 2019. - His own writings describe…

title: The Haitian Vèvè
summary: Designs traced on the temple floor in cornmeal, flour or ash by a Vodou priest or priestess to call a particular lwa, or spirit: a cross and cane for Legba, serpents for Damballa, a heart for Ezili. Each is made to be danced over and erased. Their origins in Kongo and Fon sign-traditions are still being traced.
text: Vault entry V77 · Texts & Tablets · Drawn anew for each ceremony In a Vodou temple (ounfò) in Haiti, before the drums begin, the priest (oungan) or priestess (manbo) kneels on the earthen floor of the dance space, the peristil, beside the painted centre-post, the poto mitan. Taking a handful of cornmeal, they let it trickle between thumb and fingers, tracing an intricate design on the ground: a cross with a walking stick, serpents around a pole, a heart filled with lattice. Each design is a vèvè, the sign of a particular lwa (spirit). Offerings are placed on it, songs are sung to it, and as the ceremony goes on the dancers' feet blur it into the dust. - Ritual ground drawings made in cornmeal, flour, ash, coffee grounds or powdered brick, each belonging to one lwa. - Drawn at the start of a service, to call the lwa and mark where offerings are laid. Legba's vèvè is usually drawn first, since he opens the gate between the human world and the spirits. - Vèvè vary between houses and priests. Collections of them have been published, notably Milo Rigaud's Vè-Vè: Diagrammes rituels du Voudou (1974). - They are also painted on temple walls, flags and, since the mid-twentieth century, in Haitian art. The interactive floor above traces schematic vèvè for four lwa: - Legba, the old man at the crossroads, keeper of the gate: a cross and a cane. - Damballa, the white serpent of the sky and waters, with his wife Ayida-Wedo, the rainbow: serpents rising around a pole or an egg. - Ezili Freda, lwa of love, beauty and luxury: a heart, often latticed. Her fierce counterpart Ezili Dantor's heart is pierced by a knife. - Baron Samedi, head of the Gede, the spirits of the dead: a cross on a tomb. Older writers traced vèvè to the Taíno, the Indigenous people of Hispaniola. More recent scholarship, following Robert Farris Thompson's Flash of the Spirit (1983), emphasises African roots: the Kongo cosmogram, a cross within a circle marking the boundary between the living and the dead, and the ground drawings and sign systems of the Fon and neighbouring peoples of West Africa, from whom much of Vodou's liturgy descends. Catholic imagery, and Masonic and ceremonial designs, have also shaped some vèvè. The mix is still debated. A drawing as a door. The vèvè is not a picture of the lwa but a point of contact: offerings placed on it reach the spirit, and the lwa may come to "mount" a devotee in possession. The crossroads. Many vèvè are built on a cross, the crossroads where the human and spirit worlds meet, echoing the Kongo cosmogram and Legba's role. Made to be erased. A vèvè exists only for the ceremony; its effacement by dancing feet is part of the rite. African Diaspora Religions (ch40) and African Traditional Religion (ch33). Compare the Pantheon's entries for Papa Legba, Ezili Freda and Baron Samedi, and the Tilma of Guadalupe (V13) for another meeting of Catholic and Indigenous imagery. What's well supported by the evidence - Vèvè are ritual ground drawings of Haitian Vodou, each belonging to a lwa, traced in cornmeal or other powders at ceremonies and effaced during them. - They are documented in ethnographies and collections of the twentieth century, such as…

title: The Malleus Maleficarum
summary: The 'Hammer of Witches', a Latin handbook on identifying, trying and punishing witches, written by the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer after a failed witch trial at Innsbruck. How much it was actually used in the trials, and how far Jacob Sprenger contributed, are both debated.
text: Vault entry V78 · Texts & Tablets · First printed at Speyer, 1486 In the autumn of 1485 a Dominican inquisitor named Heinrich Kramer (in Latin, Institoris) was questioning women in Innsbruck. One of them, Helena Scheuberin, a burgher's wife, had defied him; Kramer's questions about her sexual life scandalised the court. Her lawyers had the proceedings dismissed on procedural grounds, and the local bishop, Georg Golser of Brixen, told Kramer he had "presumed much that had not been proved" and ordered him out of the diocese, calling him, in a letter, a man who seemed to have become childish with age. Kramer left, and wrote a book. It was printed at Speyer in 1486 as the Malleus Maleficarum, "the Hammer of Witches". - Three parts. Part I argues that witchcraft is real and that denying it is heresy; Part II describes what witches do (pacts with the devil, harming livestock and crops, impotence, flight) and the remedies; Part III is a legal manual for prosecuting them, including the use of torture and of deception to obtain confessions. - The bull. Kramer printed at the front the papal bull Summis desiderantes affectibus, issued by Innocent VIII in 1484 at his request, which empowered him and a colleague to act against witches in German lands. Printing it made the book look papally endorsed; the bull itself endorses the inquisitors, not the book. - The approbation. The book also carried an approval from the theology faculty of the University of Cologne. The faculty had in fact given a qualified opinion, and the printed document presents it as unanimous and unreserved; most historians regard this as manipulated or partly forged by Kramer. - Sprenger. From 1519 the Dominican theologian Jacob Sprenger is named as co-author. Several historians argue that Sprenger had little or nothing to do with it, and even that he opposed Kramer; others defend a shared role. The question is contested. - Women. The book insists that witchcraft is chiefly a female crime and offers a notorious false etymology: femina from fe (faith) and minus (less), "because she is always weaker to hold and preserve the faith". The Malleus was reprinted many times: around thirteen or fourteen editions by 1520, and another burst of editions from 1574 to 1669. The Inquisition itself soon distanced itself from Kramer's procedures, and the Spanish Inquisition in 1538 warned its judges not to believe everything the book said. Its use was greatest in secular courts, especially in the German lands. How far it actually caused trials is debated: it gave prosecutors a ready-made theory and procedure, but the great waves of trials came decades later, and many courts never cite it. The hammer. The title copies the style of inquisitors' manuals that called themselves "hammers" of heretics: the book is a weapon aimed at a category of person. The printed page as authority. Its most powerful signs are paratextual: a papal bull at the front and a university approbation at the back, both used to make a private campaign look like the voice of the Church. The witch as inversion. The book builds the image of the witch as the mirror of the sacraments: a pact instead of baptism, the devil's service instead…

title: The Zohar, First Printings
summary: Kabbalah's great book was printed for the first time in two rival Italian editions, Mantua in three volumes and Cremona in one folio, over the protests of rabbis who thought secret lore should stay in manuscript. The Mantua pagination is still used to cite the Zohar today.
text: Vault entry V79 · Texts & Tablets · Mantua, 1558–1560, and Cremona, 1558–1560 In 1553, in Rome and across Italy, copies of the Talmud were heaped up and burned on the orders of the Church. Five years later, in two small Italian cities a short journey apart, presses began to print a book that had until then circulated only in manuscript among a few initiates: the Zohar, the "Book of Radiance", the great text of Kabbalah. In Mantua, two Jewish partners, Meir ben Ephraim of Padua and Jacob ben Naphtali ha-Kohen of Gazzuolo, printed it in three quarto volumes (1558–1560). In Cremona, the Christian printer Vincenzo Conti issued it as a single large folio (1558–1560). Which press put the first sheets out is reported differently; the two editions appeared in rivalry, almost together. Printing the Zohar meant making secret lore public, and some rabbis objected fiercely. Meir Katzenellenbogen of Padua and others argued that Kabbalah should be taught only by master to disciple. The Mantua printers answered with a long responsum by Isaac de Lattes, printed in their first volume, which defended publication and urged the study of the Zohar as a remedy for the corruption of the age. The Mantua text, more carefully edited, became the standard: the page numbering of the Mantua Zohar is still used to cite the book today. The Cremona edition was handsomer but less accurate. That a Christian press printed it matters too. Christian scholars had been reading Kabbalah since the fifteenth century, and some hoped the Zohar would show Jews the truth of Christianity; the Talmud was burned, and the Zohar was licensed. - Written mostly in Aramaic, the Zohar is a vast commentary on the Torah told as the wanderings and conversations of Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai, a sage of the second century, and his companions in Galilee. - It opens: "Rabbi Ḥizkiyah opened: 'Like a rose among thorns'" (Song of Songs 2:2), reading the rose as the Community of Israel and, within God, as the Shekhinah among the other sefirot. - Its central idea is the ten sefirot, the aspects of God through which the hidden divine, the Ein Sof ("without end"), becomes manifest, and the union of the masculine and feminine within God that Jewish practice helps restore. Tradition attributes the Zohar to Shimon bar Yoḥai. It first appears in Castile in the 1280s, circulated by Moses de León, who said he was copying an ancient manuscript. Gershom Scholem concluded that Moses de León wrote most of it himself; much recent scholarship sees a group of authors and a longer process of composition and editing, completed in large part by the printers of the 1550s. For many religious Jews it remains an ancient revealed text. The rose. The thirteen petals of the rose in the opening homily are read as the thirteen attributes of mercy (Exodus 34:6–7), and its colours, red and white, as judgment and mercy. Light. Zohar means "radiance", from Daniel 12:3: "the wise shall shine like the radiance of the firmament". The sefirot as a body and a tree. The ten sefirot are pictured as the limbs of a primordial human form and as a tree, the diagram that later Christian and Hermetic Kabbalah took up. Kabbalah (ch26), with Rabbinic Judaism…

title: The Sefer Yetzirah
summary: A very short Hebrew book describing creation through 'thirty-two wondrous paths': ten sefirot and the twenty-two letters, divided into three mothers, seven doubles and twelve simples and combined in 231 gates. Its date and setting are among the most disputed questions in Jewish studies.
text: Vault entry V80 · Texts & Tablets · Date of composition disputed (late antiquity to early Islamic period) It is one of the shortest books in Jewish literature, a few pages long, and one of the strangest. It begins: "With thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom Yah, the Lord of hosts, engraved and created his world." It then describes those paths: ten sefirot and the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. God, in this book, makes the world the way a scribe makes a text, by carving, weighing and combining letters. The Sefer Yetzirah, the "Book of Formation" or "Book of Creation", is the oldest surviving work of Jewish speculation about language and cosmos, and the root of much later Kabbalah. - Thirty-two paths. Ten sefirot belimah, "numbers (or spheres) of nothingness", and twenty-two letters. The sefirot here are not yet the divine attributes of later Kabbalah: they are ten dimensions, the depths of beginning and end, good and evil, above and below, east, west, north and south. - Three mothers. The letters aleph, mem and shin (א מ ש) correspond to air, water and fire. - Seven doubles. The seven letters that once had two pronunciations, bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, pe, resh, tav (ב ג ד כ פ ר ת), correspond to the seven planets, the seven days and seven openings of the head. - Twelve simples. The other twelve letters correspond to the twelve signs of the zodiac, the twelve months and twelve organs or faculties. - The 231 gates. Every letter is paired with every other, forming 231 gates (the number of pairs among twenty-two letters), and "all that is formed and all that is spoken" goes out through them. Tradition attributes the book to the patriarch Abraham. Its date is one of the most disputed questions in Jewish studies: Gershom Scholem placed it in late antique Palestine (third to sixth centuries CE); others argue for a later origin in the early Islamic world, around the eighth or ninth century. It survives in three recensions, short, long and "Saadyan", and the first known commentaries are from the tenth century, by Saadia Gaon, Dunash ibn Tamim and Shabbetai Donnolo. Letters as building blocks. The book's claim is that the Hebrew letters are not signs about things but the stuff things are made of, a view that made Hebrew a sacred technology in later Kabbalah, magic and the legends of the golem, whose makers were said to combine letters according to this book. Number. 32 is written with the letters lamed-bet, לב, lev, "heart"; later readers noticed that the Torah begins with bet and ends with lamed. Ten, three, seven and twelve structure the whole text. Correspondences. The book is an early example of a system linking letters, elements, planets, zodiac signs, months and parts of the body: the model of the "correspondences" of Western esotericism, including the Hermetic Tree of Life, whose 22 paths are the 22 letters. Kabbalah (ch26), with Rabbinic Judaism (ch19) and Theosophy & the Occult Revival (ch37). Compare the Zohar (V79) for the Kabbalah it fed, and the Picatrix (V85) for another book of correspondences. What's well supported by the evidence - The text's structure: 32 paths = 10 sefirot + 22 letters, divided into 3 mothers, 7 doubles and…

title: The Mawangdui Silk Texts
summary: Silk manuscripts from a Han tomb, including two copies of the Laozi (Daodejing), then the oldest known. They put the De section before the Dao section and write heng, 'constant', where later editions avoid an emperor's name with chang.
text: Vault entry V81 · Manuscripts · Tomb 3, Mawangdui, Changsha, sealed in 168 BCE · Hunan Museum, Changsha In December 1973, archaeologists working at Mawangdui, on the edge of Changsha in Hunan province, opened the third of a group of Han dynasty tombs belonging to the family of the Marquis of Dai. The man buried there, generally identified as a son of the marquis Li Cang, had died in 168 BCE. Inside a lacquered box lay rolls and folded sheets of silk covered in writing: some thirty texts on philosophy, medicine, astronomy, divination and war. Among them were two copies of the Laozi, the book later called the Daodejing, now known as Laozi A and Laozi B. They were, at the time, the oldest known manuscripts of the text by more than five hundred years. - Order. In both copies the section on De ("virtue", "power") comes before the section on Dao ("the way"). The received book begins with the Dao; the Mawangdui copies would be called, in that order, a Dedaojing. - The opening line. The received text begins "Dao ke dao, fei chang dao", "the way that can be spoken of is not the constant way". The silk copies read "道可道也，非恒道也", dao ke dao ye, fei heng dao ye, with heng, "constant", where later editions have chang. The substitution is usually explained as avoidance of the personal name of Emperor Wen of Han, Liu Heng (r. 180–157 BCE), whose name could not be written; the added particles ye also change how the line can be read. - Two hands. Laozi A is written in a script still close to the older seal forms and does not avoid the name of the dynasty's founder; Laozi B is in the clerical script of the Han and does avoid it, so it was copied later, probably under the first Han emperors. In 1993 a tomb at Guodian in Hubei yielded bamboo slips of about 300 BCE carrying portions of the Laozi, about a third of the received text in a different order. Mawangdui remains the oldest complete text of the book; Guodian shows that the Laozi was still being assembled in the late Warring States period. The tomb also held the "Four Classics of the Yellow Emperor", a Yijing (Book of Changes) with commentaries, medical and sexual-cultivation manuals, star charts including a list of comets, maps, and the Daoyin tu, a painted chart of exercises. Tomb 1, of the marquis's wife Xin Zhui, held her remarkably preserved body and a famous painted silk banner showing the passage to the afterlife. The taboo name. The swap of heng for chang is a small case of a large Chinese practice: a ruler's personal name was sacred and could not be written, so texts were altered around it, and editors can date copies by which names they avoid. Heng: the constant. The word the taboo hid, heng, is also the name of a hexagram of the Yijing ("Duration"), and the "constant Dao" is the unchanging source that cannot be named. Silk. Writing on silk was costly and prestigious; burying such a library placed learning among the goods the dead would need. Confucianism & Daoism (ch12), with Early China (ch09) for the Zhou background. Compare the Oracle Bones of Anyang (V55) for the oldest Chinese writing, and the Diamond Sutra (V30) for another milestone Chinese book. What's well supported by the evidence - Tomb…

title: The Bardo Thödol
summary: 'Liberation through Hearing in the Intermediate State', read aloud to the dying and the dead to guide them through the bardos of dying, of reality and of becoming. Its English title, 'The Tibetan Book of the Dead', dates from Evans-Wentz's edition of 1927.
text: Vault entry V82 · Texts & Tablets · Revealed as a treasure text by Karma Lingpa, 14th century In Tibet, when someone dies, a lama may sit beside the body and read aloud. The reading continues for days, as long as forty-nine, addressed not to the mourners but to the dead person, by name: "O child of noble family, listen without distraction. Now what is called death has arrived." The text tells the consciousness where it is, what it is seeing, and how to be free. Its Tibetan name is Bardo Thödol (bar do thos grol), "Liberation through Hearing in the Intermediate State". Since 1927, English readers have known it as The Tibetan Book of the Dead. - In Tibetan tradition the teachings were given by Padmasambhava, the Indian master who helped establish Buddhism in Tibet in the eighth century, written down by his consort Yeshe Tsogyal, and hidden as terma, "treasures", to be found when the time was right. - In the fourteenth century the treasure-revealer (tertön) Karma Lingpa (1326–1386) is said to have recovered them from Mount Gampodar in central Tibet, as part of a larger cycle, the Peaceful and Wrathful Deities: Self-Liberation through the Wisdom Mind. - It belongs to the Nyingma school, though it is used more widely, and is one of many funeral texts in Tibet. Bardo means an "in-between" state. The book guides the dead through three: - The bardo of dying (chikhai): the elements of the body dissolve and the Clear Light of reality dawns. To recognise it is to be liberated at once. - The bardo of reality (chönyi): the forty-two peaceful and fifty-eight wrathful deities appear over many days. The text insists they are the mind's own projections, and recognising them as such frees the dead. - The bardo of becoming (sidpa): if no recognition comes, the mind is driven by karma toward rebirth, and the text teaches how to choose a good womb or "close the womb door". Later teachers count six bardos in all, adding birth and life, dream, and meditation. The Sikkimese lama Kazi Dawa Samdup translated it; the American W. Y. Evans-Wentz edited it and gave it its title in 1927, by analogy with the equally misnamed Egyptian "Book of the Dead" (V20). Evans-Wentz framed it with Theosophical ideas; Carl Jung wrote a commentary for a later edition; Timothy Leary and colleagues adapted it as a manual for psychedelic experience in 1964. Newer translations (Thurman 1994; Dorje, Coleman and Jinpa 2005) work from the Tibetan and its whole cycle. Lights. In the bardo of reality each buddha appears with a brilliant coloured light and, beside it, a dull, comforting light leading to one of the six realms of rebirth. The instruction is always the same: go toward the dazzling light, not the soft one. The mandala of deities. The hundred peaceful and wrathful deities form a mandala inside the body: the peaceful in the heart, the wrathful in the brain. Hearing. Its power is said to lie in being heard: the dead are assumed to keep a subtle hearing, and the words themselves are the path. Tibetan & Vajrayana Buddhism (ch53), with Buddhism (ch11) and Tantra (ch24). Compare the Papyrus of Ani (V20) and the Egyptian idea of the afterlife journey, and the Diwan Abatur (V87) for another…

title: The Codex Boturini
summary: The 'Strip of the Pilgrimage', a 5.5-metre amate screenfold drawn in black and never coloured, telling the Mexica migration from Aztlan in footprints, place glyphs and year counts. It breaks off mid-story, during the war of Colhuacan against Xochimilco.
text: Vault entry V83 · Manuscripts · Before or just after the Spanish conquest (c. 1520s–1540s) · Biblioteca Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Mexico City It begins with an island. A man and a woman sit in a house on a small island surrounded by water; beside it, a pyramid, a date sign, and a man paddling a canoe to the shore. From the shore a line of black footprints sets out across the paper, and the footprints keep walking, page after page, for more than five metres. This is the Tira de la Peregrinación, the "Strip of the Pilgrimage", better known as the Codex Boturini: the story of how the Mexica (the people we call Aztecs) left their homeland of Aztlan and wandered for generations before coming to the Valley of Mexico. - A single strip of amate (bark paper), about 5.5 metres long, folded like a screen into 21 or 22 panels. Accounts differ on the count, depending on how the folds are read. - Drawn in black ink and left uncoloured: it may never have been finished. The story also breaks off in mid-episode. - Its date is unknown: most scholars place it shortly before or shortly after the conquest (1519–21), in a style close to pre-Hispanic painting. - It passed through the hands of the scholar Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora and the Jesuits, and was taken by the Italian collector Lorenzo Boturini in the 1730s–40s, whose name it now bears. It is held by Mexico's National Library of Anthropology and History. 1. Aztlan. The departure from the island, dated with the year sign 1 Flint (ce Tecpatl). 2. Colhuacan. The people come to a curved hill, where their god Huitzilopochtli speaks to them from a cave. 3. The tribes. They travel with eight other peoples, each shown by a name glyph. 4. The broken tree. A tree splits, a sign that the Mexica must separate from the other tribes and go on alone. 5. The first sacrifice. Huitzilopochtli gives them their mission, and the Mexica perform their first sacrifices. 6. The long walk. Footprints link place-glyph after place-glyph, and year counts show how long they stayed at each: years of wandering, building, leaving. 7. Colhuacan and war. In the Valley of Mexico they serve the lord of Colhuacan in a war against Xochimilco, bringing back their enemies' ears as proof. Here the strip stops. Footprints. In Aztec painting a line of footprints means a road or a journey; the book is read by following them, left to right. Year signs. The migration is dated in the 52-year calendar round: four year-bearers (Reed, Flint, House, Rabbit) with numbers 1 to 13, drawn as small boxes strung together to count the years spent at each stop. Place glyphs. Places are written by pictures of their names: a curved hill for Colhuacan ("place of the curved hill"), a serpent on a hill for Coatepec ("serpent hill"). Destiny. The whole strip turns a history into a sacred itinerary, guided by a god toward a promised place, the island city of Tenochtitlan that the codex never reaches. The Aztec (ch43), with The Maya (ch29) for Mesoamerican writing. Compare the Codex Mendoza (V51), which begins with the founding of Tenochtitlan where this strip leaves off, and the Codex Borgia (V41) for the ritual calendar. What's well supported by the evidence…

title: The Hinton St Mary Mosaic
summary: A Roman mosaic floor from Dorset whose central roundel shows a man before a Chi-Rho, flanked by pomegranates: probably one of the earliest pictures of Christ, though some read it as Constantine. Another room shows Bellerophon killing the Chimera.
text: Vault entry V84 · Relics & Artifacts · Hinton St Mary, Dorset, 4th century CE · British Museum, London In 1963, in the Dorset village of Hinton St Mary, the blacksmith Walter White was digging a post-hole when his spade struck a floor of small coloured stones. Excavation uncovered the mosaic pavement of two rooms of a Roman building. In the middle of the larger room was a roundel: the head and shoulders of a clean-shaven, fair-haired man in a cloak, and behind his head the monogram ☧, the Chi-Rho, the first two Greek letters of Christos. On either side of him hangs a pomegranate. If the face is Christ's, as most scholars think, it is one of the earliest known pictures of him anywhere, and the earliest from Britain. - A mosaic floor from a Roman villa or building, dated on grounds of style to the fourth century CE, and attributed to a workshop based at Durnovaria (Dorchester). - Lifted in 1965 and acquired by the British Museum. For years only the central medallion has been on display; the rest was stored, and the museum has since led new fieldwork at the site. - It covered two rooms joined by an opening: a smaller one with Bellerophon on Pegasus killing the Chimera, and a larger one with the Chi-Rho bust, surrounded by hunting scenes and four corner busts, sometimes read as the winds or the four evangelists. - The usual reading: Christ, with the Chi-Rho as his halo-like emblem. - An alternative: the emperor Constantine or another Christian ruler, the Chi-Rho being Constantine's battle standard. - Some have also asked why an image of Christ would be placed on a floor, to be walked on; later Christian law (427 CE) forbade putting the sign of Christ on pavements. The Chi-Rho. Two letters, Χ and Ρ, superimposed: a name turned into an emblem, which Constantine used after 312 and which became one of the commonest Christian signs of the fourth century. Pomegranates. In Greek myth the fruit of Persephone and return from the dead; for Christians it could signal eternal life and resurrection. Bellerophon. A pagan hero killing a monster; in a Christian house it may stand for good defeating evil. The mosaic mixes the two vocabularies in the way fourth-century Christians often did. Early Christianity (ch16), with Roman Mystery Cults (ch18) and Rome (ch13) for the pagan imagery it borrows. Compare other early images claimed to show Christ: the Shroud of Turin (V04), the Mandylion (V57) and the Veil of Veronica (V25). What's well supported by the evidence - The mosaic was found in 1963 at Hinton St Mary and is held by the British Museum. - It is fourth-century, shows a bust in front of a Chi-Rho flanked by pomegranates, and a separate Bellerophon and Chimera panel. What is not supported - That the face records what Jesus looked like. It follows Roman portrait conventions of the fourth century, three centuries after his life. What's genuinely open - Whether the bust is Christ or an emperor such as Constantine. - What the building was: a villa's dining room, a house church, or a room of mixed use. The mosaic - British Museum, "Archaeological fieldwork at Hinton St Mary, Dorset", - ASPROM, "British Museum – Hinton St Mary Mosaic" (factsheet), - Google Arts &…

title: The Picatrix
summary: The Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm, 'The Goal of the Sage', an Arabic handbook of astral magic from Muslim Spain, translated for Alfonso X and known in Latin as Picatrix. It teaches how to make talismans at the right celestial moment. Its authorship is disputed.
text: Vault entry V85 · Texts & Tablets · Arabic original compiled in al-Andalus, 10th–11th century; Castilian translation 1256–1258 Take a stone engraved at the right hour, it says, when the Moon is in the right mansion and the right planet is rising, and the power of the heavens will pour down into the image you have cut. Burn the right incense, speak the prayer to the planet in its own words, and wear the talisman. This is the teaching of the Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm, "The Goal of the Sage", an Arabic handbook of astral magic written in Muslim Spain. In Latin Europe it was called Picatrix, and for five centuries it was the most complete manual of talismanic magic that European readers had. - Written in Arabic, probably in al-Andalus in the tenth or eleventh century. It is a compilation, drawing on Hermetic, Sabian (Harranian), Neoplatonic, Indian and Persian material, and names dozens of earlier works. - Four books: on the heavens and the nature of magic; on the figures of the heavens and the making of talismans; on the properties of the planets and their prayers; on spirits, the Sabian rites, and potions and fumigations. - It teaches that the universe is one, that the lower world receives the influence of the higher, and that the sage who understands the correspondences can draw down celestial power, the rūḥāniyyāt, "spiritual forces" of the planets. - Many manuscripts name Maslama al-Majrīṭī (d. c. 1007), the Córdoban astronomer; modern scholarship calls this pseudo-Majrīṭī. - In 1996 Maribel Fierro argued for another Córdoban, Maslama ibn Qāsim al-Qurṭubī (d. 964), and later scholars (Godefroid de Callataÿ, Sébastien Moureau) have supported her. Others keep the question open. At the court of Alfonso X of Castile, the text was put into Castilian between 1256 and 1258, and from the Castilian into Latin. The Latin Picatrix shortened the philosophy and changed or dropped passages tied to Islamic practice. It was copied throughout late medieval and Renaissance Europe and was known to Marsilio Ficino and Cornelius Agrippa. The origin of the name "Picatrix" is itself uncertain; the Latin preface presents it as the name of the author. Lunar mansions. The Moon's monthly course is divided into 28 mansions, each with its own image and uses; a talisman is made when the Moon is in the mansion that suits the work. Planetary images. For each planet the book gives the figures to be engraved, the metals, stones, colours, incenses and animals that belong to it, and the hours and days it rules: a complete system of correspondences. Prayers to the planets. The planets are addressed as powers with names and costumes, drawing on the traditions attributed to the star-worshipping Sabians of Harran. Islam (ch21), with Theosophy & the Occult Revival (ch37) for the Western magical tradition that drew on it. Compare the Emerald Tablet (V03), the Sefer Yetzirah (V80) for another book of correspondences, and the Book of Soyga (V19) for a later European magical manuscript. title: The Berlin Gold Hat
era: The Vault · The Early Iron Age
summary: A 74.5 cm cone of paper-thin gold, covered with stamped circles and crescents, one of four 'Schifferstadt-type' gold hats. Wilfried Menghin read its ornament as a lunisolar calendar; the reading is contested, and the hat's find-spot is unknown.
text: Vault entry V86 · Relics & Artifacts · Late Bronze Age, c. 1000–800 BCE · Neues Museum, Berlin It stands in a dark room of the Neues Museum in Berlin, lit from above: a tall cone of beaten gold, 74.5 centimetres high, with a small brim at the bottom and a star at the tip. It weighs only about 490 grams; the gold is thinner than paper. Every centimetre is covered with bands of stamped ornament: rows of circles, discs, crescents and almond-shaped eyes, applied with small punches and wheels. Nobody knows where it was found. The museum bought it in 1996, from the art market. The Berlin hat is the best preserved of four cone-shaped gold hats of the "Schifferstadt type", all from the Late Bronze Age of central and western Europe: - Schifferstadt (near Speyer, Germany), found in 1835; short and without its point preserved; Historisches Museum der Pfalz, Speyer. - Avanton (near Poitiers, France), found in 1844, incomplete; Musée d'Archéologie nationale, Saint-Germain-en-Laye. - Ezelsdorf-Buch (near Nuremberg), found in 1953, crushed but restored to about 88 cm; Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg. - Berlin, bought in 1996; Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte, Neues Museum. The Berlin archaeologist Wilfried Menghin argued that the numbers of circles in the rows are not random: counted in certain ways, they give the number of days in lunar and solar years, and allow a lunisolar calendar to be kept, reconciling the two, even across the 19-year cycle in which the phases of the Moon return to the same dates. On this reading the hats were worn by priest-astronomers as sacred symbols of calendrical knowledge, and the star at the tip is the Sun. The circle and the Sun. Circles, wheels and discs are the most common sun signs of the European Bronze Age, from the Trundholm sun chariot to the Nebra sky disc. Counting in ornament. If Menghin is right, the ornament is the calendar: number encoded in pattern, readable by those who knew how to count it. The cone. Its shape suggests a ceremonial headdress rather than a vessel; the brim and the inner fittings of the Berlin example are consistent with its being worn, perhaps over an organic cap. The Neolithic (ch42) for the European sky-watching tradition it continues, Celtic & Germanic (ch14) for the later religion of the same lands, and Creation & the First Order (ch46). Compare the Nebra Sky Disc (V45), another Bronze Age object read as an astronomical instrument, and the Gundestrup Cauldron (V37) for later Celtic metalwork. What's well supported by the evidence - The hat is Late Bronze Age gold work of about 1000–800 BCE, 74.5 cm tall, bought by the Berlin museum in 1996, and one of four related gold cones. - Its ornament is made of repeated stamped circles and other motifs in horizontal bands. What is not supported - That the calendar reading is proven: it depends on choosing which motifs to count and how; critics see numerical patterns that could be found in any rich ornament. - Any specific find-spot: claims that it came from a particular site are unverified. What's genuinely open - Whether the hats encode a calendar or are ceremonial objects with solar symbolism but no counting function. - Where the Berlin…

title: The Diwan Abatur
summary: A Mandaean illustrated scroll over six metres long that maps the soul's road after death through the maṭarātā, or watch-houses, across the river Hitpun in the ship Shahrat, to Abatur, who weighs it. Published in English by E. S. Drower in 1950.
text: Vault entry V87 · Manuscripts · Mandaean illustrated scroll; the copy Drower published (DC 8) is 18th-century · Bodleian Library, Oxford, and Vatican Library Unrolled, it runs for more than six metres. Along it walk and sit strange figures drawn in ink: beings with human bodies and the heads of beasts, towers with animals chained at their doors, a boat on a river, and a great figure seated with a pair of scales. Between the pictures run lines of Mandaic script. This is the Diwan Abatur, the "Scroll of Abatur", a sacred illustrated scroll of the Mandaeans, the Gnostic baptising community of southern Iraq and Iran. It maps the road that a soul travels after death, through a series of watch-houses, to the place where it is weighed. - The best-known copy is DC 8 in the Drower Collection at the Bodleian Library, Oxford, an eighteenth-century scroll collected by Lady Ethel Stefana Drower, who published it with an English translation as Diwan Abatur, or Progress through the Purgatories (Vatican, Studi e Testi 151, 1950). - Another copy, MS Borgiani Siriaci 175, is in the Vatican Library; a facsimile was published by Julius Euting in 1904. - The text itself is older than these copies; like most Mandaean scriptures its date of composition is uncertain. - After death the soul must pass through the maṭarātā (sing. maṭarta), "watch-houses" or purgatories, each guarded by beings of the lower worlds. There it is held and purified according to its sins. - The scroll pictures the maṭarātā of the sons of Ptahil, the demiurge who made the material world, and of the seven planets; each is said to measure 2,000 parasangs and to lie thousands of parasangs from the next. - A ship named Shahrat, "she kept watch", ferries the souls across the river Hitpun, which divides the lower world from the World of Light. - At the end sits Abatur, "Abatur of the Scales", who weighs each soul; the soul that balances passes on to the World of Light. The scroll as map. A long roll read from one end to the other, the book is itself a road: to unroll it is to follow the soul. Animals at the gates. Chained beasts at the watch-houses stand for the passions and powers that detain the soul in the lower world. The scales. Weighing the soul links Mandaean belief to a long Near Eastern image of judgement, from Egyptian scenes of the weighing of the heart to Zoroastrian and Islamic scales. Script. The Mandaic alphabet is itself held sacred; its letters are counted and used in the community's rituals. Mandaeism (ch56), with Gnosticism (ch17) for its dualism of light and darkness. Compare the Papyrus of Ani (V20) for the Egyptian weighing of the heart, and the Bardo Thödol (V82) for another guide to the passage after death. What's well supported by the evidence - The Diwan Abatur is a Mandaean illustrated scroll over six metres long, known from copies in Oxford (DC 8, eighteenth century) and the Vatican (BS 175), published in translation by Drower (1950). - It describes the soul's passage through maṭarātā, a crossing of the Hitpun in the ship Shahrat, and a weighing by Abatur. What is not supported - That it describes what happens after death: that is Mandaean belief. Nor is it established…

title: The Skull of “Mary Magdalene” at Saint-Maximin
summary: A darkened skull in a gilded reliquary of flowing golden hair carried by four angels, venerated as Mary Magdalene's since Charles of Salerno announced her tomb in 1279. The Provence legend has no trace before the eleventh century, Vézelay claimed her first, and a 2017 study reconstructed the face of a woman of about fifty without identifying her.
text: Vault entry V88 · Relics & Sacred Objects · Crypt of the Basilica of Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, Provence, France In the crypt of the great Gothic basilica of Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, behind protective glass, a darkened human skull sits inside a gilded reliquary. The metalwork frames the skull with flowing golden hair and is carried by four golden angels. Roman numerals on the back read MDCCCLX, which points to 1860 as the reliquary's date. Tradition holds that the skull is that of Mary Magdalene, the follower of Jesus whom the Gospels name as the first witness of the empty tomb. Each year, on or around her feast day of 22 July, it is carried in procession through the town. - The Gospels say nothing of her later life or her burial. Early traditions disagree. Gregory of Tours (6th century) places her at Ephesus. Modestus, patriarch of Jerusalem in the 7th century, says she returned to Jerusalem. - The Provençal story is medieval. In it, Mary Magdalene, Lazarus, Martha, Maximinus and others arrive by boat at Marseilles and convert Provence, and Mary spends thirty years in penance in a cave at La Sainte-Baume. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), summarizing the historian Louis Duchesne, states that before the middle of the eleventh century there is no trace of the tradition that these Palestinian saints came to Provence. It says the story first appears in documents connected with Vézelay, the Burgundian abbey that then claimed her body. - Vézelay first, then Saint-Maximin. Vézelay was the great Magdalene shrine of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. In 1265 relics were exhumed there, and Louis IX attended their elevation in 1267. Then, in 1279, Charles of Salerno, later Charles II of Anjou, count of Provence, had the crypt at Saint-Maximin excavated and announced the discovery of her tomb and body. He founded a Dominican convent there. In 1295 Pope Boniface VIII recognized the Saint-Maximin relics. Vézelay's pilgrimage declined. The rival claims have never been reconciled. - The Golden Legend. The thirteenth-century Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine spread the Provençal story across Europe. - The Revolution. In 1794, during the French Revolution, the relics were despoiled. According to the account preserved by the shrine and reported by EWTN, the sacristan Joseph Bastide saved the skull, and other people saved other fragments. - The "noli me tangere." For centuries a patch of tissue on the forehead was venerated as the place the risen Christ touched her when he said "Do not hold on to me" (noli me tangere, John 20:17). It stayed on the skull until the eighteenth century. In 1780 it was placed in a glass reliquary of its own. - The 1860 reliquary is the one seen today. - In 2017 the forensic anthropologist Philippe Charlier and the forensic artist Philippe Froesch led a study of the skull and a lock of hair. The shrine did not allow the skull to be taken out of its reliquary. The team made a photogrammetric survey of several hundred photographs and examined the hair under magnification, by scanning electron microscope and by X-ray elemental analysis. - They proposed a computer-aided facial reconstruction of a woman of about fifty, of…
